United Nations
General Assembly

A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/2
Distr.: General 12 February 2026
Original: English

Human Rights Council
Working Group on the Universal Periodic Review Fifty-second session Geneva, 4-15 May 2026
Namibia
Compilation of information prepared by the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights
I. Background
1. The present report was prepared pursuant to Human Rights Council resolutions 5/1 and 16/21, taking into consideration the outcome of the previous review.1 It is a compilation of information contained in relevant United Nations documents, presented in a summarized manner owing to word-limit constraints.
II. Scope of international obligations and cooperation with human rights mechanisms
2. In 2024, the Committee against Torture and the Human Rights Committee stated that Namibia should consider ratifying the Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment with the aim of establishing a national preventive mechanism.2
3. In 2024, the Committee on the Rights of the Child and, in 2022, the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women recommended that Namibia ratify the Convention relating to the Status of Stateless Persons of 1954 and the Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness of 1961.3
4. The Committee against Torture encouraged Namibia to consider ratifying the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance.4
5. The International Labour Organization (ILO) noted that Namibia had yet to ratify the Labour Inspection (Agriculture) Convention, 1969 (No. 129).5
6. The United Nations country team noted that Namibia had not issued a standing invitation to the special procedures of the Human Rights Council and that requests for visits by mandate holders were pending.6

GE.26-00727 (E) 120226 120226

A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/2
III. National human rights framework
1. Constitutional and legislative framework
7. The Committee against Torture expressed regret that the revised bill on preventing and combating torture had been awaiting parliamentary approval since 2019, and urged Namibia to adopt the bill as soon as possible and to ensure that its provisions defined torture as a specific offence.7
8. The Human Rights Committee expressed concern about the delay in adopting bills that sought to address discriminatory aspects of the legislative framework with regard to gender, including the marriage bill, the bill on the recognition of customary marriages, the divorce bill and the uniform matrimonial property bill, and stated that Namibia should expedite the adoption of those bills.8
9. In 2024, in information provided in follow-up to the concluding observations by the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women on its sixth periodic report, Namibia stated that the Dissolution of Marriages Act (Act No. 10 of 2024) and the Marriage Act (Act No. 14 of 2024) had been passed by Parliament but that the regulations operationalizing those Acts had yet to be adopted.9
10. Noting that the bill on statelessness determination and protection remained in draft form, the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) stated that the passage of the bill was important as it would provide citizenship to those persons who did not possess the old South West African identity documents and who were therefore not covered by the Regularization of Status of Certain Residents of Namibia, Their Descendants and Foreign Spouses Act (Act No. 15 of 2024).10
11. Noting that polygamy was regulated by customary law, the Human Rights Committee stated that Namibia should review existing customary marital laws and enact legislation to increase protection for women in polygamous unions, with a view to abolishing polygamy.11
12. Noting reports of numerous incidents of data breaches and cybercrimes, the same Committee stated that Namibia should prioritize the enactment of the data protection bill in line with international standards.12
2. Institutional infrastructure and policy measures
13. The Committee on the Rights of the Child recommended that Namibia ensure that the Children's Advocate had sufficient resources to monitor children's rights and to address complaints from children in a child-sensitive manner.13
14. The Human Rights Committee expressed concern about the lack of financial and operational autonomy of the Office of the Ombudsman and about the long delay in adopting the Ombudsman bill, and stated that Namibia should expedite the adoption of amendments to the Ombudsman Act (Act No. 7 of 1990).14
IV. Promotion and protection of human rights
A. Implementation of international human rights obligations, taking into account applicable international humanitarian law
1. Equality and non-discrimination
15. In their communication of 11 June 2025 to Namibia concerning alleged human rights violations and abuses against workers and community members in the context of the activities of the Tsumeb smelter, special procedure mandate holders noted that, despite the fact that Namibia had gained independence from South Africa in 1990, its apartheid legislation, severe forms of segregation and history of colonialism had left a resounding impact. There were currently vast inequalities between white and black Namibians, with white Namibians still controlling a large share of the economy. Those inequalities were also evident in access to education, work, housing, water and healthcare.15

2

GE.26-00727

A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/2
16. The Human Rights Committee expressed concern about the prevalence of discrimination and stated that Namibia should: (a) take measures to eliminate all forms of discrimination; (b) address the de facto discrimination faced by Indigenous Peoples, most notably with regard to access to healthcare, education and employment; and (c) address the discrimination in access to healthcare faced by disadvantaged populations, including persons with disabilities and lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons, and ensure that they were provided with healthcare services that met their specific needs.16
17. The Committee on the Rights of the Child recommended that Namibia review relevant legislation to explicitly prohibit all forms of discrimination, including on the basis of language, political or other opinion, national origin, disability, place of birth, sexual orientation or gender identity.17
2. Right to life, liberty and security of person, and freedom from torture
18. The Human Rights Committee expressed concern at the reported prevalence of excessive use of force by the Namibian Police Force, including violations of the right to life, and the authorization of the use of potentially lethal force under the Criminal Procedure Act (Act No. 51 of 1977), the Public Gatherings Proclamation (A.G. No. 23 of 1989) and the Correctional Service Act (Act No. 9 of 2012), which was inconsistent with international human rights standards. It stated that Namibia should ensure that: (a) all legislative and regulatory provisions governing the use of force were in line with the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials and the United Nations Human Rights Guidance on Less-Lethal Weapons in Law Enforcement; (b) all reports of excessive use of force by law enforcement officers were promptly, effectively and impartially investigated and alleged perpetrators prosecuted and, if convicted, appropriately sentenced; (c) all law enforcement officers received training on the use of force based on international human rights standards; and (d) the principles of legality, necessity and proportionality were strictly adhered to in practice.18
19. The Committee against Torture and the Human Rights Committee stated that Namibia should ensure that all complaints of torture and ill-treatment were promptly investigated in an impartial manner by an independent body, and that suspected perpetrators were prosecuted, and if found guilty, punished commensurately with the gravity of the crime.19
20. The Committee against Torture noted that most pretrial detainees were held in police detention facilities in poor, dilapidated and severely overcrowded holding cells. It stated that Namibia should take the steps necessary to hold them in appropriate places of detention.20
21. The same Committee expressed concern about the lack of strict separation of convicted persons from pretrial detainees in correctional facilities, reported shortages of prison personnel and staff qualified to provide medical and psychological assistance to prisoners, the lack of provision of reasonable accommodation for prisoners with disabilities, the high rate of HIV/AIDS among prisoners and the imposition of solitary confinement as a disciplinary sanction without guaranteeing adequate procedural safeguards. It urged Namibia to improve the material conditions of detention in all correctional facilities, in line with the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (the Nelson Mandela Rules).21
22. The Committee on the Rights of the Child expressed concern about reports of children held in pretrial detention together with adults, and recommended that Namibia ensure that detention was used as a last resort and for the shortest appropriate period of time, and that, in cases where detention was unavoidable, children were not held together with adults.22
3. Administration of justice, including impunity, and the rule of law
23. The Committee against Torture noted shortcomings in the criminal justice system and stated that Namibia should intensify efforts to reform the criminal justice system, including by increasing judicial capacity and, whenever feasible, making more use of alternatives to pretrial detention and ensuring a more accessible and affordable bail system. The Human Rights Committee stated that Namibia should review bail conditions to ensure that bail was affordable to those entitled to it.23

GE.26-00727

3

A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/2
24. The Committee against Torture expressed concern about reports of prolonged pretrial detention, which routinely exceeded legal limits. It stated that Namibia should ensure that the provisions governing pretrial detention were respected, and that it was resorted to only in exceptional circumstances and in accordance with the law.24
25. The same Committee stated that Namibia should ensure that all fundamental legal safeguards were guaranteed in law and in practice for all detained persons from the outset of the deprivation of their liberty, including the rights to be informed immediately in a language that they understood of the charges against them, to be brought before a judge within the 48-hour legal limit, to challenge the legality of their detention at any stage of the proceedings, to be assisted by a lawyer of their choice, including during interrogations, and to have access to qualified, independent and free legal aid, if necessary.25
26. The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women recommended that Namibia increase funding for legal aid and ensure that women had effective access to justice throughout the country.26
4. Fundamental freedoms and the right to participate in public and political life
27. The Human Rights Committee stated that Namibia should consider amending its legislation and practices to ensure that individuals fully enjoyed their right of peaceful assembly and ensure that its legislation allowed the use of potentially lethal force by law enforcement officers only as a last resort and only when necessary to protect life or prevent serious injury from an imminent threat.27
28. The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women recommended that Namibia take measures to accelerate gender parity at the national and local levels of government, in particular in decision-making positions in the Cabinet, the judiciary, the public service, the foreign service and in sports commissions.28
5. Right to privacy
29. The Committee on the Rights of the Child recommended that Namibia ensure that laws and policies on the digital environment respected children's privacy and protected them from harmful content and online risks.29 The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) encouraged Namibia to ensure that a mechanism for transparency and accountability was in place for the governance of digital platforms to ensure that human rights were upheld and to mitigate the risks associated with the spread of harmful content online.30
6. Right to marriage and family life
30. The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women noted reports on the continued practice of depriving a widow of the right to the property that she had shared with her husband, and recommended that Namibia provide legal assistance to women to claim their rights upon dissolution of a marriage or union.31
31. The Committee on the Rights of the Child recommended that Namibia promote the equal sharing of parental responsibilities, including by introducing paternity leave and providing incentives for fathers to be actively involved in child-rearing.32
32. The same Committee urged Namibia to ensure that there were family- and community-based care options for children who could not stay with their families.33
7. Prohibition of all forms of slavery, including trafficking in persons
33. The United Nations country team stated that the Combating of Trafficking in Persons Act (Act No. 1 of 2018) required amendments to strengthen the protection of victims.34
34. The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women expressed concern about reports of trafficking in women and girls from, to and in transit through Namibia. It recommended that Namibia: (a) intensify awareness-raising efforts aimed at encouraging reporting of trafficking in women and girls, expedite prosecutions and strengthen cooperation with countries of origin, transit and destination; and (b) continue to

4

GE.26-00727

A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/2
strengthen the national referral mechanism and its standard operating procedures, and provide victims of trafficking with access to shelters and medical, psychosocial and legal assistance.35
35. The Committee on the Rights of the Child expressed concern about the increase in the number of children who were trafficked into Namibia and subsequently placed in domestic or hazardous work, or subjected to commercial sexual exploitation. It recommended that Namibia strengthen measures for the early identification and referral of child victims of trafficking to appropriate services.36
8. Right to work and to just and favourable conditions of work
36. ILO stated that despite relevant provisions in the Labour Act (Act No. 11 of 2007) and the regulations relating to the health and safety of employees at work, Namibia continued to face challenges in effectively implementing policies on occupational safety and health.37
37. The Committee on the Rights of the Child urged Namibia to amend the Labour Act to raise the minimum age of employment to the age of completing compulsory education and the minimum age of employment in hazardous work to 18 years.38
38. The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women recommended that Namibia: (a) increase professional training for women and girls to reduce unemployment; (b) address segregation in the labour market; (c) increase the availability of affordable childcare facilities; (d) ensure that the principle of equal pay for work of equal value was implemented; (e) take measures to prevent sexual harassment in the workplace; (f) increase the participation of women in the formal economy; and (g) ensure that women employed in the informal economy were covered by maternity and social protection.39
9. Right to social security
39. The Committee on the Rights of the Child urged Namibia to increase budget allocations for social protection programmes affecting children and strengthen their effectiveness.40
40. The same Committee recommended that Namibia strengthen support for parents of children with disabilities by increasing financial support, providing training and introducing flexible working arrangements, and ensure that they knew how to seek the necessary support.41
10. Right to an adequate standard of living
41. Noting the high incidence of poverty in Namibia, the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women recommended that Namibia take concrete measures to address poverty and ensure gender mainstreaming in its development plans.42
42. The Committee on the Rights of the Child urged Namibia to strengthen measures to end child poverty and ensure the right of all children to an adequate standard of living, and to ensure that measures to combat poverty complied with a child rights-based approach and addressed the root causes of multidimensional child poverty.43
11. Right to health
43. Noting that significant progress had been made in ensuring the right to health, the United Nations country team stated that the delivery of equitable access to health services continued to be a challenge. There was also high dependence on external funding, especially for services relating to HIV, tuberculosis and malaria.44
44. The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women recommended that Namibia: (a) amend section 3 (1) of the Abortion and Sterilization Act (Act No. 2 of 1975) to decriminalize abortion in all cases; (b) improve women's access to safe abortion and post-abortion services; (c) increase access to quality family planning services and modern contraceptives for women of reproductive age; (d) ensure safe and appropriate access to sexual and reproductive health services free from discrimination; (e) address the high prevalence of HIV/AIDS among women, implement the road map for the elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV and ensure access to free antiretroviral treatment; and

GE.26-00727

5

A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/2
(f) conduct a study on forced sterilizations of HIV-positive women, and ensure that no sterilizations were performed without the free, prior and informed consent of the woman concerned.45
45. The Committee on the Rights of the Child recommended that Namibia strengthen measures to ensure that all children had access to quality health services and strengthen efforts to reduce infant mortality rates and to eliminate malnutrition, stunting and micronutrient deficiency among children.46
46. The same Committee urged Namibia to ensure that all adolescents had access to age-appropriate family planning services and free contraceptives, and that sexual and reproductive health education included education on sexual and reproductive health rights, sexual diversity, responsible sexual behaviour and prevention of early pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections.47
47. The Committee against Torture urged Namibia to accelerate the process of reforming its mental health legislation to bring it into compliance with international human rights standards.48
12. Right to education
48. UNESCO and the United Nations country team noted the announcement by the President of Namibia that the Government would fully subsidize tuition and registration fees at all State-run universities and vocational training centres from 2026.49
49. UNESCO referred to relevant recommendations from the previous review that had been supported by Namibia.50 It stated that while the Basic Education Act (Act No. 3 of 2020) codified universal primary education and universal secondary education, there remained a persistent shortage of classrooms and basic facilities that hindered access to quality education, especially in rural areas. There was also limited access to inclusive education for learners with disabilities due to inadequate infrastructure, insufficient assistive devices and a shortage of specialized teachers.51
50. The Committee on the Rights of the Child expressed concern about the poor quality of education, and urged Namibia to ensure that reforms to improve the quality of education included measures to, inter alia, integrate life skills training and modern teaching methods into school curricula, strengthen the training of teachers and education professionals, and improve educational outcomes for all children.52
51. The same Committee recommended that Namibia ensure that all children with disabilities had access to inclusive education in mainstream schools and expand the provision of quality multilingual education, particularly for children belonging to Indigenous or ethnic minority groups.53
52. The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women recommended that Namibia: (a) ensure that all girls and boys had access to age-appropriate, evidence-based and scientifically accurate education on sexual and reproductive health and rights; 54 (b) provide adequate sanitation facilities and free sanitary pads for girls in schools, including through the dignity project, and include age-appropriate training on menstrual management in school curricula;55 (c) strengthen the implementation of programmes in place to reduce school dropout rates due to early pregnancy and to promote the re-entry into school of mothers after giving birth; 56 (d) promote the participation of women and girls in non-traditional fields of study and career paths, in particular in science, technology, engineering, mathematics and information and communications technology;57 and (e) fully implement the sector policy on inclusive education (2013), and ensure support to girls with disabilities in schools and the accessibility of school buildings.58
13. Cultural rights
53. Noting that Namibia was a State Party to the Convention for the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage, the Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage and the Convention on the Protection and Promotion of the Diversity of Cultural Expressions, UNESCO encouraged Namibia to fully implement the relevant

6

GE.26-00727

A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/2
provisions of those Conventions that promoted access to and participation in cultural heritage and creative expression.59
14. Development, the environment, and business and human rights
54. The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women urged Namibia to recognize women as the driving force of its sustainable development and to adopt relevant policies and strategies to that effect. The Committee on the Rights of the Child urged Namibia to ensure the meaningful participation of children in the design and implementation of policies and programmes aimed at achieving all 17 Sustainable Development Goals insofar as they concerned children.60
55. The United Nations country team stated that climate change disproportionately affected marginalized groups and that, although Namibia had demonstrated its commitment to climate action through various initiatives, the application of a human right-based approach in addressing climate change was still limited.61
56. The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women recommended that Namibia conduct environmental and human rights impact assessments in relation to oil and gas exploration activities in the country, and ensure that any decisions on oil and gas exploitation in the Kavango region were subject to the full, prior and informed consent of local communities.62
57. In their communication of 11 June 2025 to Namibia, special procedure mandate holders noted that, based on information received: (a) the Tsumeb smelter, in Tsumeb, which produced blister copper, had caused the release of smelting by-products into the environment, which had contaminated the air, soil and water, creating a danger to human health and the environment; (b) the Government, among others, had repeatedly attempted to delegitimize research on water, environment and community health in Tsumeb, and had barred researchers from publishing their findings in scientific journals; and (c) the "grandfather clause", a legal provision that shielded smelter owners from liability for the environmental and human rights harm that they had caused, was of great concern and was not in alignment with international standards.63
B. Rights of specific persons or groups
1. Women
58. The Human Rights Committee stated that Namibia should take appropriate steps to tackle the root causes of gender-based violence, such as inequality, poverty, social exclusion and drug and alcohol abuse, including through engagement programmes and training for men.64
59. The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women recommended that Namibia initiate in-depth participatory research on the communities and contexts in which harmful practices, including polygamy, violent sexual initiation, grooming and cleansing, persisted, continue to engage traditional leaders and communities in addressing gender stereotypes and harmful practices through awareness-raising programmes and develop a national strategy on the prevention of harmful practices.65
60. The same Committee noted with concern reports on the high prevalence of intimate partner violence and other forms of gender-based violence against women, and the limited access for women to protection orders, reparations, shelters and psychological treatment and counselling. Similar concerns were also expressed by the Committee against Torture and the Human Rights Committee.66
61. The Human Rights Committee expressed concern about the low number of prosecutions and convictions handed down to perpetrators of gender-based violence. It stated that Namibia should remove all barriers to prosecuting and punishing perpetrators of domestic violence and implement the Combating of Domestic Violence Act (Act No. 4 of 2003), including by increasing the availability of specialized courts and ensuring that the

GE.26-00727

7

A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/2

gender-based violence protection units run by the Namibian Police Force were provided with appropriate resources.67
62. The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women recommended that Namibia ensure effective access to protection orders, reparations, shelters and psychosocial treatment and counselling for women and girls who were victims of gender-based violence.68
63. In information provided in follow-up to the concluding observations by the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women on its sixth periodic report, Namibia stated that capacity-building for the judiciary, healthcare workers and civil society organizations had been conducted on preventing and responding to cases of gender-based violence.69
64. The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women recommended that Namibia: (a) ensure women's equal access to bank loans, mortgages and other forms of financial credit; (b) increase women's access to entrepreneurship grants, training and support; (c) increase women's access to land and their representation in related decision-making processes; and (d) ensure rural women's access to social protection and basic services, such as healthcare, food, housing, electricity, mobile money-transfer systems, transportation, water and sanitation.70
2. Children
65. The Committee on the Rights of the Child recommended that Namibia: (a) ensure that the principle of the best interests of the child was consistently interpreted and applied in all legislation, policies and programmes affecting children, and by public or private social welfare institutions, courts of law, administrative authorities and legislative bodies, in accordance with section 3 (1) of the Child Care and Protection Act (Act No. 3 of 2015);71 (b) ensure the effective implementation of the Child Care and Protection Act and develop mandatory child-rights impact assessment procedures for all legislation and policies relevant to children;72 (c) address the root causes of child abandonment and ensure the right of all children to life, survival and development;73 (d) consider adopting a regulatory framework for protecting the rights of children born through surrogacy;74 (e) promote the meaningful and empowered participation of all children within the family, communities and schools, in all relevant judicial and administrative proceedings, and include children in decision-making in all matters related to them.75
66. The Committee against Torture expressed concern that the harmful traditional practice of child marriage under customary law persisted in some communities, despite its prohibition in section 226 of the Child Care and Protection Act, and stated that Namibia should enforce that legislation and address the harmful consequences of the practice. The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women and the Human Rights Committee stated that Namibia should address the root causes of child marriage.76
67. The Committee on the Rights of the Child expressed concern about the growing number of children in street situations, and recommended that Namibia ensure that they had access to food, education, healthcare and housing, and establish mechanisms to prevent them from falling victim to trafficking and economic and sexual exploitation.77
3. Persons with disabilities
68. The same Committee recommended that Namibia continue its efforts to fully adopt a human rights-based approach to disability, including by aligning relevant policies with international standards.78
69. The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women recommended that Namibia amend the Labour Act and the Affirmative Action (Employment) Act (Act No. 29 of 1998) to include a rights-based model of disability and promote access to employment opportunities and leadership positions by women with disabilities.79
70. The United Nations country team stated that access for persons with disabilities to services remained limited, with many buildings, transport systems and essential facilities lacking ramps, tactile signage or auditory cues.80

4. Indigenous Peoples and minorities
71. The Human Rights Committee expressed concern that Namibia did not recognize certain communities as Indigenous Peoples, instead referring to them as marginalized communities. It stated that Namibia should consider recognizing communities such as the San, Himba, Ovatue, Ovatjimba and Ovazemba as Indigenous Peoples with the concomitant rights recognized in international standards.81
72. The same Committee stated that Namibia should ensure that Indigenous Peoples benefited fully from the National Resettlement Policy and that land allocation criteria took account of ancestral land ties. It should also take appropriate measures with a view to promoting the restitution of ancestral lands to affected communities, including Indigenous Peoples.82
73. The same Committee expressed concern about the very low level of participation by Indigenous Peoples in political life and public administration, and stated that Namibia should take the measures necessary to increase the representation of all Indigenous Peoples in governance structures and public administration.83
74. In their communication of 12 September 2024 to Namibia, special procedure mandate holders noted that, based on information received, the planned extension of the harbour in L�deritz, would endanger an important heritage site that memorialized the 1904-1908 genocide. The decision to expand the harbour in L�deritz did not seem to have given sufficient attention to the requests from the Nama and Ovaherero peoples concerned, in violation of their cultural rights, their right to recognition and their right to know the truth about the gross human rights violations against them and to fully take part in decision-making processes that affected their land, culture and memory of those violations. International law required States to obtain the free, prior and informed consent of the Indigenous Peoples concerned through their own representatives before adopting and implementing measures that might affect them.84
75. In their communication of 23 February 2023, special procedure mandate holders brought to the attention of Namibia information that they had received concerning the lack of meaningful participation of the Ovaherero and Nama peoples in the negotiations leading to the issuance of the "Joint Declaration by the Federal Republic of Germany and the Republic of Namibia: United in remembrance of our colonial past, united in our will to reconcile, united in our vision of the future", as well as the lack of effective reparative measures afforded to them, including an unqualified recognition of the genocide committed against those communities between 1904 and 1908. They expressed grave concern at the alleged failure to ensure the right of the Ovaherero and Nama peoples to meaningful participation, through self-elected representatives, in the discussions on the recognition and redress of the 1904-1908 genocide. They recalled that the legal status of the Ovaherero and Nama peoples and their representatives as Indigenous Peoples under international and national law was different and separate from that of the Namibian Government itself, and thus they required a place of their own in the negotiations.85
76. In its response of 30 May 2023, Namibia stated that the affected communities had been invited to nominate representatives to serve on the technical committee tasked with negotiations. The Ovaherero and Ovambanderu Traditional Leaders and the Nama Traditional Authorities Association had rejected the invitation. Namibia indicated that the Government would continue to extend a hand of collaboration to those groups.86
5. Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex persons
77. The Human Rights Committee stated that Namibia should amend the Labour Act, the Combating of Domestic Violence Act and the Combating of Rape Act (Act No. 8 of 2000) to extend the protection provided under those Acts to lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons.87
78. The Committee against Torture expressed concern about the criminalization of consensual sexual relations between persons of the same sex, and recommended that Namibia decriminalize consensual same-sex relations. It also expressed concern about the reported persistent violence, including harassment, hate speech and hate crimes, against individuals

on the basis of their actual or perceived sexual orientation or gender identity, and stated that Namibia should take effective measures to prevent such violence and ensure that all acts of violence were investigated and prosecuted promptly.88
6. Migrants, refugees and asylum-seekers
79. The same Committee stated that Namibia should repeal section 24 (1) of the Namibia Refugees (Recognition and Control) Act (Act No. 2 of 1999) with a view to guaranteeing the absolute principle of non-refoulement.89
80. UNHCR and the United Nations country team noted that Namibia maintained its reservation to article 26 of the Convention relating to the Status of Refugees of 1951, thus limiting the freedom of movement of refugees and preventing their participation in meaningful livelihood opportunities.90
81. The Human Rights Committee stated that Namibia should regularly review conditions in the Osire settlement and ensure an adequate standard of living for those settled there.91
82. UNHCR stated although the Namibia Refugees (Recognition and Control) Act prescribed a 30-day time limit for the adjudication of asylum applications, there were significant delays in receiving decisions from the authorities.92
7. Stateless persons
83. UNHCR stated that although the Civil Registration and Identification Act (Act No. 13 of 2024) and the Regularization of Status of Certain Residents of Namibia, Their Descendants and Foreign Spouses Act had yet to come into force, they nonetheless represented a significant step forward in ensuring the fundamental right to identity and addressing long-standing issues of statelessness within the country.93
84. The Committee on the Rights of the Child recommended that Namibia: (a) ensure that safeguards were in place for the protection of stateless children, in line with its Harambee Prosperity Plan and the pledge made at the Global Refugee Forum to prevent and reduce statelessness;94 and (b) strengthen its efforts to achieve universal birth registration and ensure that all children had access to birth registration and identity documents.95

1	United Nations
2	General Assembly
3	
4	A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/3
5	Distr.: General 26 January 2026
6	Original: English
7	
8	Human Rights Council
9	Working Group on the Universal Periodic Review Fifty-second session Geneva, 4-15 May 2026
10	Summary of stakeholders' submissions on Namibia*
11	Report of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights
12	I. Background
13	1. The present report was prepared pursuant to Human Rights Council resolutions 5/1 and 16/21, taking into consideration the periodicity of the universal periodic review and the outcome of the previous review.1 It is a summary of 13 stakeholders' submissions2 for the universal periodic review, presented in a summarized manner owing to word-limit constraints. A separate section is provided for the contribution by the national human rights institution that is accredited in full compliance with the Paris Principles.
14	II. Information provided by stakeholders
15	A. Scope of international obligations3 and cooperation with human rights mechanisms
16	2. JS6 noted that Namibia had not ratified the Indigenous and Tribal Peoples Convention, 1989 (No. 169) of the International Labour Organization, which left significant gaps in the protection of the rights of Indigenous Peoples.4 3. JS2 stated that at the previous review, Namibia had supported a recommendation to extend a standing invitation to the special procedures of the Human Rights Council, which had not been implemented. Also, although Namibia had hosted visits by special procedure mandate holders, it had yet to host the Independent Expert on protection against violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity.5
17	B. National human rights framework
18	1. Constitutional and legislative framework 4. JS7 stated that the enforceability of most of the internationally recognised economic, social and cultural rights had not been guaranteed in the Constitution. As a result, those rights had been treated as aspirational policy goals.6
19	* The present document is being issued without formal editing.
20	GE.26-00913 (E)
21	
22	A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/3
23	5. JS1 stated that Namibia lacked comprehensive laws on cybercrime, data protection and personal data privacy. A National Cybersecurity Strategy had been adopted in March 2022, but the absence of a national cybersecurity framework and the delay in the enactment of the Cybercrime Bill, which had been drafted in 2014, had hindered an effective response and an alignment with global standards.7
24	6. BWS encouraged Namibia to enact legislation in full compliance with CAT to create avenues for victims of torture to claim relief, as well as for the families of those who died due to torture and extrajudicial killings.8
25	7. JS7 stated that the Ombudsman Bill (2024), which sought to clarify the mandate of the Office of the Ombudsman, strengthen its independence, and enhance its operational effectiveness, had been withdrawn for further consultations following parliamentary objections. Debate had arisen around the appointment process for the Ombudsman and Deputy Ombudsman, which allowed the President to appoint these officials on recommendation of the Judicial Service Commission, in line with Article 90 of the Constitution. This process centralized authority within the Executive and Judiciary and exposed the Office of the Ombudsman to potential political influence, compromising its neutrality.9
26	8. JS2 stated that in 2021, the Office of the Ombudsman submitted a bill on combating discrimination, discriminatory harassment and hate speech to the government which had yet to be enacted. In addition, it was unclear whether the bill prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity.10
27	9. JS4 stated that the draft Hate Speech Bill (2024), which aimed to criminalize the incitement of hatred on the basis of race, religion, ethnicity, and gender, was significantly weakened by the omission of sexual orientation, gender identity, and expression.11
28	10. JS4 stated that there was an urgent need for statutory gender recognition legislation that recognized and respected bodily autonomy, as evidenced by reports of transgender individuals facing humiliation and often misgendered or detained in facilities inconsistent with their gender identity.12
29	2. Institutional infrastructure and policy measures
30	11. JS7 stated that the effectiveness of the Office of the Ombudsman had remained constrained due to persistent financial and staffing shortages, which had limited its investigative capacity and ability to reach communities across the country. Concerns had also been expressed about the recommendations made by the Office of the Ombudsman being frequently ignored by ministers and lawmakers.13
31	12. JS7 noted that: (a) The modest increase in the budget of the Anti-Corruption Commission for the 2025/2026 financial year had remained inadequate; (b) The current level of funding did not allow for the establishment of specialized units, particularly an anti-money laundering unit, which was required to address deficiencies identified by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) and facilitate the removal of Namibia from the FATF's grey list; and (c) The persistent under-resourcing of the Commission had hampered its ability to address increasingly sophisticated corruption schemes; and (d) The majority of citizens believed that corruption had worsened and that government efforts to combat corruption had remain ineffective.14
32	13. NMT stated that while Namibia had been consistently ranked as having one of Africa's freest press environments, institutional independence had remained fragile. The Namibia Broadcasting Corporation and the Communications Regulatory Authority of Namibia operated under statutes that allowed executive appointments without public consultation. NMT recalled that in its national report during the previous review, Namibia had acknowledged the need to strengthen governance and ensure independent functioning of regulatory institutions and stated that legislative amendments had not been advanced in that regard. Namibia should amend the Namibian Broadcasting Corporation Act (1991), and the Communications Act, 2009 (2009), as amended by the Communications Amendment Act, 2020 (2020), to ensure the independence envisioned in Article 21 of the Constitution.15
33	2
34	
35	A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/3
36	14. Referring to a relevant recommendation from the previous review which Namibia had supported, JS2 stated that while some police officers had received ad hoc training on human rights, there was a lack of a consistent and comprehensive curriculum to ensure that all public officials, particularly those in law enforcement, received adequate human rights training.16
37	C. Promotion and protection of human rights
38	1. Implementation of international human rights obligations, taking into account applicable international humanitarian law
39	Equality and non-discrimination
40	15. Noting the lack of comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation, JS5 stated that the ethnic and Indigenous groups had limited legal protection again systemic exclusion. National development strategies had often prioritised urban growth and had sidelined rural communities in infrastructure, digital access and service delivery.17
41	16. JS6 stated that Indigenous Peoples had continued to experience structural and systemic forms of discrimination that had affected nearly every aspect of their lives. Despite Namibia supporting recommendations at the previous review aimed at addressing racial, linguistic, and social inequalities, progress had been limited. Discrimination manifested in healthcare, education, political participation, the labour market, and in access to natural resources and traditional knowledge, reinforcing entrenched patterns of marginalization, poverty, and exclusion.18
42	17. JS3 stated that transgender and gender diverse individuals had faced significant discrimination from both government institutions and non-government actors, which had impacted their fundamental rights, including access to comprehensive affirming healthcare services, fair and timely access to justice, and the legal recognition of their gender identity through appropriate documentation and legal processes. The Constitution did not explicitly safeguard individuals against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity and expression.19
43	Right to life, liberty and security of person, and freedom from torture
44	18. BWS stated that during the liberation struggle between 1960 and 1989, trumped-up charges of spying for the apartheid regime in South Africa had been levelled against cadres in the liberation movement, the South West Africa People's Organisation (SWAPO), who had been tortured and imprisoned in exile. Consequently, nnly 153 prisoners had been officially released as result of the United Nations Security Council Resolution 435 and repatriated to Namibia by UNHCR and an additional 16 detainees had escaped from the prison camps ("dungeons") and returned to Namibia, while an estimated 2000 persons had been listed as disappeared. According to BWS, by denying the families of the missing persons the right to know the fate and whereabouts of their loved ones, and by failing to ensure effective remedy to the survivors, Namibia had not complied with ICPPED, CAT, and ICCPR.20
45	19. JS3 stated that the period under review had witnessed a concerning escalation in violence directed at LGBTQI+ individuals, with reports indicating a substantial increase in hate crimes and homicides. While many of those heinous acts had been committed by nonstate actors, such violence had been aggravated by a hostile socio-political and legal environment, including discriminatory legislation and societal animosity that embolden perpetrators.21
46	Administration of justice, including impunity, and the rule of law
47	20. JS3 noted reports that had suggested that the police had exhibited apathy or insensitivity, especially when transgender individuals or gender non-conforming persons had attempted to report crimes. It stated that the failure to effectively investigate, prosecute, and secure convictions against perpetrators, particularly in cases where evidence had pointed to hate crimes or bias-motivated violence, had perpetuated a climate of impunity. This
48	3
49	
50	A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/3
51	ineffective legal response had not only undermined the rule of law but had also failed to meet the State's positive obligation under international human rights standards to protect all citizens from violence and to ensure justice for victims.22
52	Fundamental freedoms and the right to participate in public and political life
53	21. JS1 stated that in 2024, Namibia had faced persistent challenges in protecting human rights online, particularly in relation to freedom of expression and privacy. Although the Constitution guaranteed the rights to freedom of expression and privacy, they were not explicitly extended to digital spaces.23
54	22. NMT noted that media pluralism had been limited due to a dependence on state advertising and inconsistent funding mechanisms. In the absence of a clear public service media policy, editorial autonomy remained vulnerable to fiscal pressure. NMT noted instances where media outlets had self-censored coverage on governance and corruption due to reliance on government advertising. These structural weaknesses had direct implications for the safety and security of journalists, whose working conditions had become increasingly precarious amid the wider sustainability crisis confronting the media. Government had a positive obligation under international human rights law to create an enabling environment for independent and safe journalism.24
55	23. JS4 stated that the Financial Intelligence Act (2012), while aimed at combating money laundering and terrorism financing, has inadvertently imposed restrictive compliance obligations on civil society organisations. In parallel, the Draft National Policy on Civic Space (2024), which sought to safeguard freedom of association and participation, lacked explicit inclusion of marginalized groups, such as those representing LGBTQI+ persons.25
56	24. Noting the enactment of the Access to Information Act (2022), JS7 stated that the delay in bring this Act into force had undermined the work of journalists, civil society organizations, and oversight bodies that relied on access to official information. In addition, the Whistleblower Protection Act (2017), had remained non-operational due to unresolved policy, infrastructural, and budgetary challenges.26
57	25. JS1 stated that digital connectivity had improved but there were gaps in internet access in rural areas, limited smartphone use, and weak legal protections, which had underscored the need for robust reforms to ensure inclusive digital rights and democratic integrity.27
58	26. JS1 stated that in the absence of a national artificial intelligence strategy or regulatory framework, there was limited scope for the coordinated development on artificial intelligence.28
59	27. Noting that Namibia had made notable strides in digital connectivity, JS1 stated that despite the increase in digital access, stark disparities had persisted as only 16.2 percent of the rural households had mobile internet access as compared to 50.3 percent in urban areas. While 93 percent of Namibians had basic telecom access, many rural schools and clinics lacked reliable infrastructure.29
60	28. JS5 stated that minority groups had experienced political exclusion due to underrepresentation in decision-making bodies and limited access to political platforms, among others, which meant that their voices, concerns, and rights had not been sufficiently address in policy and governance. Their political participation had been further hindered by language barriers, lack of resources, and historical marginalization.30
61	29. JS1 stated that the 2024 presidential and parliamentary elections had been accompanied by a surge in misinformation, particularly on social media. Gendered disinformation, including AI generated content, had targeted female candidates. Namibia did not have legislation to enforce content moderation.31
62	30. JS1 stated that the elections had been marred by ballot shortages and technical failures, which had prompted a controversial voting extension. During this period, the digital environment had been rife with misinformation and disinformation, amplified by social media platforms. Youth voters, who had relied heavily on these platforms had become particularly vulnerable due to low media literacy.32
63	4
64	
65	A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/3
66	Right to privacy
67	31. NMT recalled that at the previous review, concerns had been raised over surveillance and data protection and noted that Namibia had reported that a data protection bill was under development to safeguard privacy rights. A civil society review of the draft bill which was introduced in 2022 was found to have had insufficient guarantees of independence for the proposed Data Protection Authority and excessive ministerial discretion in granting exemptions. In addition, data subjects were afforded minimal remedies, and state security interests had been prioritised without judicial oversight.33
68	Right to marriage and family life
69	32. CCI stated that family in Namibia had been historically recognized as the natural and fundamental unit of society, and the preservation of the family was essential for social stability, the up bringing of children, and the transmission of cultural values. It noted that Article 14(1) of the Constitution provided that "Men and women of full age, without any limitation due to race, colour, ethnic origin, nationality, religion, creed or social or economic status, shall have the right to marry and to found a family. They shall be entitled to equal rights as to marriage, during marriage and at its dissolution."34
70	33. JS4 stated that the persistence of administrative and legal uncertainty, particularly regarding parental recognition, citizenship, and custody had continued to infringe upon the rights of LGBTQI+ families. Those issues were symptomatic of the absence of a comprehensive legal framework governing assisted reproduction, surrogacy, and family formation for sexual minorities. Addressing those gaps required legislative reform to protect the best interests of the child.35
71	Prohibition of all forms of slavery, including trafficking in persons
72	34. ECLJ stated that Namibia was primarily a destination country for both labour and sex trafficking, with victims typically deceived by traffickers and forced into exploitative situations. It referred to a relevant supported recommendation from the previous review and, in that regard, took positive note of the implementation of the National Plan of Action on Combating Trafficking in Persons (2023 to 2027) and the National Referral Mechanisms and Standard Operating Procedures on Trafficking in Persons. Additionally, a training manual on trafficking in persons had been created for police and prosecutors, training had been provided to social workers and police, and funding for protective services for victims had been increased. According to ECLJ, those measures had led to an increase in the number of cases that had been investigated and prosecuted.36
73	Right to work and to just and favourable conditions of work
74	35. JS6 stated that although the Affirmative Action (Employment) Act (1998) identified "women" as a designated group for affirmative action measures designed to ensure equal employment opportunities at all levels of employment and equitable representation in the workforce, it overlooked the specific barriers faced by Indigenous women. It recalled that at the previous review, Namibia had supported a recommendation to accelerate affirmative action policies that would improve access to decent jobs for Indigenous women.37
75	36. JS8 stated that the fair labour standards, as provided for in the Constitution, had remained unrealised for sex workers. Namibia must approach sex work and sex workers from a human rights perspective. While sex work was not criminalized per se, key aspects associated with sex work including solicitation, the keeping of a brothel for the purposes of prostitution and living of the proceeds of prostitution were criminalized.38
76	Right to social security
77	37. JS7 noted that steps had been taken to strengthen social protection, including a substantial increase in the universal old-age pension and the launch of the Social Protection Policy (2021-2030), but stated that that Policy remained weak in scope and excluded many citizens who lacked basic social protection coverage.39
78	5
79	
80	A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/3
81	38. JS7 stated that despite the demonstrated success of the Basic Income Grant pilot project in Otjivero-Omitara (2008), this project had not been expanded nationally.40
82	39. JS7 stated that the National Pension Fund and the National Medical Benefit Fund, intended to provide retirement and medical benefits for both public and private sector employees, had faced delays of nearly three decades in implementation.41
83	Right to an adequate standard of living
84	40. JS7 stated that Namibia had continued to face severe socio-economic challenges marked by high unemployment, deep income inequality, and persistent multidimensional poverty. With a Gini coefficient of 59.1 (as of 2022), Namibia had remained the second most unequal country in the world in terms of income distribution. The COVID-19 pandemic had further worsened economic vulnerability, and had pushed many households into poverty, making recovery difficult without targeted social and economic reforms.42
85	41. JS7 stated that more 40 percent of the total population and approximately 80 percent of the urban population lived in informal settlements, often without access to basic services or secure land tenure. Namibia had faced a persistent shortage in the delivery of services and urban land, driven by high infrastructure costs, administrative delays, and limited municipal capacity. In 2023, the Cabinet approved the revised National Housing Policy and Implementation Action Plan, which aimed to accelerate the upgrading of informal settlements and improve access to affordable housing.43
86	42. JS7 noted that according to Namibia Statistic Agency, white citizens and foreign nationals owned 70.1 percent of the country's freehold (commercial) agricultural land. Implementation of the 60 resolutions from the Second National Land Conference in 2018 had been slow. There had also been little progress in implementing the recommendations of Presidential Commission of Inquiry into the Claims of Ancestral Land Rights and Restitution, whose report was released in 2021.44
87	Right to health
88	43. JS7 noted that in February 2025, the Cabinet of Namibia approved the universal health coverage policy framework, aimed at ensuring equitable access to quality healthcare services without financial hardship.45
89	44. Noting that the Abortion and Sterilization Act of 1975 allowed for the termination of pregnancy under certain restricted conditions, CCI stated that in 2020, two petitions had been submitted to Parliament, one had urged liberalization of the law, and another had affirmed the existing protections for unborn children. The public dialogue had revealed a wide gap between advocacy groups pressing for greater access to abortion and stakeholders who had emphasized alternatives such as family support, social assistance, and the establishment of crisis pregnancy services. CCI further stated that the persistence of illegal abortions had demonstrated the existence of gaps in practical support for women, especially those facing poverty or social exclusion.46
90	45. JS3 stated that transgender persons had continued to face pervasive stigma and discrimination within the health care sector, as they had often encountered biased attitudes from healthcare providers that had hindered their access to appropriate care.47
91	46. JS2 stated that the HIV/AIDS response, which had previously achieved significant success, was now at risk due to the withdrawal of foreign aid. The historical reliance on external donors had left Namibia unprepared to sustain its own public health programmes, which threatened to undo decades of progress and left vulnerable populations at risk.48 JS8 stated that sex workers had faced discrimination in access to HIV and sexual and reproductive health services.49
92	Right to education
93	47. GERG considered a relevant supported recommendation from the previous review to ensure free and compulsory education for all children to have been implemented. In that regard, it noted, inter alia, the per capita education expenditure, the implementation of Strategic Plan for 2025-2030 with 2 of its 8 pillars addressing equitable access to quality
94	6
95	
96	A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/3
97	education, the adoption of the San Development Programme, the implementation of the teacher capacity building programmes, and the increase in the number of schools.50
98	48. GERG noted an increase in pregnancy-related school dropouts and considered a relevant supported recommendation from the previous review to have been partially implemented.51
99	49. CCI stated that Namibia faced a persistent challenge of teenage pregnancy, which directly affected access to education for girls, with school drop-out rates especially high in the Kavango and Zambezi regions, where poverty and limited access to schools had intensified the problem. Despite government policies that allowed pregnant learners to return to school after giving birth, stigma and lack of family or community support had often prevented reintegration. Teenage pregnancy therefore not only disrupted education but also perpetuated cycles of poverty and social exclusion. Comprehensive Sexuality Education, which had been integrated in government programmes, such as the School Health and the Life Skills Education programmes, had not been effective in addressing the real drivers of adolescent pregnancy, such as poverty, peer pressure, and the breakdown of family and community structures. JS2 stated that there had been a lack of funding for the full implementation of these programmes and teachers had not been properly trained to teach the curriculum.52
100	2. Rights of specific persons or groups
101	Women
102	50. JS2 referred to eight recommendations from the previous review relating to genderequality and gender-based violence which had been supported by Namibia and considered seven of those recommendations to have been partially implemented and one recommendation to have not been implemented. Despite positive initiatives including the enactment of Combating of Rape Amendment Act (2022) and the Combating of Domestic Violence Amendment Act (2022) and the promulgated the National Plan of Action on Gender-Based Violence, 2019-2023, significant gaps had persisted not only in the legal and policy framework, but also in obtaining protection orders, ensuring robust data collection, and providing adequate shelters and institutional support for victims. With the expiration of the aforementioned Plan in 2023, no replacement plan had been put in place, which diminished the ability of the government to address gender-based violence. In addition, there was a critical discriminatory gap in the Combating of Domestic Violence Amendment Act (2022), as it did not cover domestic violence between same-sex partners. There was also a lack of safe shelters and protective spaces, as well as mental health and counselling services for survivors of gender-based violence.53
103	51. JS1 stated that: (a) Technology-facilitated gender-based violence, which had the same roots as other forms of gender-based violence, have been on an increase; (b) Women in leadership roles, including politicians, journalists and human rights defenders, had been disproportionately affected by technology-facilitated gender-based violence; (c) Although there were several laws that addressed gender-based violence, there were no laws that specifically addressed technology-facilitated gender-based violence, which remained underreported and poorly addressed; and (d) Law enforcement and social service sectors lacked capacity, training, protocols and legal frameworks to respond effectively to technology-facilitated gender-based violence.54
104	52. JS2 recalled that at the previous review, Namibia had supported two recommendations relating to the eradication of harmful traditional practices against women and girls and considered both recommendations to have been partially implemented. It stated that such practices had remained largely unaddressed due to both inadequate enforcement of existing laws and a reluctance to recognize the extent of these practices. While many organizations had conducted research and thoroughly documented harmful practices across various ethnic groups, the government and traditional authorities had often refused to acknowledge the existence of the documented practices. This lack of recognition had stemmed from the reluctance to challenge deeply ingrained patriarchal structures, which had led to a significant data gap that had prevented meaningful action.55
105	7
106	
107	A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/3
108	Children
109	53. JS2 stated that while the Child Care and Protection Act (2015) commendably set the legal age of marriage at 18 years for both civil and customary marriages, there had been significant challenges in the implementation of this Act.56
110	54. JS5 stated that youth in rural areas had suffered from socioeconomic marginalization and had been disproportionately affected by poverty, food insecurity, school dropouts, and limited access to skills training or entrepreneurship.57
111	Indigenous Peoples and minorities
112	55. JS6 stated that the Traditional Authorities Act did not explicitly recognize the rights of Indigenous Peoples and that Indigenous Peoples such as the San, Ovatue and Ovahimba continued to be officially referred to as "marginalized communities". It referred to two supported recommendations from previous review concerning the implementation of the White Paper on Indigenous Rights that had been drafted by the Office of the Ombudsman and noted that the White Paper had not been adopted nor implemented by Namibia and consequently considered the recommendations to have not been implemented.58
113	56. JS2 referred to two relevant recommendations from the previous reviews that had been supported by Namibia and stated that that the systemic marginalization of indigenous communities had continued to be perpetuated. Indigenous Peoples had limited educational opportunities and had been excluded from the mainstream economy. There had also been an erosion of indigenous culture and language.59
114	57. JS5 noted that the lack of realization of linguistic rights of Indigenous Peoples and the discrimination against Indigenous languages had limited the access of Indigenous Peoples to public services and had led to high illiteracy and unemployment rates.60
115	58. JS5 stated that the San Peoples had remained one of the most marginalised and disadvantages communities in Namibia, particularly with a history of dispossession of ancestral land.61 The San Peoples had continued to experience poverty, food insecurity, and social exclusion, and had faced barriers in the realization of its land rights, and in accessing education, healthcare, employment and political participation. While taking positive note of the San Development Programme, JS5 stated that additional financial and human resources should be allocated to the Programme.62
116	59. JS5 stated that regions in Namibia that were populated by minority groups had remained underdeveloped, which had led to few schools, clinics, and trained professionals in those regions.63
117	Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex persons
118	60. JS3 noted that since 2022, disturbing trends had been observed, including an escalation in violent attacks, increased incidence of hate crimes, and the introduction of restrictive legislation that undermines gender freedom and rights.64
119	61. JS2 recalled that at the previous review, Namibia had supported three recommendations relating to the rights of LGBTI persons. It noted that same-sex sexual relationships between males was criminalized under Roman Dutch common law, which the government had made no attempt to repeal. In 2024, the High Court had struck down the common law offences of sodomy and unnatural offences,65 and the government has since filed an appeal against this decision to the Supreme Court.66
120	62. CCI noted that in May 2023, the Supreme Court of Namibia held that same-sex marriages legally contracted abroad must be recognised in Namibia for immigration purposes. The Court reasoned that failure to recognise such marriages violated constitutional guarantees of dignity and equality, though it did not legalise same-sex marriages within Namibia itself. In July 2023, lawmakers passed the Marriage Amendment Bill and the Divorce Amendment Bill, both of which defined marriage exclusively as a union between "a man and a woman" and explicitly prohibited the recognition of same-sex marriages concluded outside the country. However, these amendments had not been signed into law be the President of Namibia, which left them without legal effect. In October 2024, the President
121	8
122	
123	Notes
124	
125	A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/3
126	of Namibia had assented to a consolidated Marriage Act (2024), which similarly defined marriage in strictly heterosexual terms. The Act also restricted the recognition of foreign marriages to those between opposite-sex partners, thus directly aiming to reverse the findings of the Supreme Court's 2023 judgment. JS4 stated that the Act's heteronormative framing was inconsistent with Articles 10 and 14 of the Constitution, which guaranteed equality before the law and protected family life; and that Namibia faced both a constitutional and moral imperative to amend the Act to ensure consistency with the rule of law and the fundamental values of justice and inclusivity.67
