United Nations
General Assembly

A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/1
Distr.: General 27 March 2026
Original: English

Human Rights Council
Working Group on the Universal Periodic Review Fifty-second session Geneva, 4-15 May 2026
National report submitted pursuant to Human Rights Council resolutions 5/1 and 16/21*
Namibia

* The present document is being issued without formal editing. GE.26-04314 (E)

A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/1
I. Process for preparation of the report
1. The report was prepared by obtaining information in writing and holding consultative meetings from Offices, Ministries, and Agencies O/M/A's) which are members of the InterMinisterial Committee on Human Rights and Humanitarian Law (IMC).
2. Two meetings were held to verify the information submitted by O/M/A's. The meetings were attended by members of the IMC. The report underwent a process of approval by the Minister of Justice and Labour Relations and the Cabinet of the Republic of Namibia. Institutional consultations were held with civil society organisations and their views were taken into account.
3. Beyond the institutional consultations held, the Government is committed to broadening its engagement and to hold further public consultations to ensure that the perspectives of a wide array of civil society actors, community leaders, and the general public are reflected in the final report and in the ongoing implementation of human rights commitments.
II. Developments since the previous cycle
4. Namibia is a sovereign, secular, democratic and unitary State founded upon the principles of democracy, rule of law and justice for all. Namibia held its 8th Presidential and National Assembly elections during November 2024. Namibia also held its Regional and Local Authorities elections during November 2025. During the year 2023, Namibia conducted its population and housing census. The population of Namibia grew by 43.1% between 2011 and 2023, which increased from 2.11 million in 2011 to 3.02 million in 2023.
5. During the period under review, Namibia co-facilitated the Summit of the future; participated in the Human Rights 75 High Level Event; participated in the case of Obligations of States in Respect of Climate Change; hosted the 25th Anniversary of the United Nations Security Council Resolution 1325 on Women, Peace and Security. Namibia continues to implement the National Plan of Action on Women Peace and Security 2019-2024 (under review) and the National Gender Equality and Equity Policy for 2025-2035.
III. Promotion and protection of human rights on the ground
Recommendations (138.71-77, 244) (SDGs: 3, 4, 5, 10, 16)
6. The National Plan of Action on Gender Based Violence (GBV) places survivors first and stimulates a culture of care amongst families, communities and institutions which promotes early help-seeking behaviours. The Government in Collaboration with other Stakeholders and Partners creates awareness on GBV through campaigns on GBV prevention and response. Gender Liaison Officers in all fourteen regions also address GBV at regional level and sensitize community members daily on GBV and how to respond to it. Coordination of GBV interventions is done through national and regional GBV clusters.
7. To ensure access to justice by victims of gender-based violence (GBV), members of the GBV Protection Division conduct awareness campaigns and operations in collaboration with other stakeholders, to educate the public on GBV, rights of victims and survivors, the consequences of GBV, and available legal remedies to empower victims to come forth and report crimes. Information is shared with the public through media outlets as well community affairs offices. Annexure C - Table#12.
Recommendations (138.41, 45, 47, 48, 49, 50, 123, 222, 149) (SDGs: 5, 16)
8. The Government will determine upon request from special procedure mandate holders of the Human Rights Council, whether to grant or reject a request. Namibia enacted the Education Act which prohibits corporal punishment in school. Corporal punishment is prohibited by the Namibian constitution in all settings. Furthermore, the Government has implemented a number of measures to address recommendations which it supported during
2

A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/1
the last review. However, some recommendations were not addressed due to the prolonged effects of the Covid-19 pandemic.
Recommendations (138.51, 259-260, 262, 46) (SDGs: 3, 5, 10, 16, 17)
9. In 2024 Cabinet issued a directive that the Government should conduct a review of the National Human Rights Action Plan (NHRAP) 2015-2019 and develop a successor plan. Namibia will continue with its efforts to fulfil its international obligations by developing and implementing comprehensive national plans and programmes. Furthermore, Namibia continues to implement its national programme for children and its harmonization with other strategies, such as the national strategic framework for the fight against HIV/AIDS and gender equality and child welfare framework.
10. The Government established the Inter-Ministerial Committee on Human Rights and Human Rights and Humanitarian Law (IMC). The IMC is a standing coordinating committee for implementation and Reporting. The IMC has been in existence since 2002.
Recommendation (138.49) (SDG: 16)
11. Namibia continues to support operations of civil society organisations. There are a number of civil society organisations which operate in the country. Civil society are members of the IMC and are consulted when reports are prepared for submission to the Universal Periodic Review Working Group, treaty bodies and the African Union. A meeting with civil society organisations was held to discuss this report on 24 November 2025.
Recommendation (138.231) (SDGs: 5, 10, 16)
12. The Government has provided financial resources to the relevant Ministries to tackle gender-based violence. The budget of the Ministry of Gender Equality and Child Welfare was increased by 23.2% to N$8.0 billion in financial fear 2024/2025. The budget includes N$824.7 million to maintain real value of the social safety nets. The Government increased the frequency of food distribution to marginalized communities at a cost of N$170.0 million, and N$284.5 million to ensure full coverage of the Orphan and Vulnerable Children Grant.
13. The Ministry of Home Affairs, Immigration, Safety and Security received N$7.4 billion in the financial year 2024/2025. N$70 million was allocated to roll-out electronic identification cards (e-IDs) and ensure full coverage of civil registration through mass registration for national documents countrywide. During the 2025/2026 financial year, health and social services received N$12.26 billion. Investment in the social sector for the Medium Term Expenditure Framework (MTEF) for the 2025/2026 to 2027/2028 financial years is earmarked for the implementation of programmes such as veteran's welfare, youth training and development programmes, tertiary and clinical health care services, health system planning and management, capacity building for gender mainstreaming, Early Child Development facilities, Primary Education, Senior Secondary Education, High Education and Vocational Education and Training. This sector is the second highest recipient of the Development Budget over the MTEF period with 21% allocation inside the State Revenue Fund and 20% benefits from outside the State Revenue Fund.
IV. Implementation of accepted/supported recommendations from the previous cycle
14. The information contained in this part relates to accepted/supported recommendations and their level of implementation are contained in Annexure A - Matrix of Recommendations.
15. Recommendations which were noted and comments on the level of implementation are contained in Annexure A - Matrix of Recommendations.
3

A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/1
A. Constitutional, legislative framework and international instruments
Recommendations (138.2-39) (SDGs: 5, 11, 13, 16)
16. The position remains the same since the last national report of the 3rd cycle. However, Namibia became a state party to the International Labour Organisation (ILO) Convention 190 on sexual harassment and ILO Convention 156 on workers with families and responsibilities ratified on the 14 August 2025.
Recommendation (138.44) (SDG: 16)
17. Namibia fully cooperates and will continue cooperating with treaty bodies and special procedures of the United Nations. Namibia has no overdue reports and has submitted all the reports to all UN treaty bodies. During 2024, Namibia was reviewed by the Committee against Torture and the Human Rights Committee. In 2024, Namibia accepted a request from special rapporteur on freedom of expression and the Government is currently liaising with the special rapporteur for scheduled visit.
Recommendations (138.54-68, 111, 257, 258, 261, 269) (SDGs: 2, 4, 3, 5, 10, 12, 16)
18. The Constitution of the Republic of Namibia remains unchanged since the submission of the previous report. A number of legislative amendments and enactments were made during the period under review. A list of new laws and amendments since the last national report is annexed as Annexure B.
19. The Namibian Constitution; Child Care and Protection Act, 2015; Criminal Procedure Act 1977, Combating of Domestic Violence Act; and Education Act, 2020; prohibits corporal punishment in all settings for adults and children. The Code of Conduct for the Teaching Service issued in terms of the Education Act 2004, states that a teacher "may not administer corporal punishment or any other degrading punishment upon a learner". The Criminal Procedure Act 1977 and other legislation which previously allowed whipping or caning as punishments for crimes committed by adults or juveniles were declared invalid by the Supreme Court of the Republic of Namibia. Consequently, corporal punishment is outlawed and prohibited in Namibia. The Child Care and Protection Act of 2015, effective from 2019, prohibits corporal punishment in settings such as schools, foster care, shelters, prisons, and police cells, and reaffirms its ban in judicial and traditional courts, while requiring parents to respect children's dignity. However, it does not explicitly outlaw corporal punishment in the home, leaving some ambiguity. To address this gap, the Government and stakeholders developed a Parenting Manual on Positive Parenting, which promotes non-violent childrearing practices. The manual provides parents with practical tools for positive discipline such as setting boundaries, praising good behaviour, using non-violent consequences, fostering emotional bonds while raising awareness about the harms of corporal punishment, encouraging nurturing and respectful approaches that uphold children's rights and wellbeing.
20. To ensure that people who live near to resource rich areas benefit from social services and development projects, Namibia has a mining policy and law. The Mineral (Prospecting and Mining) Act 1992 stipulates that no persons shall carry any reconnaissance, prospecting or mining operations in Namibia except in accordance with the licence granted. Licence conditions which require operators to provide social services and other benefits or projects, are usually stipulated to improve the lives of people who live near mines. Namibia has a Policy on Community based Natural Resource Management 2013. Community Based Natural Resources Management (CBNRM) Policy is built on the basis that espouses sound environmental management and promotes the sustainable use of natural resources, in a manner that empowers local communities who should share the responsibilities and benefits of such management.
Recommendations (138.60, 63, 82, 83, 124, 136-139, 270) (SDGs: 5, 6, 10, 12, 16)
21. The Republic of Namibia enacted several laws during the period under review to promote and protect human rights of its citizens.
4

A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/1
22. The Water Act, 2013 was brought into force in 2023.
23. To address gender inequality the Government developed the third National Gender Equality and Equity Policy (NGEEP) 2025-2035 a policy based on article 10 of the Constitution.
24. Old Persons are protected by the provisions of all laws which apply to all persons in Namibia. The Criminal Procedure Act proscribes criminal offences which protects all persons living in the Republic of Namibia including, older persons. Furthermore, the Namibian Constitution, the Labour Act 2007, the Combating of Rape Act 2000, Combating of Domestic Violence Act 2003, protect the rights and bodily integrity of all persons including older persons. The Ministry of Health and Social Services has developed the National Health Policy on the Care and Protection of Older Persons.
25. Namibia has a fully functioning independent judiciary. The Office of the Judiciary was established by the Judiciary Act 2015. The permanent structure of the Magistracy consists of 104 Magistrates. Currently there are 94 magistrates in the country. With regards to punishment after the enactment of the Correctional Act 2012, Namibia moved away from retributive forms of punishment to rehabilitative and restorative forms of punishment.
26. The High Court Act 1990, was amended to insert a definition of "primary home"; to impose restrictions on the sale in executions of immovable property; to empower the JudgePresident to make rules regulating the procedure for cession of rights for matters brought before the court by certain litigants; to make rules regulating the procedure for the adjudication of commercial disputes; to make rules relating to the appointment, administration, security, jurisdiction and the fees of deputy-sheriffs and assistants to deputysheriffs; to make rules relating to the conduct and disciplinary procedure of deputy-sheriffs and Assistants to deputy-sheriffs.
27. The Namibia Correctional Service continues to recruit cadets to serve as Correctional Officers to enhance exiting rehabilitative programmes.
28. To improve the right to fair trial, Namibia continues to provide legal aid to persons who qualify to be represented in civil and criminal cases. The qualifying amount is determined on the basis of a persons monthly salary or earning. Therefore, persons who earn more than the qualifying amount are not eligible for legal aid. The qualifying amount for legal aid was increased from N$ 3500.00 to N$7000.00. Annexure C - Table#1.
29. The Dissolution of Marriages Act 2024 provides jurisdiction to Regional Magistrates Court to hear divorce cases. Previously, divorce cases were only heard in the High Court which is situated in Windhoek and Oshakati. The Magistrate Courts Act was amended in 2023 to increase their monetary jurisdiction. This improves access to courts since most towns have magistrates courts. Namibia has 104 magistrates courts which are composed as follows: 9 Regional Courts, 21 Circuit Regional Courts, 37 District Courts and 37 Periodic Courts.
30. There are 3 victim friendly courts in Namibia located at Katima Mulilo, Keetmanshoop and Windhoek.
Recommendation (138.69) (SDG: 16)
31. The Ombudsman was accredited as an A status institution in 2019 by the subcommittee on accreditation of the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions. It was rated as fully compliant with the Paris Principles with the understanding that the Ombudsman Act 1990 should be amended to fully incorporate the Paris Principles. Consequently, the Ombudsman Bill 2024 was drafted and tabled during 2025. However, it was withdrawn for further consultations. The Ombudsman's Office was allocated the following amounts over the years: N$ 18,552,200.00 during the 2020-2021 financial year which increased to N$ 22,637,360.00 during 2024-2025 financial year. The budget of the Ombudsman's Office increased by 22.02% from the year 2020-2025 to ensure that it executes its mandate. The Office has been capacitated and decentralised into six regional offices to bring services closer to the people. In addition, staff members of the Ombudsman's Office conduct regular visits to other parts of the country where it does not have representatives or Offices. Annexure C - Table # 2.
5

A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/1
32. During the past 35 years, the Ombudsman's Office has been operating as an independent institution while its budget and procurement is administered by the Ministry of Justice and Labour Relations. Government resolved to enhance the independence of the Ombudsman in accordance with Article 89 of the Constitution and the Paris Principles on National Human Rights Institutions.
33. The Ombudsman Bill once enacted will de-link the Ombudsman's Office from the Ministry of Justice and Labour Relations and have its own accounting officer. The accounting officer will be responsible for the recruitment of staff in terms of the Public Service Act 1995 in consultation with the Ombudsman. The Bill will be re-tabled in Parliament in future.
B. Cross cutting issues
Recommendations (138.79, 81, 84-86, 89, 92, 99) (SDGs: 3, 4, 5, 10, 16)
34. The Constitution and its legislative framework prohibit discrimination on the grounds of sex, race, colour, ethnic origin, religion, creed or social or economic status. The Labour Act 2007 provides that - "A person must not discriminate in any employment decision directly or indirectly, or adopt any requirement or engage in any practice which has the effect of discrimination against any individual on one or more of the following grounds - (a) race, colour, or ethnic origin;(b) sex, marital status or family responsibilities; (c) religion, creed or political opinion; (d) social or economic status; (e) degree of physical or mental disability; (f) AIDS or HIV status; or (g) previous, current or future pregnancy".
35. Namibia is implementing the Third NGEEP 2025-2035. The Third NGEEP is anchored on Article 10 of the Namibian Constitution, which states that "(1) All persons shall be equal before the law. (2) No persons may be discriminated against on the grounds of sex, race, colour, ethnic origin, religion, creed or social or economic status". The Third NGEEP is aligned to the provisions of various regional and global commitments on gender equality.
36. Namibia has closed its gender gap by at least 81.1%. The Country is number 8 globally while in Sub-Saharan Africa, it is number 1. These improvements were in the areas of: Education; Economic Participation and Opportunity; Political Empowerment; and Health. Namibia has achieved full parity on both the Health and Survival and Educational Attainment sub-indexes.
37. Since 21 March 2025, Namibia has a female President, Vice President, Speaker of the National Assembly and the majority of Cabinet Ministers in Namibia are female. Currently, Namibia's Cabinet is composed of a majority of women (57%). The Government continues to lobby for the 50/50 representation in the political decision-making sector. The Government, through collaborations with International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (IDEA) continues to implement and hold capacity building workshops for women in Political and decision making roles, to enhance gender equality in these sectors.
38. To combat racial discrimination, the Government enacted and enforces the Racial Discrimination Prohibition Act, 1991 and is a state party to International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination.
39. There is a quota reserved for indigenous people/marginalised communities namely, the San, Ovatue and Ovatjimba at the University of Namibia and, Namibia University of Science and Technology. There is standing Cabinet Directive and policy to reserve certain vacancies in the Public Service to indigenous persons with disabilities and women.
40. The Government through its social services departments continues to hold awareness campaigns against the stigmatisation of HIV affected people.
41. The Third NGEEP 2025-2035 has strategies in place, to escalate civic education campaigns on HIV and AIDS targeting communities, schools, men, boys, Traditional Authorities, Persons with Disabilities and Marginalised Communities to address some of the gender-related barriers, toxic masculinities and harmful practices that fuel the spread of HIV and AIDs, and STIs.
6

A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/1
Recommendations (138.112, 113, 172, 223) (SDGs: 1, 5, 10, 16)
42. Namibia will continue to promote sustainable economic and social development in order to provide a solid foundation for its people by developing and implementing its economic and social National development policies and plans. In 2025, Namibia launched its National Development Plan Six (NDP 6) which focuses on four (4) pillars, namely: Economic Recovery, and Resilience; Human Development and Community Resilience; Sustainable Development and Green Growth Opportunities, and Effective Governance and Public Service Delivery. NDP 6 also has an Implementation, Monitoring and Evaluation Plan (IMEP). The IMEP outlines the programmes and Sub-Programmes that will be implemented in the NDP6 period. It also outlines their cost. Under the 8th Government administration poverty eradication is a cross-cutting issue in all sectors. Government appointed National Planning Commissioners during August 2025, for a period of three years to monitor the implementation of the NDP6.
Recommendations (138.116-120) (SDGs: 11, 13)
43. The Government recognises and embraces the fundamental rights of people and further recognises the prediction that the most severe effects of climate change will be felt by poor people in rural areas, women, children and marginalised groups/ individuals. In accordance with article 95 of the constitution, the Government actively promotes and maintains the welfare of the people by adopting policies which address the impact of climate change on human rights.
44. Namibia has a National Policy on Climate Change (2011). The third NGEEP 20252035 makes provision for the implementation of strategies to address the impact of climate change by recognizing its disproportionate impacts on women and children, especially in rural and vulnerable communities, and by integrating gender-responsive strategies into adaptation, resilience, and disaster risk reduction efforts. Climate change continues to affect Namibia and increase risks of natural disasters emanating from climate change related drought and floods. Namibia has a Disaster and Risk Management Act 2012, which provides for disaster risk management in Namibia.

Consequently, during 2025 Namibia amended the National Disability Council Act 2004, which contains the amended National Policy of Disability. The amended National Disability Policy 2025 provides all the relevant information on international instruments ratified by Namibia, Namibian legislation and statistics about persons with disability in Namibia. A copy of the amended National Disability Policy is attached hereto for ease of reference as Annexure D.
Recommendations (138.263-264) (SDGs: 5, 10, 16)
119. The Child Care and Protection Act 2015 (CCPA) defines a child under Section 1, as a person who has not attained the age of 18 years. This definition complies with international human rights law and is in alignment with the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC). The CCPA also provides for the age of majority under section 10. Furthermore, Namibia has made the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (schedule 2) and the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (schedule 3) part of the CCPA.
120. Namibia enacted the Child Care and Protection Act 2015 and the Marriage Act 2024 which prohibits practices of marrying of children. The government provides learners with knowledge and skills and information on sexual and reproductive health, especially in connection with HIV prevention through programmes such as the "Window of Hope" and "My Future My Choice". Development of Ending Child Marriage strategy is underway. The main goal of the Ending Child Marriage Strategy is to eliminate child marriage by addressing its root causes, strengthening legal and policy frameworks, empowering children particularly girls and mobilizing families, communities, and institutions to protect the rights, health, and well-being of all children.
121. Government has developed and adopted the National Plan of Action on Violence against children 2021 -2025. Child friendly version materials were developed on harmful
16

A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/1
practices. The National Agenda for Children 2025-2030 has a specific pillar addressing violence against children. There is also a specific focus area in the National Development Plan 6 on child protection with specific strategies addressing violence against children including indicator on child marriage rate.
Recommendations (138.280, 274-278) (SDGs: 4, 10, 16) 122. Namibia continues to promote and provide free education as contemplated in Article 20 of the Namibian Constitution. The Government has since independence strengthened efforts to ensure that every child residing in Namibia has access to education. Such efforts include the building of mobile schools for marginalised groups such as the San and Ovatwe/Ovahimba who live a nomadic life. The White Paper on indigenous peoples' rights in Namibia has been finalized with input from stakeholders, under the leadership of the Ombudsman. The White Paper on indigenous people has been submitted to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Agriculture, Environment and Natural Resources and Standing Committee on Urban, Rural Development and Land reform, to consider recommendations. The Government recognises marginalised communities and there are specialised programmes designed to support them.
V. Status of implementation of voluntary pledges
123. Namibia made four pledges to the Human Rights 75 Secretariat during December 2023 and is engaged in implementing those pledges. The pledges are included in the sixth National Development Plan (NDP6) which has an implementation and monitoring plan. Financing of NDP6 will be based on the Integrated Financing Framework consisting mainly of conventional and non-conventional sources of finance.

124. The Ombudsman has started a National dialogue on Business and Human Rights in 2025 and has proposed to incorporate a component on business and Human Rights in the successor plan post review of the National Human Rights Action Plan (2015-2020).

125. Namibia is experiencing a high unemployment rate and requires assistance from the international community to assist with modalities aimed at reducing the high unemployment. 126. Challenges highlighted are:
(a) The non-legislated quota of the 50.0 percent target risks regression after elections as political parties are not obliged by the Electoral Act, 2024 to field equal numbers of men and women as candidates;
(b) While there has been an increase of female enrolment from primary, secondary, high education and TVET there has been a decrease in enrolment and completion for males;
(c) The HIV prevalence rate is still high among females with 15.7% while among males stands at 12.6%;
(d) Gender-Based Violence (GBV) and Violence Against Children (VAC); (e) Unemployment and poverty rate still high especially among the youth; and (f) Access to water and sanitation is still limited. 127. Priorities for the next five years identified include: (a) Gender Based Violence and Violence against children;

Marginalised Communities and Persons with Disabilities; (c) Sexual reproductive health and rights for women and men with special focus
on Maternal Health, and HIV/AIDS; (d) Reduction of Poverty; (e) Address high unemployment; and (f) Implementation, monitoring and evaluation of Universal Period Review
recommendations.

1	United Nations

5	Distr.: General 24 February 2026 English Original: English/Spanish

7	Human Rights Council
8	Working Group on the Universal Periodic Review Fifty-second session Geneva, 4-15 May 2026
9	Paraguay
10	Compilation of information prepared by the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights
11	I. Background
12	1. The present report was prepared pursuant to Human Rights Council resolutions 5/1 and 16/21, taking into consideration the outcome of the previous review.1 It is a compilation of information contained in relevant United Nations documents, presented in a summarized manner owing to word-limit constraints.
13	II. Scope of international obligations and cooperation with human rights mechanisms
14	2. The Special Rapporteur on minority issues noted that Paraguay still had not ratified an international instrument, despite the commitment that it had made during the second review cycle. The Special Rapporteur, together with the United Nations country team and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), recommended that Paraguay ratify the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.2 3. The Special Rapporteur on the implications for human rights of the environmentally sound management and disposal of hazardous substances and wastes, together with the United Nations country team, recommended that Paraguay fully comply with the Views of the Human Rights Committee in the cases relating to Campo Agua' and Colonia Yerut�.3 4. The Committee on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families and the Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities acknowledged the SIMORE recommendations monitoring mechanism, as an outcome of a cooperation project between Paraguay and OHCHR.4
15	III. National human rights framework
16	1. Constitutional and legislative framework 5. The Special Rapporteur on minority issues noted that the Paraguayan legislative framework did not protect the full range of human rights. He recommended that Paraguay adopt comprehensive national human rights legislation to cover the full range of human rights that it had accepted by ratifying human rights treaties, and recognize the competence of the
17	GE.26-01460 (E) 250226 250226
18	
19	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/2
20	Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination to receive and examine individual communications.5
21	6. The Committee on Migrant Workers took note of the migration bill. However, it was concerned that the bill was still pending more than five years after it had been introduced. The Committee urged Paraguay to adopt and publish the migration law and ensure that its content was fully in line with the International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Their Families.6
22	2. Institutional infrastructure and policy measures
23	7. The United Nations country team noted that the Ombudsman's Office had been reaccredited with category A status by the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions, thereby initiating a process of institutional strengthening in line with the principles relating to the status of national institutions for the promotion and protection of human rights (the Paris Principles). The budget allocated to the institution had been increased, but it continued to have one of the lowest budgets of any agency.7 The Special Rapporteur on minority issues recommended that the national human rights institution comply fully with the Paris Principles, having a broad mandate on universal human rights standards and being autonomous and independent.8
24	8. The country team stated that a bill to establish a ministry of the family by merging the Ministry for Women, the Ministry for Children and Adolescents and the National Secretariat for Youth was being considered and that this initiative could have restricted the visibility of, and responses to, structural inequalities and different types of gender-based violence.9
25	9. The country team noted that improvements had been made to the National Institute of Indigenous Affairs. However, challenges remained, such as a lack of inter-agency coordination, a shortage of specific resources and a limited capacity to enforce compliance with consultation procedures.10
26	10. The Committee on Migrant Workers recommended that Paraguay strengthen its institutional structure for dealing with migration-related issues by creating mechanisms and engaging in capacity-building at the different entities coordinating work on those issues.11
27	11. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities recommended endowing the National Secretariat for the Human Rights of Persons with Disabilities with sufficient resources to allow it to fulfil its function effectively.12
28	IV. Promotion and protection of human rights
29	A. Implementation of international human rights obligations, taking into account applicable international humanitarian law
30	1. Equality and non-discrimination
31	12. The Special Rapporteur on minority issues was concerned about the persistent discrimination suffered by women, persons of African descent, Indigenous Peoples and persons with disabilities and about the high level of impunity regarding hate crimes against those groups.13 The same Special Rapporteur and the Committee on Migrant Workers were concerned that Paraguay still had not adopted a law against all forms of discrimination, despite the numerous international recommendations.14
32	13. The Special Rapporteur on minority issues, the Committee on Migrant Workers, the Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and the United Nations country team recommended that Paraguay promptly adopt a law against all forms of discrimination.15 The Committee on the Rights of the Child recommended putting in place laws and regulations to explicitly prohibit all forms of discrimination on the grounds of social origin, ethnicity, disability, sex, gender identity and sexual orientation.16
33	14. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities recommended that Paraguay establish accessible and effective procedures, including judicial, administrative and
34	
35	2
36	
37	GE.26-01460
38	
39	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/2
40	
41	complaints procedures, for victims of discrimination, and ensure that victims received reparation and perpetrators were punished.17
42	2. Right to life, liberty and security of person, and freedom from torture
43	15. The Committee on the Rights of the Child found that Paraguay was accountable for grave human rights violations concerning the killings of two 11-year-old girls during an operation conducted by the Joint Task Force of Paraguay against the Paraguayan People's Army, a guerrilla group. The Committee recommended that Paraguay take further steps to establish the truth, acknowledge the facts and accept responsibility for the failures in the investigation procedures, including considering the assistance of an international expert mission; strengthen its legal and regulatory framework regarding its law enforcement officials; and ensure that the police, law enforcement agents, armed forces and other agents acting on behalf of or with the consent or acquiescence of the State act with restraint and in conformity with international human rights law and international humanitarian law, including the principles of proportionality and necessity.18
44	16. The same Committee was concerned at cases of torture or ill-treatment of children in police stations and centres of deprivation of liberty. It recommended enforcing the prohibition of torture and ensuring that allegations of torture or ill-treatment or punishment of children were duly investigated, that perpetrators were punished and that children who were victims received effective remedies and psychosocial services.19
45	17. According to the United Nations country team, although initiatives had been undertaken to improve detention conditions and reduce overcrowding, the prison system continued to face a structural crisis. A total of 70% of the prison population was in pretrial detention, and overcrowding had reached 435% nationwide, with some facilities operating at more than 1,100% of their capacity. Conditions of extreme isolation had been documented in maximum security units. Women deprived of their liberty faced a simultaneous restriction of multiple rights, inhuman and degrading treatment and disproportionate penalties.20
46	18. The Committee on Migrant Workers was concerned about the lack of information on the number of migrants detained, the conditions under which the period of "administrative delay" during entry proceedings was imposed and the length of time that that period lasted. It urged Paraguay to ensure that detention of migrants was an exceptional measure of last resort, to adopt alternatives to administrative detention for migrant workers and members of their families during proceedings relating to their entry into or expulsion from the country, and to ensure adequate and decent conditions in places of restriction of liberty and, where applicable, the effective separation of migrant workers and members of their families from persons under criminal investigation.21
47	19. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities was concerned at the involuntary treatment to which persons with disabilities were subjected at the psychiatric hospital. It recommended explicitly prohibiting by law the use of isolation, mechanical restraints, forced medication, electroconvulsive therapy, confinement in individual cells and isolation rooms, and forced treatment in crisis situations; and establishing accessible complaint and investigation mechanisms so that persons with disabilities in institutions could report instances of ill-treatment, receive legal assistance and have an effective remedy.22
48	3. Administration of justice, including impunity, and the rule of law
49	20. According to the Special Rapporteur on hazardous substances and wastes, Paraguay faced several challenges in terms of access to justice. In particular, the country's judicial system was slow and inefficient, with most reports of human rights violations not being investigated. He recommended ensuring that people had effective access to mechanisms, resources and support to help them understand and use the judicial system, and addressing the inequalities and discrimination that hindered access to justice for some groups.23
50	21. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities recommended that Paraguay adopt the protocol on access to justice for persons with disabilities and ensure that it was strictly enforced. The Committee also recommended that Paraguay put in place ageand gender-sensitive procedural accommodation in all judicial proceedings to ensure that persons with disabilities could participate effectively, including as judges, legal advisers or
51	
52	GE.26-01460
53	
54	3
55	
56	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/2
57	witnesses, in such proceedings, and that it make the necessary procedural changes at the provincial level to afford such accommodation.24
58	22. The Committee on the Rights of the Child recommended strengthening restorative mechanisms and non-custodial sanctions for the social insertion of adolescents in conflict with the law and actively promoting non-judicial measures.25
59	4. Fundamental freedoms and the right to participate in public life
60	23. The United Nations country team noted that attacks, reprisals and assaults against human rights defenders, particularly defenders of sexual and reproductive rights, continued to be carried out. It also noted that the majority of murders of journalists remained unpunished. It added that, although the Inter-American Court of Human Rights had issued a ruling ordering the establishment of a mechanism for protecting journalists and defenders, the bill presented for this purpose had not made any progress through the parliament since 2021.26 The country team recommended that the law establishing this mechanism be adopted.27 The Special Rapporteur on hazardous substances and wastes recommended adopting a programme for the protection of human rights defenders.28
61	24. UNESCO stated that, since 2006, when systematic monitoring had begun, its Observatory of Killed Journalists had recorded nine killings of journalists in Paraguay.29 UNESCO encouraged Paraguay to continue investigating unresolved cases of killed journalists.30
62	25. UNESCO recommended decriminalizing defamation and placing it within civil defamation legislation that was in accordance with international standards, 31 ensuring a transparency and accountability mechanism on the governance of digital platforms to ensure the upholding of human rights and mitigate the risks associated with the spread of harmful content online,32 and assessing the system of supervision of the broadcasting sector in order to ensure that that process was transparent and independent.33
63	5. Prohibition of all forms of slavery, including trafficking in persons
64	26. The Committee on Migrant Workers was concerned that Paraguay had not yet achieved satisfactory standards in its fight against trafficking in persons and that children, especially those living on the street in the tri-border area, continued to be subjected to exploitation in-country. The Committee recommended that Paraguay include specific provisions in the Criminal Code to penalize trafficking in persons and smuggling of migrants; ensure that all offences of trafficking in persons, in particular those related to sexual exploitation and those in which public officials were complicit, were effectively and impartially investigated, prosecuted and punished; and allocate sufficient resources for the provision of assistance to victims.34
65	27. The United Nations country team noted that Indigenous Peoples were particularly vulnerable to forced labour and debt bondage owing to the structural conditions of poverty and exclusion under which they lived.35
66	28. The Committee on the Rights of the Child recommended that Paraguay withdraw all children involved in the worst forms of child labour, especially in rural areas and in domestic labour, and ensure their reintegration into the education and social protection systems, and that it eliminate the practice of criadazgo (forced child servitude) and provide full protection to children who were victims.36 The Committee also recommended that Paraguay develop a national strategy to combat trafficking in persons.37
67	6. Right to work and to just and favourable conditions of work
68	29. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities was concerned about the limited implementation of the National Action Plan for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 2015-2030 regarding the creation of more jobs. 38 The Committee recommended that Paraguay develop and apply a constructive strategy to implement effectively pillar 13 of the National Action Plan and include affirmative measures and incentives that encouraged the employment of persons with disabilities in the public and private sectors, in urban, rural and remote areas.39

76	30. The Committee on Migrant Workers recommended that Paraguay provide resources and put in place procedures to break the vicious circle where, in order to work, migrants needed permanent residence documents, but in order to obtain those documents, they needed to have income from a job.40
77	31. The United Nations country team recommended ratifying the Violence and Harassment Convention, 2019 (No. 190) and the Violence and Harassment Recommendation, 2019 (No. 206) of the International Labour Organization (ILO) concerning violence and harassment in the workplace.41
78	7. Right to social security
79	32. The Committee on the Rights of the Child recommended that Paraguay increase budget allocations for social protection programmes affecting children and strengthen their effectiveness, in particular by improving multi-agency coordination in the identification and disbursement of grants, expanding coverage of the child grant programme to cover all groups of children in disadvantaged situations, and addressing barriers that prevented certain groups of children from acquiring access to social assistance.42
80	8. Right to an adequate standard of living
81	33. The Committee on the Rights of the Child was concerned about the large number of children living in poverty and the regional disparities in access to rights.43 It recommended that Paraguay strengthen measures to end child poverty and ensure the right of all children to an adequate standard of living, including their access to adequate housing, water and sanitation, paying particular attention to children living in rural areas and urban informal settlements.44
82	34. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities was concerned at the rate of poverty among Indigenous persons with disabilities. It recommended that Paraguay increase the budget allocated to social programmes, and the amounts provided, in order to achieve a real reduction in poverty among persons with disabilities, especially Indigenous persons with disabilities and persons with disabilities living in rural and remote areas.45
83	35. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities recommended ensuring that persons with disabilities had access to housing alternatives in their communities.46
84	9. Right to health
85	36. The United Nations country team noted that, despite the efforts made, challenges continued to surround the quality of healthcare, especially in rural areas and Indigenous communities. Food insecurity, poverty and exposure to violence had a serious impact on the well-being of Indigenous children, who also faced forced evictions, displacement and the pollution of their ancestral lands, directly affecting their health and access to basic services.47
86	37. The Committee on the Rights of the Child was also concerned about the quality of healthcare.48 It recommended increasing access to quality and culturally sensitive healthcare, particularly in rural areas and Indigenous communities, and improving vaccination coverage and providing accurate information about the importance of vaccines.49
87	38. The country team recommended strengthening health information systems with data disaggregated by gender, age, ethnicity, socioeconomic status and disability in order to inform evidence-based policies.50 The country team also recommended ensuring intercultural health services tailored to the needs of Indigenous Peoples, who should participate effectively in the design and implementation of such services.51
88	39. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities was concerned at the limited implementation of the National Sexual and Reproductive Health Plan 2019-2023 and the failure to adopt the bill on sexual, reproductive, maternal and perinatal health.52 The country team stated that the budget allocated to the sexual and reproductive health programme had been insufficient, undermining the sustainability of the progress made. 53 It also noted persistent challenges in guaranteeing sexual and reproductive rights, especially the rights of adolescents, Indigenous women, persons with disabilities and members of the LGTBIQ+ community.54 The country team recommended ensuring access to sexual and reproductive

96	40. The Committee on the Rights of the Child was concerned about the high number of adolescent pregnancies and about the prohibition by the Ministry of Education and Science on disseminating age-appropriate information on sexual and reproductive health in educational institutions.56 It recommended repealing resolution No. 933/2023 of the Ministry of Education and Sciences and adopting a comprehensive sexual and reproductive health policy for adolescents; ensuring that sexual and reproductive health and gender-related education was part of the mandatory school curriculum and was targeted at adolescents, with special attention paid to preventing early pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections; and decriminalizing abortion in all circumstances and ensuring access to safe, timely and quality abortion and post-abortion care services.57

The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities was concerned about barriers encountered by persons with disabilities in obtaining health services, and the persistence of the medical model of disability in Act No. 7018/2022.58 It recommended ensuring that all persons with disabilities had access to high-quality gender-sensitive and culturally sensitive health services; decentralizing health services, and placing a special focus on the care of Indigenous persons with disabilities; adopting promptly the bill on sexual, reproductive, maternal and perinatal health; and aligning Act No. 7018/2022 on mental health, and the regulations thereto, with the human rights model of disability set out in the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.59

102	45. 109	GE.26-01460

111	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/2
112	communities in order to fully implement the International Labour Organization (ILO) Indigenous and Tribal Peoples Convention, 1989 (No. 169) and better integrate it into judicial processes and the education system.69
113	48. The United Nations country team recommended ensuring the cultural rights of the entire population, including people of African descent, migrants, persons with disabilities and Indigenous Peoples, by promoting access to and equitable participation in culture, the protection of tangible and intangible cultural heritage, and cultural diversity through the development of a new national culture plan.70
114	12. Development, the environment, and business and human rights
115	49. According to the Special Rapporteur on hazardous substances and wastes, Paraguay had been taking steps in hazardous waste management. However, the country faced significant challenges. Rural communities and Indigenous Peoples faced an alarming level of exposure to toxic substances, particularly hazardous pesticides and most of the country's environmental laws were not observed.71 The Special Rapporteur recommended helping companies handling hazardous wastes to develop plans for the environmentally sound management and disposal of that waste; implementing emergency measures to stop the contamination of soils and the Pati�o aquifer with methyl tert-butyl ether; addressing the human rights abuses related to the use of pesticides, in a structural and decisive manner, including by implementing accessible educational and awareness-raising programmes, in Spanish and Guaran�, to inform pesticide users and communities of the dangers of pesticide misuse and of the necessary protective measures; and conducting health cohort studies and environmental pollution monitoring studies to identify and prevent the negative health effects of pesticides.72
116	B. Rights of specific persons or groups
117	1. Women
118	50. The United Nations country team noted that cases of femicide had been observed in Paraguay in previous years and, according to a national survey, the level of violence against women was very high.73 It recommended that a comprehensive system of prevention, support and redress be implemented to combat violence against women, girls, and adolescents.74
119	51. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities highlighted the insufficient measures taken to prevent and eliminate multiple discrimination and violence against women with disabilities, Indigenous women with disabilities and women with disabilities living in rural areas.75 It recommended that, with the effective participation of women and girls with disabilities, Paraguay mainstream a disability perspective in its laws and policies on gender equality and incorporate a gender perspective into its laws and policies on disability.76
120	52. The same Committee recommended that Paraguay adopt a national strategy to promote a gender- and age-sensitive human rights model of disability and effectively involve persons with disabilities in the development, implementation and regular evaluation of the strategy.77
121	53. Concerned at the persistence of early marriage, the Committee on the Rights of the Child and UNESCO recommended that Paraguay amend the legislation to ensure that the minimum age of marriage was 18 years, without exception.78
122	54. The country team stated that the economic and social crisis arising from the pandemic had disproportionately affected women, which showed that the persistence of gender norms restricted their full participation in the labour market and society.79 It added that only 36.8% of farms belonged to women, representing only 11.6% of the total area of agricultural land. Furthermore, according to the country team, women owned only 13.4% of plots of land with firm titles.80
123	55. The country team noted that women's representation in governance spaces remained limited.81
124	
125	GE.26-01460
126	
127	7
128	
129	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/2
130	2. Children
131	56. The Committee on the Rights of the Child was concerned at the high rates of missing children, in particular girls and in the context of criadazgo. The Committee recommended that Paraguay take immediate and effective measures to prevent children going missing, addressing the root causes of this, including criadazgo, and that the country's National Police and Office of the Public Prosecutor follow up on cases of missing children.82
132	57. The same Committee was concerned at high rate of child sexual abuse, in particular of girls and Indigenous children, both online and in the context of tourism, and at the lack of a comprehensive system and strategy for preventing and combating child abuse and sexual violence and for protecting the children who were victims.83 It recommended extending, on the basis of an evaluation, the national plan to end violence against children, and the scope of the strategy for preventing and combating child abuse and sexual violence; and amending the Penal Code so as to clearly criminalize all acts of sexual violence, regardless of the sex and gender, against children, with penalties proportionate to the seriousness of the offences.84
133	58. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities was concerned about the persistent poverty among children with disabilities, particularly Indigenous children with disabilities and children with disabilities living in rural and remote areas.85
134	59. The Committee on the Rights of the Child recommended implementing targeted policies and programmes to eliminate discrimination against children, in particular children with disabilities, Indigenous children, children living with HIV/AIDS, children in street situations and lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or intersex children, and ensuring their equal access to health services, education and a decent standard of living.86
135	60. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities recommended that Paraguay reduce poverty among children with disabilities, paying particular attention to the situations of Indigenous children with disabilities and children with disabilities living in rural and remote areas, and reinforce the Abrazo Programme; and that it put in place, in close coordination with the institutions comprising the National System for the Comprehensive Protection and Advancement of Children and Adolescents, monitoring and oversight measures to ensure strict compliance with Act No. 5659/16 on the protection of children and adolescents against physical punishment in homes, schools and institutions in both urban and rural areas, and report on complaints and the follow-up given to them.87
136	3. Persons with disabilities
137	61. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities appreciated the National Action Plan for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 2015-2030 and related legislative measures.88
138	62. The same Committee noted the continuing difficulties that individuals faced in obtaining a disability certificate 89 and was concerned at the little progress made in implementing Act No. 4934/13 on accessibility.90 It recommended updating and extending the 2016-2018 Strategic Plan, and ensuring that municipalities harmonized their laws with Act No. 4934/13 and that the Basic Guide on Accessibility of the Physical Environment for Persons with Disabilities was applied.91
139	63. The same Committee recommended that Paraguay actively promote the participation of persons with disabilities, especially women with disabilities, in political parties, so that they may be put forward as candidates for elected office.92
140	64. The United Nations country team took note of the enactment of the Mental Health Act and its National Plan 2024-2030. However, it added that serious shortcomings persisted, including the use of prolonged institutionalization without consent.93
141	65. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities recommended that Paraguay ensure that all public information was accessible to persons with disabilities, and that it allocate sufficient funding for the development, promotion and use of accessible communication formats and alternative means of communication.94
142	
143	8
144	
145	GE.26-01460
146	
147	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/2
148	4. Indigenous Peoples and minorities
149	66. The United Nations country team noted the persistent discrimination directed at Indigenous Peoples, which was reflected in the difficulties that they experienced in gaining equitable access to the rights to health, education, water and basic services such as electricity and sanitation. The country team noted the difficulties that Indigenous Peoples faced in fully exercising their cultural rights.95 It also stated that 66.2% of members of Indigenous Peoples lived in poverty while 34.4% lived in extreme poverty, these figures being three times the national average.96
150	67. While acknowledging some progress, the Special Rapporteur on minority issues expressed concerns at the fact that Indigenous Peoples were often victims of hate crimes, of hate speech and of direct discrimination in public services, including in hospitals and schools, and in access to basic services.97
151	68. The Special Rapporteur on minority issues stated that Indigenous Peoples' lands were not adequately protected, and noted an increase in forced evictions affecting Indigenous Peoples, together with a significant rise in protests, both peaceful and violent.98
152	69. According to the country team, forced evictions of Indigenous communities, the parcelling out of communal lands and the pollution of rivers particularly affected women and children. In addition, the housing conditions of the Indigenous population were poor.99 It recommended developing an inter-agency protocol for the prevention of forced evictions that would guarantee the protection of human rights, including those of the Indigenous Peoples, ensure their access to their ancestral lands and provide redress to those who have been evicted.100
153	70. According to the Special Rapporteur on minority issues, the Afrodescendent minority of Paraguay was often invisible and unacknowledged, and there was a lack of empowerment and self-recognition by Afrodescendent peoples themselves. He recommended including questions on Afrodescendent identity in all future national censuses, in consultation with the interested parties, including all Afrodescendent communities.101
154	71. The country team stated that the adoption of Act No. 6940, which established mechanisms to prevent and punish racism and discrimination against people of African descent, constituted partial progress and that its implementation was still pending.102
155	5. Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex persons
156	72. The Committee on the Rights of the Child was concerned at failure to implement the provisions banning "conversion therapy" in Act No. 7018/2022 on mental health. It recommended that Paraguay develop policies and allocate sufficient resources to promote the mental health of children, and eradicate "conversion therapies".103
157	73. The United Nations country team recommended repealing decision No. 29.664 of the Ministry of Education and Science, which prohibited the teaching of topics related to gender theory in schools.104
158	6. Migrants and refugees
159	74. The Special Rapporteur on minority issues noted that some migrants and refugees still faced obstacles and challenges in access to employment, education or other public services.105 The Committee on Migrant Workers recommended that Paraguay take effective measures, with deadlines, indicators, and monitoring and evaluation benchmarks, to implement the migration policy; and provide sufficient human, technical and financial resources for its implementation. 106 The same Committee also recommended establishing ordinary regularization mechanisms that were regulated by law, in accordance with the International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Their Families, and that applied to all migrants.107
160	75. The Committee on Migrant Workers was concerned at Emergency Act No. 6524/2020, which made migrants and refugees ineligible for the aid offered to workers in the informal sector.108
161	
162	GE.26-01460
163	
164	9
165	
166	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/2
167	76. The same Committee recommended ensuring that, in practice, migrant workers and members of their families, including those in an irregular situation, were informed about migration procedures and the documents needed, about the possibility of applying for regularization even in the case of rejection, about their rights upon arrival and during transit and about the fact that they had access to remedies, complaint mechanisms and other forms of redress.109
168	77. The same Committee recommended collecting information on school enrolment rates for migrant children, including those in an irregular situation.110
169	78. The Special Rapporteur on minority issues recommended setting up a migrant and refugee assistance service, accessible online or by telephone, free of charge, in order to provide assistance and practical information to migrants and refugees.111
170	7. Stateless persons
171	79. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities was concerned about the 30 per cent underregistration rate for births. It recommended that Paraguay step up the activities of the "Right to an Identity" programme, including in rural and remote areas.112 The Committee on the Rights of the Child recommended ensuring comprehensive free-of-charge birth registration and the issuance of birth certificates for all children born in the territory of Paraguay, immediately after the birth, regardless of their or their parents' immigration status.113
