United Nations
General Assembly

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/2
Distr.: General 24 February 2026 English Original: English/Spanish

Human Rights Council
Working Group on the Universal Periodic Review Fifty-second session Geneva, 4-15 May 2026
Paraguay
Compilation of information prepared by the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights
I. Background
1. The present report was prepared pursuant to Human Rights Council resolutions 5/1 and 16/21, taking into consideration the outcome of the previous review.1 It is a compilation of information contained in relevant United Nations documents, presented in a summarized manner owing to word-limit constraints.
II. Scope of international obligations and cooperation with human rights mechanisms
2. The Special Rapporteur on minority issues noted that Paraguay still had not ratified an international instrument, despite the commitment that it had made during the second review cycle. The Special Rapporteur, together with the United Nations country team and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), recommended that Paraguay ratify the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.2 3. The Special Rapporteur on the implications for human rights of the environmentally sound management and disposal of hazardous substances and wastes, together with the United Nations country team, recommended that Paraguay fully comply with the Views of the Human Rights Committee in the cases relating to Campo Agua' and Colonia Yerut�.3 4. The Committee on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families and the Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities acknowledged the SIMORE recommendations monitoring mechanism, as an outcome of a cooperation project between Paraguay and OHCHR.4
III. National human rights framework
1. Constitutional and legislative framework 5. The Special Rapporteur on minority issues noted that the Paraguayan legislative framework did not protect the full range of human rights. He recommended that Paraguay adopt comprehensive national human rights legislation to cover the full range of human rights that it had accepted by ratifying human rights treaties, and recognize the competence of the
GE.26-01460 (E) 250226 250226

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/2
Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination to receive and examine individual communications.5
6. The Committee on Migrant Workers took note of the migration bill. However, it was concerned that the bill was still pending more than five years after it had been introduced. The Committee urged Paraguay to adopt and publish the migration law and ensure that its content was fully in line with the International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Their Families.6
2. Institutional infrastructure and policy measures
7. The United Nations country team noted that the Ombudsman's Office had been reaccredited with category A status by the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions, thereby initiating a process of institutional strengthening in line with the principles relating to the status of national institutions for the promotion and protection of human rights (the Paris Principles). The budget allocated to the institution had been increased, but it continued to have one of the lowest budgets of any agency.7 The Special Rapporteur on minority issues recommended that the national human rights institution comply fully with the Paris Principles, having a broad mandate on universal human rights standards and being autonomous and independent.8
8. The country team stated that a bill to establish a ministry of the family by merging the Ministry for Women, the Ministry for Children and Adolescents and the National Secretariat for Youth was being considered and that this initiative could have restricted the visibility of, and responses to, structural inequalities and different types of gender-based violence.9
9. The country team noted that improvements had been made to the National Institute of Indigenous Affairs. However, challenges remained, such as a lack of inter-agency coordination, a shortage of specific resources and a limited capacity to enforce compliance with consultation procedures.10
10. The Committee on Migrant Workers recommended that Paraguay strengthen its institutional structure for dealing with migration-related issues by creating mechanisms and engaging in capacity-building at the different entities coordinating work on those issues.11
11. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities recommended endowing the National Secretariat for the Human Rights of Persons with Disabilities with sufficient resources to allow it to fulfil its function effectively.12
IV. Promotion and protection of human rights
A. Implementation of international human rights obligations, taking into account applicable international humanitarian law
1. Equality and non-discrimination
12. The Special Rapporteur on minority issues was concerned about the persistent discrimination suffered by women, persons of African descent, Indigenous Peoples and persons with disabilities and about the high level of impunity regarding hate crimes against those groups.13 The same Special Rapporteur and the Committee on Migrant Workers were concerned that Paraguay still had not adopted a law against all forms of discrimination, despite the numerous international recommendations.14
13. The Special Rapporteur on minority issues, the Committee on Migrant Workers, the Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and the United Nations country team recommended that Paraguay promptly adopt a law against all forms of discrimination.15 The Committee on the Rights of the Child recommended putting in place laws and regulations to explicitly prohibit all forms of discrimination on the grounds of social origin, ethnicity, disability, sex, gender identity and sexual orientation.16
14. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities recommended that Paraguay establish accessible and effective procedures, including judicial, administrative and

2

GE.26-01460

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/2

complaints procedures, for victims of discrimination, and ensure that victims received reparation and perpetrators were punished.17
2. Right to life, liberty and security of person, and freedom from torture
15. The Committee on the Rights of the Child found that Paraguay was accountable for grave human rights violations concerning the killings of two 11-year-old girls during an operation conducted by the Joint Task Force of Paraguay against the Paraguayan People's Army, a guerrilla group. The Committee recommended that Paraguay take further steps to establish the truth, acknowledge the facts and accept responsibility for the failures in the investigation procedures, including considering the assistance of an international expert mission; strengthen its legal and regulatory framework regarding its law enforcement officials; and ensure that the police, law enforcement agents, armed forces and other agents acting on behalf of or with the consent or acquiescence of the State act with restraint and in conformity with international human rights law and international humanitarian law, including the principles of proportionality and necessity.18
16. The same Committee was concerned at cases of torture or ill-treatment of children in police stations and centres of deprivation of liberty. It recommended enforcing the prohibition of torture and ensuring that allegations of torture or ill-treatment or punishment of children were duly investigated, that perpetrators were punished and that children who were victims received effective remedies and psychosocial services.19
17. According to the United Nations country team, although initiatives had been undertaken to improve detention conditions and reduce overcrowding, the prison system continued to face a structural crisis. A total of 70% of the prison population was in pretrial detention, and overcrowding had reached 435% nationwide, with some facilities operating at more than 1,100% of their capacity. Conditions of extreme isolation had been documented in maximum security units. Women deprived of their liberty faced a simultaneous restriction of multiple rights, inhuman and degrading treatment and disproportionate penalties.20
18. The Committee on Migrant Workers was concerned about the lack of information on the number of migrants detained, the conditions under which the period of "administrative delay" during entry proceedings was imposed and the length of time that that period lasted. It urged Paraguay to ensure that detention of migrants was an exceptional measure of last resort, to adopt alternatives to administrative detention for migrant workers and members of their families during proceedings relating to their entry into or expulsion from the country, and to ensure adequate and decent conditions in places of restriction of liberty and, where applicable, the effective separation of migrant workers and members of their families from persons under criminal investigation.21
19. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities was concerned at the involuntary treatment to which persons with disabilities were subjected at the psychiatric hospital. It recommended explicitly prohibiting by law the use of isolation, mechanical restraints, forced medication, electroconvulsive therapy, confinement in individual cells and isolation rooms, and forced treatment in crisis situations; and establishing accessible complaint and investigation mechanisms so that persons with disabilities in institutions could report instances of ill-treatment, receive legal assistance and have an effective remedy.22
3. Administration of justice, including impunity, and the rule of law
20. According to the Special Rapporteur on hazardous substances and wastes, Paraguay faced several challenges in terms of access to justice. In particular, the country's judicial system was slow and inefficient, with most reports of human rights violations not being investigated. He recommended ensuring that people had effective access to mechanisms, resources and support to help them understand and use the judicial system, and addressing the inequalities and discrimination that hindered access to justice for some groups.23
21. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities recommended that Paraguay adopt the protocol on access to justice for persons with disabilities and ensure that it was strictly enforced. The Committee also recommended that Paraguay put in place ageand gender-sensitive procedural accommodation in all judicial proceedings to ensure that persons with disabilities could participate effectively, including as judges, legal advisers or

GE.26-01460

3

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/2
witnesses, in such proceedings, and that it make the necessary procedural changes at the provincial level to afford such accommodation.24
22. The Committee on the Rights of the Child recommended strengthening restorative mechanisms and non-custodial sanctions for the social insertion of adolescents in conflict with the law and actively promoting non-judicial measures.25
4. Fundamental freedoms and the right to participate in public life
23. The United Nations country team noted that attacks, reprisals and assaults against human rights defenders, particularly defenders of sexual and reproductive rights, continued to be carried out. It also noted that the majority of murders of journalists remained unpunished. It added that, although the Inter-American Court of Human Rights had issued a ruling ordering the establishment of a mechanism for protecting journalists and defenders, the bill presented for this purpose had not made any progress through the parliament since 2021.26 The country team recommended that the law establishing this mechanism be adopted.27 The Special Rapporteur on hazardous substances and wastes recommended adopting a programme for the protection of human rights defenders.28
24. UNESCO stated that, since 2006, when systematic monitoring had begun, its Observatory of Killed Journalists had recorded nine killings of journalists in Paraguay.29 UNESCO encouraged Paraguay to continue investigating unresolved cases of killed journalists.30
25. UNESCO recommended decriminalizing defamation and placing it within civil defamation legislation that was in accordance with international standards, 31 ensuring a transparency and accountability mechanism on the governance of digital platforms to ensure the upholding of human rights and mitigate the risks associated with the spread of harmful content online,32 and assessing the system of supervision of the broadcasting sector in order to ensure that that process was transparent and independent.33
5. Prohibition of all forms of slavery, including trafficking in persons
26. The Committee on Migrant Workers was concerned that Paraguay had not yet achieved satisfactory standards in its fight against trafficking in persons and that children, especially those living on the street in the tri-border area, continued to be subjected to exploitation in-country. The Committee recommended that Paraguay include specific provisions in the Criminal Code to penalize trafficking in persons and smuggling of migrants; ensure that all offences of trafficking in persons, in particular those related to sexual exploitation and those in which public officials were complicit, were effectively and impartially investigated, prosecuted and punished; and allocate sufficient resources for the provision of assistance to victims.34
27. The United Nations country team noted that Indigenous Peoples were particularly vulnerable to forced labour and debt bondage owing to the structural conditions of poverty and exclusion under which they lived.35
28. The Committee on the Rights of the Child recommended that Paraguay withdraw all children involved in the worst forms of child labour, especially in rural areas and in domestic labour, and ensure their reintegration into the education and social protection systems, and that it eliminate the practice of criadazgo (forced child servitude) and provide full protection to children who were victims.36 The Committee also recommended that Paraguay develop a national strategy to combat trafficking in persons.37
6. Right to work and to just and favourable conditions of work
29. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities was concerned about the limited implementation of the National Action Plan for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 2015-2030 regarding the creation of more jobs. 38 The Committee recommended that Paraguay develop and apply a constructive strategy to implement effectively pillar 13 of the National Action Plan and include affirmative measures and incentives that encouraged the employment of persons with disabilities in the public and private sectors, in urban, rural and remote areas.39

4

GE.26-01460

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/2

30. The Committee on Migrant Workers recommended that Paraguay provide resources and put in place procedures to break the vicious circle where, in order to work, migrants needed permanent residence documents, but in order to obtain those documents, they needed to have income from a job.40
31. The United Nations country team recommended ratifying the Violence and Harassment Convention, 2019 (No. 190) and the Violence and Harassment Recommendation, 2019 (No. 206) of the International Labour Organization (ILO) concerning violence and harassment in the workplace.41
7. Right to social security
32. The Committee on the Rights of the Child recommended that Paraguay increase budget allocations for social protection programmes affecting children and strengthen their effectiveness, in particular by improving multi-agency coordination in the identification and disbursement of grants, expanding coverage of the child grant programme to cover all groups of children in disadvantaged situations, and addressing barriers that prevented certain groups of children from acquiring access to social assistance.42
8. Right to an adequate standard of living
33. The Committee on the Rights of the Child was concerned about the large number of children living in poverty and the regional disparities in access to rights.43 It recommended that Paraguay strengthen measures to end child poverty and ensure the right of all children to an adequate standard of living, including their access to adequate housing, water and sanitation, paying particular attention to children living in rural areas and urban informal settlements.44
34. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities was concerned at the rate of poverty among Indigenous persons with disabilities. It recommended that Paraguay increase the budget allocated to social programmes, and the amounts provided, in order to achieve a real reduction in poverty among persons with disabilities, especially Indigenous persons with disabilities and persons with disabilities living in rural and remote areas.45
35. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities recommended ensuring that persons with disabilities had access to housing alternatives in their communities.46
9. Right to health
36. The United Nations country team noted that, despite the efforts made, challenges continued to surround the quality of healthcare, especially in rural areas and Indigenous communities. Food insecurity, poverty and exposure to violence had a serious impact on the well-being of Indigenous children, who also faced forced evictions, displacement and the pollution of their ancestral lands, directly affecting their health and access to basic services.47
37. The Committee on the Rights of the Child was also concerned about the quality of healthcare.48 It recommended increasing access to quality and culturally sensitive healthcare, particularly in rural areas and Indigenous communities, and improving vaccination coverage and providing accurate information about the importance of vaccines.49
38. The country team recommended strengthening health information systems with data disaggregated by gender, age, ethnicity, socioeconomic status and disability in order to inform evidence-based policies.50 The country team also recommended ensuring intercultural health services tailored to the needs of Indigenous Peoples, who should participate effectively in the design and implementation of such services.51
39. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities was concerned at the limited implementation of the National Sexual and Reproductive Health Plan 2019-2023 and the failure to adopt the bill on sexual, reproductive, maternal and perinatal health.52 The country team stated that the budget allocated to the sexual and reproductive health programme had been insufficient, undermining the sustainability of the progress made. 53 It also noted persistent challenges in guaranteeing sexual and reproductive rights, especially the rights of adolescents, Indigenous women, persons with disabilities and members of the LGTBIQ+ community.54 The country team recommended ensuring access to sexual and reproductive

GE.26-01460

5

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/2
health services, including abortion services in cases permitted by law, and implementing comprehensive measures to reduce the maternal mortality rate.55
40. The Committee on the Rights of the Child was concerned about the high number of adolescent pregnancies and about the prohibition by the Ministry of Education and Science on disseminating age-appropriate information on sexual and reproductive health in educational institutions.56 It recommended repealing resolution No. 933/2023 of the Ministry of Education and Sciences and adopting a comprehensive sexual and reproductive health policy for adolescents; ensuring that sexual and reproductive health and gender-related education was part of the mandatory school curriculum and was targeted at adolescents, with special attention paid to preventing early pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections; and decriminalizing abortion in all circumstances and ensuring access to safe, timely and quality abortion and post-abortion care services.57
41. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities was concerned about barriers encountered by persons with disabilities in obtaining health services, and the persistence of the medical model of disability in Act No. 7018/2022.58 It recommended ensuring that all persons with disabilities had access to high-quality gender-sensitive and culturally sensitive health services; decentralizing health services, and placing a special focus on the care of Indigenous persons with disabilities; adopting promptly the bill on sexual, reproductive, maternal and perinatal health; and aligning Act No. 7018/2022 on mental health, and the regulations thereto, with the human rights model of disability set out in the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.59
42. The Committee on Migrant Workers noted the 2015-2030 National Health Policy and programmes aimed at ensuring universal access to healthcare. 60 It recommended that Paraguay take specific steps to give all migrant workers and members of their families access to its healthcare system.61
10. Right to education
43. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities expressed concern at the lack of investment in the right to education of persons with disabilities.62 The Committee recommended increasing the budget, staffing and resources allocated to the Directorate General for Inclusive Education so that it could carry out its functions throughout the country. 63 The Committee also recommended that Paraguay redouble its efforts to end segregated special education, including through a national action plan on high-quality inclusive education that guaranteed access to mainstream schools for all students with disabilities, including in rural and remote areas,64 and that it ensure that schools were fully accessible and that augmentative and alternative modes and systems of communication were used.65
44. The same Committee was concerned that little progress had been made in the capacity-building and training of teachers working in schools located in Indigenous communities under Act No. 5136/13 on inclusive education.66
45. The Committee on the Rights of the Child recommended that Paraguay ensure that all children completed free, equitable and quality primary and secondary education leading to achieving effective learning outcomes, and that it develop gender-sensitive strategies for school retention and reintegration, in particular for adolescent mothers, pregnant girls and those in early unions.67
46. UNESCO recommended that Paraguay strengthen efforts to increase enrolment rates, especially at the pre-primary and secondary levels, which were both compulsory; and continue efforts to ensure gender equality in education.68
11. Cultural rights
47. The Special Rapporteur on minority issues noted that among the 19 Indigenous languages spoken in Paraguay, six of those languages were in danger of extinction. He recommended enacting new legislation to ensure equal and effective bilingualism in the use of the Spanish and Guaran� languages in State institutions, services and public media and in particular in official documents and laws, and respecting the linguistic rights of Indigenous

6

GE.26-01460

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/2
communities in order to fully implement the International Labour Organization (ILO) Indigenous and Tribal Peoples Convention, 1989 (No. 169) and better integrate it into judicial processes and the education system.69
48. The United Nations country team recommended ensuring the cultural rights of the entire population, including people of African descent, migrants, persons with disabilities and Indigenous Peoples, by promoting access to and equitable participation in culture, the protection of tangible and intangible cultural heritage, and cultural diversity through the development of a new national culture plan.70
12. Development, the environment, and business and human rights
49. According to the Special Rapporteur on hazardous substances and wastes, Paraguay had been taking steps in hazardous waste management. However, the country faced significant challenges. Rural communities and Indigenous Peoples faced an alarming level of exposure to toxic substances, particularly hazardous pesticides and most of the country's environmental laws were not observed.71 The Special Rapporteur recommended helping companies handling hazardous wastes to develop plans for the environmentally sound management and disposal of that waste; implementing emergency measures to stop the contamination of soils and the Pati�o aquifer with methyl tert-butyl ether; addressing the human rights abuses related to the use of pesticides, in a structural and decisive manner, including by implementing accessible educational and awareness-raising programmes, in Spanish and Guaran�, to inform pesticide users and communities of the dangers of pesticide misuse and of the necessary protective measures; and conducting health cohort studies and environmental pollution monitoring studies to identify and prevent the negative health effects of pesticides.72
B. Rights of specific persons or groups
1. Women
50. The United Nations country team noted that cases of femicide had been observed in Paraguay in previous years and, according to a national survey, the level of violence against women was very high.73 It recommended that a comprehensive system of prevention, support and redress be implemented to combat violence against women, girls, and adolescents.74
51. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities highlighted the insufficient measures taken to prevent and eliminate multiple discrimination and violence against women with disabilities, Indigenous women with disabilities and women with disabilities living in rural areas.75 It recommended that, with the effective participation of women and girls with disabilities, Paraguay mainstream a disability perspective in its laws and policies on gender equality and incorporate a gender perspective into its laws and policies on disability.76
52. The same Committee recommended that Paraguay adopt a national strategy to promote a gender- and age-sensitive human rights model of disability and effectively involve persons with disabilities in the development, implementation and regular evaluation of the strategy.77
53. Concerned at the persistence of early marriage, the Committee on the Rights of the Child and UNESCO recommended that Paraguay amend the legislation to ensure that the minimum age of marriage was 18 years, without exception.78
54. The country team stated that the economic and social crisis arising from the pandemic had disproportionately affected women, which showed that the persistence of gender norms restricted their full participation in the labour market and society.79 It added that only 36.8% of farms belonged to women, representing only 11.6% of the total area of agricultural land. Furthermore, according to the country team, women owned only 13.4% of plots of land with firm titles.80
55. The country team noted that women's representation in governance spaces remained limited.81

GE.26-01460

7

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/2
2. Children
56. The Committee on the Rights of the Child was concerned at the high rates of missing children, in particular girls and in the context of criadazgo. The Committee recommended that Paraguay take immediate and effective measures to prevent children going missing, addressing the root causes of this, including criadazgo, and that the country's National Police and Office of the Public Prosecutor follow up on cases of missing children.82
57. The same Committee was concerned at high rate of child sexual abuse, in particular of girls and Indigenous children, both online and in the context of tourism, and at the lack of a comprehensive system and strategy for preventing and combating child abuse and sexual violence and for protecting the children who were victims.83 It recommended extending, on the basis of an evaluation, the national plan to end violence against children, and the scope of the strategy for preventing and combating child abuse and sexual violence; and amending the Penal Code so as to clearly criminalize all acts of sexual violence, regardless of the sex and gender, against children, with penalties proportionate to the seriousness of the offences.84
58. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities was concerned about the persistent poverty among children with disabilities, particularly Indigenous children with disabilities and children with disabilities living in rural and remote areas.85
59. The Committee on the Rights of the Child recommended implementing targeted policies and programmes to eliminate discrimination against children, in particular children with disabilities, Indigenous children, children living with HIV/AIDS, children in street situations and lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or intersex children, and ensuring their equal access to health services, education and a decent standard of living.86
60. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities recommended that Paraguay reduce poverty among children with disabilities, paying particular attention to the situations of Indigenous children with disabilities and children with disabilities living in rural and remote areas, and reinforce the Abrazo Programme; and that it put in place, in close coordination with the institutions comprising the National System for the Comprehensive Protection and Advancement of Children and Adolescents, monitoring and oversight measures to ensure strict compliance with Act No. 5659/16 on the protection of children and adolescents against physical punishment in homes, schools and institutions in both urban and rural areas, and report on complaints and the follow-up given to them.87
3. Persons with disabilities
61. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities appreciated the National Action Plan for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 2015-2030 and related legislative measures.88
62. The same Committee noted the continuing difficulties that individuals faced in obtaining a disability certificate 89 and was concerned at the little progress made in implementing Act No. 4934/13 on accessibility.90 It recommended updating and extending the 2016-2018 Strategic Plan, and ensuring that municipalities harmonized their laws with Act No. 4934/13 and that the Basic Guide on Accessibility of the Physical Environment for Persons with Disabilities was applied.91
63. The same Committee recommended that Paraguay actively promote the participation of persons with disabilities, especially women with disabilities, in political parties, so that they may be put forward as candidates for elected office.92
64. The United Nations country team took note of the enactment of the Mental Health Act and its National Plan 2024-2030. However, it added that serious shortcomings persisted, including the use of prolonged institutionalization without consent.93
65. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities recommended that Paraguay ensure that all public information was accessible to persons with disabilities, and that it allocate sufficient funding for the development, promotion and use of accessible communication formats and alternative means of communication.94

8

GE.26-01460

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/2
4. Indigenous Peoples and minorities
66. The United Nations country team noted the persistent discrimination directed at Indigenous Peoples, which was reflected in the difficulties that they experienced in gaining equitable access to the rights to health, education, water and basic services such as electricity and sanitation. The country team noted the difficulties that Indigenous Peoples faced in fully exercising their cultural rights.95 It also stated that 66.2% of members of Indigenous Peoples lived in poverty while 34.4% lived in extreme poverty, these figures being three times the national average.96
67. While acknowledging some progress, the Special Rapporteur on minority issues expressed concerns at the fact that Indigenous Peoples were often victims of hate crimes, of hate speech and of direct discrimination in public services, including in hospitals and schools, and in access to basic services.97
68. The Special Rapporteur on minority issues stated that Indigenous Peoples' lands were not adequately protected, and noted an increase in forced evictions affecting Indigenous Peoples, together with a significant rise in protests, both peaceful and violent.98
69. According to the country team, forced evictions of Indigenous communities, the parcelling out of communal lands and the pollution of rivers particularly affected women and children. In addition, the housing conditions of the Indigenous population were poor.99 It recommended developing an inter-agency protocol for the prevention of forced evictions that would guarantee the protection of human rights, including those of the Indigenous Peoples, ensure their access to their ancestral lands and provide redress to those who have been evicted.100
70. According to the Special Rapporteur on minority issues, the Afrodescendent minority of Paraguay was often invisible and unacknowledged, and there was a lack of empowerment and self-recognition by Afrodescendent peoples themselves. He recommended including questions on Afrodescendent identity in all future national censuses, in consultation with the interested parties, including all Afrodescendent communities.101
71. The country team stated that the adoption of Act No. 6940, which established mechanisms to prevent and punish racism and discrimination against people of African descent, constituted partial progress and that its implementation was still pending.102
5. Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex persons
72. The Committee on the Rights of the Child was concerned at failure to implement the provisions banning "conversion therapy" in Act No. 7018/2022 on mental health. It recommended that Paraguay develop policies and allocate sufficient resources to promote the mental health of children, and eradicate "conversion therapies".103
73. The United Nations country team recommended repealing decision No. 29.664 of the Ministry of Education and Science, which prohibited the teaching of topics related to gender theory in schools.104
6. Migrants and refugees
74. The Special Rapporteur on minority issues noted that some migrants and refugees still faced obstacles and challenges in access to employment, education or other public services.105 The Committee on Migrant Workers recommended that Paraguay take effective measures, with deadlines, indicators, and monitoring and evaluation benchmarks, to implement the migration policy; and provide sufficient human, technical and financial resources for its implementation. 106 The same Committee also recommended establishing ordinary regularization mechanisms that were regulated by law, in accordance with the International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Their Families, and that applied to all migrants.107
75. The Committee on Migrant Workers was concerned at Emergency Act No. 6524/2020, which made migrants and refugees ineligible for the aid offered to workers in the informal sector.108

GE.26-01460

9

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/2
76. The same Committee recommended ensuring that, in practice, migrant workers and members of their families, including those in an irregular situation, were informed about migration procedures and the documents needed, about the possibility of applying for regularization even in the case of rejection, about their rights upon arrival and during transit and about the fact that they had access to remedies, complaint mechanisms and other forms of redress.109
77. The same Committee recommended collecting information on school enrolment rates for migrant children, including those in an irregular situation.110
78. The Special Rapporteur on minority issues recommended setting up a migrant and refugee assistance service, accessible online or by telephone, free of charge, in order to provide assistance and practical information to migrants and refugees.111
7. Stateless persons
79. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities was concerned about the 30 per cent underregistration rate for births. It recommended that Paraguay step up the activities of the "Right to an Identity" programme, including in rural and remote areas.112 The Committee on the Rights of the Child recommended ensuring comprehensive free-of-charge birth registration and the issuance of birth certificates for all children born in the territory of Paraguay, immediately after the birth, regardless of their or their parents' immigration status.113

9	Summary of stakeholders' submissions on Paraguay*
10	Report of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights
11	I. Background
12	1. The present report was prepared pursuant to Human Rights Council resolutions 5/1 and 16/21, taking into consideration the periodicity of the universal periodic review and the outcome of the previous review.1 It is a summary of 22 stakeholders' submissions2 for the universal periodic review, presented in a summarized manner owing to word-limit constraints. A separate section is provided for the contribution by the national human rights institution that is accredited in full compliance with the Paris Principles.
13	II. Information provided by the national human rights institution accredited in full compliance with the Paris Principles
14	2. In 2025, the Ombudsman's Office of Paraguay regained category A status from the Subcommittee on Accreditation of the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions.3 3. The Ombudsman's Office recommended ensuring that State agencies acted in accordance with the law and in the public interest,4 in accordance with Act No. 7445/2025 on Public Service and the Civil Service, under which the State was authorized to sue public servants who engaged in misconduct.5 4. The Ombudsman's Office recommended strengthening the mechanism for compensating victims of human rights violations during the dictatorship.6 5. The Ombudsman's Office expressed concern about Act No. 7363/64 on the Oversight, Transparency and Accountability of Non-profit Organizations as it imposed requirements and procedures that restricted the exercise of the right of association.7 It called for the Act to be brought into line with the principles of necessity and proportionality and with international human rights standards.8
15	* The present document is being issued without formal editing.
16	GE.26-02004 (E) 240226 250226
17	
18	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/3
19	
20	6. The Ombudsman's Office stated that a bill on the protection of journalists, media workers and human rights defenders9 was still pending and recommended prioritizing it, ensuring a participatory legislative process and allocating financial resources to it.10
21	7. The Ombudsman's Office recommended reforming the law on conscientious objection, ensuring that persons who opted for alternative civilian service would receive the same benefits as those who completed mandatory military service.11
22	8. The Ombudsman's Office reported that rates of total and extreme monetary poverty had fallen, although they remained very high in rural areas.12 It considered it essential to implement targeted public policies to reduce disparities between urban and rural areas, paying particular attention to Indigenous populations,13 and to step up investment in social inclusion and employment programmes, with a focus on young persons.14
23	9. The Ombudsman's Office pointed to the low public investment in health15 and the lack of access to treatments, supplies and medications, in connection with which lawsuits were continuously being brought.16 It recommended establishing effective public policies and adequate budgets 17 and bringing investment in public health into line with the recommendations of the World Health Organization (6% of gross domestic product).18
24	10. The Ombudsman's Office recommended effectively implementing the National Plan for Human Rights Education, ensuring that it was allocated the necessary budget.19
25	11. The Ombudsman's Office noted that regulatory progress had been made in respect of the environment and that there were challenges relating to agricultural expansion, illicit crops, deforestation in protected areas20 and artisanal gold mining that posed risks to human health and the environment.21 It recommended adopting the National Forest Restoration Plan, 22 strengthening the capacity of the Ministry of the Environment and Sustainable Development and the municipal governments,23 and managing socioenvironmental conflicts through dialogue and respect for human and environmental rights, with the participation of local governments and the Ombudsman's Office.24
26	12. The Ombudsman's Office referred to the persistent violations of Indigenous Peoples' 25 rights to land, drinking water and sanitation 26 and the delays and obstacles hindering the regularization, titling and restitution of lands.27 It recommended designing and implementing a national plan for the regularization of Indigenous territories with an allocated budget and sustainable inter-agency mechanisms.28 It also called for the strengthening of drinking water infrastructure and the adoption of sustainable solutions that would guarantee permanent and safe access to water in rural and Indigenous areas.29
27	
28	III. Information provided by other stakeholders
29	
30	A. Scope of international obligations30 and cooperation with human rights mechanisms
31	13. Amnesty International and Joint Submission 3 (JS3) noted the failure to ratify the Regional Agreement on Access to Information, Public Participation and Justice in Environmental Matters in Latin America and the Caribbean (Escaz� Agreement), in connection with which the Government of Paraguay had stated that it would move forward with a process of analysis, dialogue and exchange among stakeholders.31
32	14. Amnesty International drew attention to the non-ratification of the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights and the Ljubljana-The Hague Convention on International Cooperation in the Investigation and Prosecution of the Crime of Genocide, Crimes against Humanity, War Crimes and Other International Crimes.32 JS3 called for the ratification of the Inter-American Convention on Protecting the Human Rights of Older Persons,33 which has been pending since the previous universal periodic review, 34 during which a commitment was made to ratify it.
33	15. JS3 urged Paraguay to ratify the Inter-American Convention against Racism, Racial Discrimination and Related Forms of Intolerance and the Inter-American Convention against All Forms of Discrimination and Intolerance.35
34

39	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/3
40	16. Amnesty International and JS3 welcomed the visits of the Special Rapporteur on hazardous substances and wastes and the Special Rapporteur on minority issues in 2022.36 JS3 referred to the failure to provide the reparations ordered by the Human Rights Committee in a number of cases. JS3 urged Paraguay to strengthen its cooperation with all United Nations human rights mechanisms and to grant the reparations ordered by the treaty bodies.37
41	B. National human rights framework
42	17. JS5 reported some progress in the implementation of the National Human Rights Plan (PNDH) 2013-2017. Nevertheless, authorities had prepared the III Action Plan 2021-2023 without broad citizen participation and so far, there was no evidence of a comprehensive new national plan.38
43	18. Joint Submission 12 (JS12) recommended re-incorporating gender mainstreaming in the fourth National Equality Plan 2018-2024 and in all national policies.39
44	Institutional infrastructure and policy measures
45	19. JS3 referred to the lack of political independence of the Ombudsman's Office, which resulted from the lack of a regulated, merit-based selection process, the Office's lack of transparency and its vulnerability to political collusion. 40 Amnesty International recommended establishing a transparent and participatory procedure for electing the Ombudsman that would guarantee pluralism and independence and be based on a track record of defending human rights, in line with the Paris Principles.41 JS3 requested that Paraguay comply with the recommendations of the Subcommittee on Accreditation of the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions with a view to establishing a transparent, participatory selection process based on the verifiable merits of competence and a track record of defending human rights and pluralism.42 Joint Submission 11 (JS11) recommended strengthening the Ombudsman's Office and improving its capacity to respond to, and follow up on, cases.43
46	C. Promotion and protection of human rights
47	1. Implementation of international human rights obligations, taking into account applicable international humanitarian law
48	Equality and non-discrimination
49	20. A number of communications expressed concern about the lack of comprehensive laws against all forms of discrimination,44 which, according to the Red Paraguaya de Artistas LGBTQ+, leaves LGBTIQ+ persons in a situation of structural vulnerability to violence, exclusion and the denial of their fundamental rights, preventing access to protective mechanisms and redress for victims of violence and exclusion. 45 JS12 recommended adopting legislation prohibiting all forms of discrimination, including on the grounds of gender, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, race, ethnicity, disability and age.46
50	21. Amnesty International expressed regret about impunity for hate speech and the promotion of discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex persons. 47 Joint Submission 2 (JS2) recommended strengthening the implementation of inclusive public policies and awareness-raising campaigns at all levels of Government, ensuring equitable access to rights for Indigenous Peoples, persons with disabilities, people of African descent, LGBTQ+ persons and other excluded groups.48
51	
52	GE.26-02004
53	
54	3
55	
56	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/3
57	
58	Right to life, liberty and security of person, and freedom from torture
59	22. Joint Submission 6 (JS6) expressed alarm about the disappearance of persons, which heightened the risk of trafficking in persons. It stated that institutional responses were inadequate, as there were no effective search and location protocols, investigations were not conducted with due diligence and no risk analysis was undertaken, leaving families to conduct searches alone.49
60	Administration of justice, including impunity, and the rule of law
61	23. JS3 expressed concern about systematic impunity for crimes against humanity committed during the civil-military dictatorship of 1954-1989, with convictions being secured against only eight oppressors. It mentioned the defunding of, and lack of government support for, the programme to search for and identify disappeared persons, the delays and red tape surrounding reparation measures and the statute of limitations applicable to civil compensation proceedings, which excluded victims from the protections to which they were entitled. JS3 recommended investigating and prosecuting crimes against humanity; guaranteeing prompt, fair and effective access to comprehensive reparation for all victims and their families; and funding a programme to search for and locate persons who were disappeared during the dictatorship, ensuring the identification and return of disappeared persons' remains.50
62	24. JS3 noted that Paraguay had not taken measures to guarantee the independence and impartiality of the judiciary. 51 According to JS6, the judicial system was marked by procedural delays, a lack of human rights perspectives and discriminatory biases that perpetuated impunity.52 JS3 recommended guaranteeing the independence and impartiality of the judiciary by improving the transparency of judicial proceedings and accountability, restricting political influence over the appointment and dismissal of judges, and ensuring a balance of powers in selection and prosecution bodies.53
63	25. The National Mechanism for the Prevention of Torture of Paraguay expressed concern about the persistent abuse of pretrial detention; overcrowding; maximum security regimes that constitute torture; corruption and control of prisons by criminal groups; the lack of gender-sensitive policies; the failure to register the children of incarcerated women; the failure to change the budget assigned to the National Mechanism for the Prevention of Torture; and the failure to professionalize prison staff.54 It also highlighted prolonged periods of detention in inhumane conditions and cases of torture for which no charges were brought.55 It recommended reducing the use of pretrial detention, eliminating prolonged solitary confinement, and adopting a gender- and child-sensitive prison policy.56
64	26. JS11 noted that penalties were becoming harsher in the juvenile justice system and recommended vetoing bills that would lower the age of criminal responsibility and/or increase penalties for adolescents.57 The National Mechanism for the Prevention of Torture of Paraguay recommended strengthening the Restorative Justice Programme.58
65	Fundamental freedoms and the right to participate in public and political life
66	27. JS5 expressed concern about attacks and a growing hostile environment for civil society, particularly those working on environmental and land rights and anti-corruption and transparency. 59 A number of communications mentioned that, against a backdrop of shrinking civic space, Act No. 7363 (the Garrote Act), adopted in 2024, abusively restricted freedom of association with vague provisions and unclear penalties. 60 JS1 stressed that penalties for non-compliance were severe and disproportionate, and threatened non-profit organisations;61 compromising the privacy and security of their members.62 According to JS5, the civic space was obstructed.63 A number of communications recommended repealing Act No. 7363 and guaranteeing freedom of association in accordance with international human rights law.64
67	28. JS1 stated that despite supporting most previous recommendations on freedom of expression, implementation remained weak, with women journalists impacted the most.65 JS3 recorded 122 cases of violence directed at journalists by the authorities and criminal organizations and two journalists killed since the previous universal periodic review, bringing the number of journalists killed between 1991 and 2025 to 21.66 JS3 recommended
68	
69	4
70	
71	GE.26-02004
72	
73	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/3
74	investigating and punishing those responsible for murders, assaults and threats targeted at journalists, and forming a working group to investigate the murders of journalists in the exercise of their profession, as instructed by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights in the case of Santiago Leguizam�n v. Paraguay.67
75	29. JS3 expressed concern about the use of the criminal justice system to harass human rights defenders, noting that Paraguay was failing to comply with its commitments to stop criminalizing them and to investigate attacks.68 JS5 detailed harassment, intimidation and attacks against campesino leaders, Indigenous and environmental Human Rights defenders, and journalists, highlighting a pattern of state complicity and structural impunity.69 JS3 and JS1 recommended conducting independent, effective and impartial investigations into attacks against human rights defenders; adopting measures to prevent and bring an end to their criminalization; 70 refraining from using surveillance technologies against them; and establishing a protection mechanism that incorporates an intersectional gender perspective.71 Amnesty International regretted the lack of progress made towards adopting the bill to protect journalists and human rights defenders, despite the commitments made,72 and recommended that it be adopted.73
76	30. JS5 affirmed that the government supported one recommendation on freedom of peaceful assembly but had not implemented it.74 JS1 noted that during peaceful "Gen Z" demonstrations in September 2025 authorities used open-source intelligence systems and cyber-patrol tools to monitor participants without judicial authorisation, and demonstrations were violently suppressed.75 JS5 expressed concern that Law No. 1.066/1997 (March�dromo Law) proscribed time and place restrictions on demonstrations and the obligation to notify the police, granting authorities excessive discretion to restrict them.76 JS5 recommended repealing or amending Law No. 1.066/97, eliminating arbitrary restrictions; dropping charges against peaceful protesters; ensuring judicial recourse and effective remedy; ensuring protest observers monitor police conduct without fear; and updating existing human rights training for police and security forces according to the UN Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms.77
77	31. JS12 reported that women accounted for only 23.2% of members of Congress and recommended the adoption of the bill on democratic parity, in accordance with the Constitution.78
78	Right to privacy
79	32. Tecnolog�a, Educaci�n, Desarrollo, Investigaci�n y Comunicaci�n (TEDIC) referred to the lack of transparency of surveillance policies and practices, and that Paraguay had obtained tools to conduct surveillance without an appropriate legal framework. 79 The regulation of drones remained fragmented and weak.80 JS1 expressed concern at the lack of independent oversight mechanisms in the acquisition and use of mass surveillance technologies, raising serious privacy-related concerns.81
80	33. TEDIC recommended adopting an adequate regulatory framework in line with international principles and standards to guarantee the transparency and accountability in the acquisition of surveillance technology and regulate the use of surveillance technology by the State or other state authorised actors. This framework should protect people against potential abusers, by ensuring any surveillance measures respect the principles of necessity and proportionality; by guaranteeing independent judicial authorisation, appropriate reporting procedures and meaningful information regarding the scope and extent of the use of private surveillance technology; and by establishing independent oversight bodies to audit, investigate and prosecute abuse in the use of surveillance technologies.82
81	Prohibition of all forms of slavery, including trafficking in persons
82	34. European Centre for Law and Justice (ECLJ) reported that, according to the 2023 Global Slavery Index, an estimated 46,000 people lived in conditions of modern slavery in Paraguay, exploited for labor and sexual services83 via false promises.84 Joint Submission 11 (JS11) stated that Paraguay was among the countries with the highest number of victims of trafficking in persons, with alarming numbers of disappeared children and adolescents and a lack of systematic records, protocols and rapid response mechanisms.85 ECLJ stated that,
83	
84	GE.26-02004
85	
86	5
87	
88	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/3
89	although between 2019 and 2023 authorities had opened cases, the number of human trafficking cases that opened every year had decreased since 2019 86 due to corruption, impunity, lack of resources and inadequate victim support.87 Two communications noted that trafficking in persons and sexual and economic exploitation mainly affected women, girls, boys and adolescents belonging to vulnerable groups.88
90	35. Several submissions recommended that Paraguay weed out corruption, provide resources, open shelters, and offer help to victims,89 as well as strengthen inter-institutional coordination, comprehensive protection, training, and prevention measures.90
91	Right to work and to just and favourable conditions of work
92	36. Joint Submission 9 (JS9) reported that various forms of abuse and exploitation, including violence and sexual harassment, had been directed at Indigenous domestic workers by their employers,91 and recommended that labour inspections and reporting mechanisms be strengthened.92
93	Right to an adequate standard of living
94	37. According to JS3, Paraguay was marked by a high concentration of land ownership, low levels of public investment in the rural sector and the increasing criminalization of campesino activism. Campesinos had limited access to land, despite the regulations in force. A national commission for exploring mechanisms for recovering public agricultural land illegally awarded during the 1954-1989 dictatorship has not been established. JS3 recommended establishing mechanisms for recovering public land to ensure the right to adequate food for the rural population; implementing policies for land redistribution; ensuring the participation of campesinos in decisions relating to agricultural policy; and promoting food sovereignty.93
95	Right to health
96	38. JS3 emphasized that free public healthcare was not guaranteed and that public spending was insufficient to increase access to, and the quality of, services.94 JS11 regretted the low level of funding allocated to mental health.95 JS9 stated that Indigenous women and girls faced additional barriers to healthcare.96
97	39. Joint Submission 13 (JS13) referred to the criminalization of abortion in Paraguay, which is authorized only when a woman's life or health is at risk and is not governed by a clear protocol.97 In 2024, the Ministry of Health registered 4,691 abortions and, as of June 2025, 19 women had died. Under current legislation, women were forced to seek clandestine abortions. 98 Two communications recommended guaranteeing the right to terminate a pregnancy when the person's life and mental or physical health are at risk; decriminalizing abortion, at least in cases of rape or abuse;99 adopting a law on sexual and reproductive health that guarantees universal access to safe abortion;100 and offering humane, non-stigmatizing and confidential services.101
98	40. Center for Family and Human Rights (C-Fam) recommended to ensure adequate and affordable maternal health care, investing in infrastructure and ensuring pregnant women in remote areas have access to adequate antenatal care.102
99	41. JS13 noted that no significant progress had been made towards preventing early pregnancies and protecting the sexual and reproductive rights of women and girls.103 In 2024, the Ministry of Health recorded 350 births to girls aged between 10 and 14 years who were not given the option of terminating the pregnancy, 104 putting their lives, life plans and physical and mental health at risk.105 JS6 stated that the lack of comprehensive sexuality education undermined efforts to prevent sexual violence and forced pregnancy.106 JS2 noted that access to sexual and reproductive health services was limited and responses to sexual violence were ineffective.107 JS13 recommended budgeting for the National Sexual and Reproductive Health Plan 2024-2030 and the National Comprehensive Adolescent Health Plan;108 adopting measures to prevent sexual abuse, such as implementing comprehensive sexuality education109 and a comprehensive national plan for preventing and responding to sexual violence;110 ensuring the provision of comprehensive support with measures to prevent
100	
101	6
102	
103	GE.26-02004
104	
105	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/3
106	
107	revictimization; 111 establishing a single registry of cases of sexual violence; 112 and strengthening the training of judges and justice officials.113
108	Right to education
109	42. JS2 noted that school attendance rates had improved but dropout rates remained high among rural and low-income students as a result of poverty, the lack of infrastructure, poor quality education, violence and lack of vocational guidance.114 It also noted that there was a marked disparity between State and private schools.115 Two communications referred to the persistent educational gap and structural restrictions affecting access to education for Indigenous Peoples,116 disproportionately affecting Indigenous girls.117
110	43. JS2 considered that the implementation of the National Plan for Human Rights Education had been partial and uneven. Despite the legislative developments made, significant gaps remained that would require urgent measures to be taken in relation to infrastructure, teacher training, inclusive policies and educational reform.118 It recommended increasing investment in infrastructure and educational resources in rural areas and Indigenous communities in order to ensure appropriate conditions for access and retention, with a focus on inclusive and bilingual secondary and technical education; and implementing programmes to reduce school dropout rates and discrimination.119 Joint Submission 10 (JS10) mentioned the low quality of early childhood education.120
111	Development, the environment, and business and human rights
112	44. JS3 stated that Paraguay had taken insufficient action to tackle the challenges of climate change, particularly with regard to halting deforestation caused by the expansion of monoculture farming and the use of forest fires to expand agricultural land. JS3 recommended institutionally strengthening the agencies responsible for preventing deforestation and expanding their coverage to the entire territory.121
113	2. Rights of specific persons or groups
114	Women
115	45. According to Amnesty International, 78.5% of women experienced gender-based violence and, in 2024, an average of 103 people per day submitted reports of domestic violence.122 Despite the commitments made by Paraguay,123 legislative initiatives such as a bill to ban gender mainstreaming and another to eliminate the Ministry for Women involved a serious risk of regression.124 A number of communications recommended including in the national budget the resources necessary to implement Act No. 5777 on Comprehensive Protection for Women against All Forms of Violence;125 strengthening the fourth National Equality Plan;126 and strengthening the independence of the Ministry for Women127 and comprehensive care services for victims, particularly victims of sexual violence.128
116	46. A number of communications referred to cases of femicide,129 with the majority of victims being murdered by their current or former partners. 130 JS2 questioned the effectiveness of early warning systems.131 Two communications recommended including resources for the implementation of Act No. 6806132 and adopting a national protocol for the prevention of femicide to ensure swift inter-agency responses.133
117	47. Madres Aut�nomas Paraguay (Madresaut�nomaspy) stated that vicarious violence was a form of gender-based violence that involved sons and daughters being weaponized in order to cause pain to their mothers.134 It pointed out that, according to the Public Prosecution Service, there were 4,251 cases involving failure to comply with legal maintenance obligations in 2025, which constituted economic and institutional violence135 in a context of impunity, with a conviction rate of only 1%.136 Madresaut�nomaspy recommended that vicarious violence be recognized and that the misuse of the child court system be halted.137
118	48. JS4 highlighted violence against women in digital spaces. 138 Act No. 5777/16 recognized cyberviolence. 139 However, according to JS1, this legislation was limited in scope, leaving other forms of technology-facilitated gender-based harassment and abuse uncovered and creating legal and protection gaps. 140 A number of communications recommended developing regulatory frameworks on cybersecurity; recognizing online
119	
120	GE.26-02004
121	
122	7
123	
124	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/3
125	gender-based violence as a violation of human rights; amending article 6 of Act No. 5777/16 to include the various forms of online violence against women;141 preventing misuse of the Act to unjustifiably restrict journalistic work;142 and training justice officials to respond appropriately to digital violence.143
126	49. Unidas en la Esperanza explained that stigma and discrimination against sex workers facilitated violations of rights,144 including violations that harmed their physical integrity145 and resulted in arbitrary detention146 and the denial of access to justice.147 Unidas en la Esperanza recommended training law enforcement agents and justice officials and treating violence against women sex workers as gender-based violence.148
127	Children
128	50. JS2 expressed concern about discrimination, structural exclusion and the unequal progress made in improving the health situation of various groups of children, particularly in Indigenous and rural communities, where access to education, healthcare, drinking water and legal documentation is limited.149
129	51. JS11 noted that unpaid domestic child labour (criadazgo), which involved placing poor children and adolescents in other people's homes on the promise that they will receive food, housing and education, continued to be practised. 150 According to JS9, criadazgo particularly affected Indigenous girls, who performed domestic work without compensation and were exposed to abuse, receiving insufficient support and care from the State.151 JS6 argued that this practice exposed children and adolescents to multiple violations, exploitation, and sexual violence152 and that no policies have been adopted to tackle it.153 It also pointed out that the National Congress had rejected a bill aimed at protecting children against criadazgo on the grounds that it was part of Paraguayan culture. 154 A number of communications recommended prohibiting criadazgo in law, ensuring school retention and adopting a national strategy based on a preventive, comprehensive and systemic approach.155
130	52. JS11 expressed concern about the persistence of child unions and marriages, including those endorsed by the State, given that the law continued to allow marriage from the age of 16 years with the authorization of a court.156 JS9 highlighted the vulnerability of Indigenous adolescents to early marriage and pregnancy.157 JS12 recommended eliminating exceptions to the minimum age for marriage.158
131	Persons with disabilities
132	53. JS2 drew attention to the fact that Indigenous children and children with disabilities faced significant barriers and discrimination in gaining access to education and greater obstacles to remaining in the education system. 159 JS2 recommended strengthening the implementation of inclusive public policies and awareness-raising campaigns, ensuring equitable access. 160 JS12 recommended adopting legislation against all forms of discrimination, including on grounds of disability.161
133	54. JS12 referred to the clear difference between men with disabilities in employment and women with disabilities. It recommended implementing measures to reduce the wage and employment gap for women with disabilities and to promote their full inclusion in public and private employment.162
134	Indigenous Peoples
135	55. JS9 reported that Paraguay had made no progress in implementing the recommendations on Indigenous Peoples emanating from the third cycle. It expressed concern about poverty resulting from land dispossession and the requirement to have an identity card to gain access to social programmes intended to reduce poverty.163 It also referred to the precarious nature of Indigenous housing, which is subject to significant gaps in access to electricity, drinking water and sanitation services.164
136	56. Amnesty International reported that the National Plan for Indigenous Peoples 2020-2030 lacked adequate funding and that the National Institute of Indigenous Affairs165 had been weakened. According to JS9, the Indigenous Peoples had reported that there was a lack of political will and limited State financial capacity for the effective implementation of
137	
138	8
139	
140	GE.26-02004
141	
142	Notes
143	
144	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/3
145	the Plan. 166 Two communications recommended strengthening the Plan with sufficient funding167 and enhancing the operational and legal capacity of the National Institute of Indigenous Affairs.168
146	57. JS3 reported that little progress had been made towards the restitution of Indigenous territories.169 JS9 mentioned conceptual limitations in land restitution policies, under which areas of land were conceived as physical spaces rather than as territories essential for the exercise of self-determination by the Indigenous Peoples. 170 Two communications denounced the legal uncertainty faced by Indigenous communities in respect of their territories, the lack of land titles, the slow and fragmented administrative procedures, forced evictions, the lack of comprehensive public policies on access to drinking water, health and education in Indigenous territories171 and encroachments on these territories.172
147	58. Joint Submission 8 (JS8) stated that the protocol on consultation and free, prior and informed consent had structural shortcomings that hindered its effective implementation: the protocol lacked binding legal mechanisms or sanctions for non-compliance and failed to ensure substantive participation by Indigenous Peoples based on their own timelines, languages and organizational structures.173 JS9 expressed concern about projects carried out without free, prior and informed consent, causing the destruction of ecosystems, displacement and the fragmentation of the social fabric.174 JS8 recommended ensuring that consent procedures were binding and in compliance with the right of Indigenous Peoples to self-determination. 175 JS3 recommended strengthening land restitution mechanisms, guaranteeing Indigenous participation in the formulation of public policy and ensuring equitable access to essential resources in their territory.176
148	59. JS8 reported that sacred sites had been violated.177
149	60. JS9 expressed concern about the selective and unequal implementation of the ZavalaRiera Act, which increased penalties for encroaching on private property, affecting poor and rural communities and Indigenous Peoples. It recommended amending the Zavala-Riera Act and the national unified registry to prevent them from being used in a discriminatory manner and from having a regressive impact.178
150	Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex persons
151	61. REPAR+ stressed that the situation of the LGBTQ+ population in Paraguay remained marked by the absence of legislation, by institutional and social discrimination, and the rise of hate speech.179 Ultra-conservative political and religious sectors targeted the LGBTQ+ community as a threat to the family and national values resulting in increased violence against them, normalising harassment in public and private life and stigmatisation.180 REPAR+ stated that the lack of legal recognition of civil unions between same sex couples generated inability to access certain rights and benefits as well as indirect discrimination in housing policies.181
152	62. REPAR+ noted the absence of an administrative procedure for the legal recognition of self-perceived gender and the change of name under civil legislation being obstructed when requested by a trans person.182 It recommended to establish an agile, accessible and free administrative procedure for that purpose.183
