United Nations
General Assembly

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/3
Distr.: General 17 February 2026 English Original: English/Spanish

Human Rights Council
Working Group on the Universal Periodic Review Fifty-second session Geneva, 4-15 May 2026
Summary of stakeholders' submissions on Paraguay*
Report of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights
I. Background
1. The present report was prepared pursuant to Human Rights Council resolutions 5/1 and 16/21, taking into consideration the periodicity of the universal periodic review and the outcome of the previous review.1 It is a summary of 22 stakeholders' submissions2 for the universal periodic review, presented in a summarized manner owing to word-limit constraints. A separate section is provided for the contribution by the national human rights institution that is accredited in full compliance with the Paris Principles.
II. Information provided by the national human rights institution accredited in full compliance with the Paris Principles
2. In 2025, the Ombudsman's Office of Paraguay regained category A status from the Subcommittee on Accreditation of the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions.3 3. The Ombudsman's Office recommended ensuring that State agencies acted in accordance with the law and in the public interest,4 in accordance with Act No. 7445/2025 on Public Service and the Civil Service, under which the State was authorized to sue public servants who engaged in misconduct.5 4. The Ombudsman's Office recommended strengthening the mechanism for compensating victims of human rights violations during the dictatorship.6 5. The Ombudsman's Office expressed concern about Act No. 7363/64 on the Oversight, Transparency and Accountability of Non-profit Organizations as it imposed requirements and procedures that restricted the exercise of the right of association.7 It called for the Act to be brought into line with the principles of necessity and proportionality and with international human rights standards.8
* The present document is being issued without formal editing.
GE.26-02004 (E) 240226 250226

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/3

6. The Ombudsman's Office stated that a bill on the protection of journalists, media workers and human rights defenders9 was still pending and recommended prioritizing it, ensuring a participatory legislative process and allocating financial resources to it.10
7. The Ombudsman's Office recommended reforming the law on conscientious objection, ensuring that persons who opted for alternative civilian service would receive the same benefits as those who completed mandatory military service.11
8. The Ombudsman's Office reported that rates of total and extreme monetary poverty had fallen, although they remained very high in rural areas.12 It considered it essential to implement targeted public policies to reduce disparities between urban and rural areas, paying particular attention to Indigenous populations,13 and to step up investment in social inclusion and employment programmes, with a focus on young persons.14
9. The Ombudsman's Office pointed to the low public investment in health15 and the lack of access to treatments, supplies and medications, in connection with which lawsuits were continuously being brought.16 It recommended establishing effective public policies and adequate budgets 17 and bringing investment in public health into line with the recommendations of the World Health Organization (6% of gross domestic product).18
10. The Ombudsman's Office recommended effectively implementing the National Plan for Human Rights Education, ensuring that it was allocated the necessary budget.19
11. The Ombudsman's Office noted that regulatory progress had been made in respect of the environment and that there were challenges relating to agricultural expansion, illicit crops, deforestation in protected areas20 and artisanal gold mining that posed risks to human health and the environment.21 It recommended adopting the National Forest Restoration Plan, 22 strengthening the capacity of the Ministry of the Environment and Sustainable Development and the municipal governments,23 and managing socioenvironmental conflicts through dialogue and respect for human and environmental rights, with the participation of local governments and the Ombudsman's Office.24
12. The Ombudsman's Office referred to the persistent violations of Indigenous Peoples' 25 rights to land, drinking water and sanitation 26 and the delays and obstacles hindering the regularization, titling and restitution of lands.27 It recommended designing and implementing a national plan for the regularization of Indigenous territories with an allocated budget and sustainable inter-agency mechanisms.28 It also called for the strengthening of drinking water infrastructure and the adoption of sustainable solutions that would guarantee permanent and safe access to water in rural and Indigenous areas.29

III. Information provided by other stakeholders

A. Scope of international obligations30 and cooperation with human rights mechanisms
13. Amnesty International and Joint Submission 3 (JS3) noted the failure to ratify the Regional Agreement on Access to Information, Public Participation and Justice in Environmental Matters in Latin America and the Caribbean (Escaz� Agreement), in connection with which the Government of Paraguay had stated that it would move forward with a process of analysis, dialogue and exchange among stakeholders.31
14. Amnesty International drew attention to the non-ratification of the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights and the Ljubljana-The Hague Convention on International Cooperation in the Investigation and Prosecution of the Crime of Genocide, Crimes against Humanity, War Crimes and Other International Crimes.32 JS3 called for the ratification of the Inter-American Convention on Protecting the Human Rights of Older Persons,33 which has been pending since the previous universal periodic review, 34 during which a commitment was made to ratify it.
15. JS3 urged Paraguay to ratify the Inter-American Convention against Racism, Racial Discrimination and Related Forms of Intolerance and the Inter-American Convention against All Forms of Discrimination and Intolerance.35

2

GE.26-02004

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/3
16. Amnesty International and JS3 welcomed the visits of the Special Rapporteur on hazardous substances and wastes and the Special Rapporteur on minority issues in 2022.36 JS3 referred to the failure to provide the reparations ordered by the Human Rights Committee in a number of cases. JS3 urged Paraguay to strengthen its cooperation with all United Nations human rights mechanisms and to grant the reparations ordered by the treaty bodies.37
B. National human rights framework
17. JS5 reported some progress in the implementation of the National Human Rights Plan (PNDH) 2013-2017. Nevertheless, authorities had prepared the III Action Plan 2021-2023 without broad citizen participation and so far, there was no evidence of a comprehensive new national plan.38
18. Joint Submission 12 (JS12) recommended re-incorporating gender mainstreaming in the fourth National Equality Plan 2018-2024 and in all national policies.39
Institutional infrastructure and policy measures
19. JS3 referred to the lack of political independence of the Ombudsman's Office, which resulted from the lack of a regulated, merit-based selection process, the Office's lack of transparency and its vulnerability to political collusion. 40 Amnesty International recommended establishing a transparent and participatory procedure for electing the Ombudsman that would guarantee pluralism and independence and be based on a track record of defending human rights, in line with the Paris Principles.41 JS3 requested that Paraguay comply with the recommendations of the Subcommittee on Accreditation of the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions with a view to establishing a transparent, participatory selection process based on the verifiable merits of competence and a track record of defending human rights and pluralism.42 Joint Submission 11 (JS11) recommended strengthening the Ombudsman's Office and improving its capacity to respond to, and follow up on, cases.43
C. Promotion and protection of human rights
1. Implementation of international human rights obligations, taking into account applicable international humanitarian law
Equality and non-discrimination
20. A number of communications expressed concern about the lack of comprehensive laws against all forms of discrimination,44 which, according to the Red Paraguaya de Artistas LGBTQ+, leaves LGBTIQ+ persons in a situation of structural vulnerability to violence, exclusion and the denial of their fundamental rights, preventing access to protective mechanisms and redress for victims of violence and exclusion. 45 JS12 recommended adopting legislation prohibiting all forms of discrimination, including on the grounds of gender, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, race, ethnicity, disability and age.46
21. Amnesty International expressed regret about impunity for hate speech and the promotion of discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex persons. 47 Joint Submission 2 (JS2) recommended strengthening the implementation of inclusive public policies and awareness-raising campaigns at all levels of Government, ensuring equitable access to rights for Indigenous Peoples, persons with disabilities, people of African descent, LGBTQ+ persons and other excluded groups.48

GE.26-02004

3

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/3

Right to life, liberty and security of person, and freedom from torture
22. Joint Submission 6 (JS6) expressed alarm about the disappearance of persons, which heightened the risk of trafficking in persons. It stated that institutional responses were inadequate, as there were no effective search and location protocols, investigations were not conducted with due diligence and no risk analysis was undertaken, leaving families to conduct searches alone.49
Administration of justice, including impunity, and the rule of law
23. JS3 expressed concern about systematic impunity for crimes against humanity committed during the civil-military dictatorship of 1954-1989, with convictions being secured against only eight oppressors. It mentioned the defunding of, and lack of government support for, the programme to search for and identify disappeared persons, the delays and red tape surrounding reparation measures and the statute of limitations applicable to civil compensation proceedings, which excluded victims from the protections to which they were entitled. JS3 recommended investigating and prosecuting crimes against humanity; guaranteeing prompt, fair and effective access to comprehensive reparation for all victims and their families; and funding a programme to search for and locate persons who were disappeared during the dictatorship, ensuring the identification and return of disappeared persons' remains.50
24. JS3 noted that Paraguay had not taken measures to guarantee the independence and impartiality of the judiciary. 51 According to JS6, the judicial system was marked by procedural delays, a lack of human rights perspectives and discriminatory biases that perpetuated impunity.52 JS3 recommended guaranteeing the independence and impartiality of the judiciary by improving the transparency of judicial proceedings and accountability, restricting political influence over the appointment and dismissal of judges, and ensuring a balance of powers in selection and prosecution bodies.53
25. The National Mechanism for the Prevention of Torture of Paraguay expressed concern about the persistent abuse of pretrial detention; overcrowding; maximum security regimes that constitute torture; corruption and control of prisons by criminal groups; the lack of gender-sensitive policies; the failure to register the children of incarcerated women; the failure to change the budget assigned to the National Mechanism for the Prevention of Torture; and the failure to professionalize prison staff.54 It also highlighted prolonged periods of detention in inhumane conditions and cases of torture for which no charges were brought.55 It recommended reducing the use of pretrial detention, eliminating prolonged solitary confinement, and adopting a gender- and child-sensitive prison policy.56
26. JS11 noted that penalties were becoming harsher in the juvenile justice system and recommended vetoing bills that would lower the age of criminal responsibility and/or increase penalties for adolescents.57 The National Mechanism for the Prevention of Torture of Paraguay recommended strengthening the Restorative Justice Programme.58
Fundamental freedoms and the right to participate in public and political life
27. JS5 expressed concern about attacks and a growing hostile environment for civil society, particularly those working on environmental and land rights and anti-corruption and transparency. 59 A number of communications mentioned that, against a backdrop of shrinking civic space, Act No. 7363 (the Garrote Act), adopted in 2024, abusively restricted freedom of association with vague provisions and unclear penalties. 60 JS1 stressed that penalties for non-compliance were severe and disproportionate, and threatened non-profit organisations;61 compromising the privacy and security of their members.62 According to JS5, the civic space was obstructed.63 A number of communications recommended repealing Act No. 7363 and guaranteeing freedom of association in accordance with international human rights law.64
28. JS1 stated that despite supporting most previous recommendations on freedom of expression, implementation remained weak, with women journalists impacted the most.65 JS3 recorded 122 cases of violence directed at journalists by the authorities and criminal organizations and two journalists killed since the previous universal periodic review, bringing the number of journalists killed between 1991 and 2025 to 21.66 JS3 recommended

4

GE.26-02004

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/3
investigating and punishing those responsible for murders, assaults and threats targeted at journalists, and forming a working group to investigate the murders of journalists in the exercise of their profession, as instructed by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights in the case of Santiago Leguizam�n v. Paraguay.67
29. JS3 expressed concern about the use of the criminal justice system to harass human rights defenders, noting that Paraguay was failing to comply with its commitments to stop criminalizing them and to investigate attacks.68 JS5 detailed harassment, intimidation and attacks against campesino leaders, Indigenous and environmental Human Rights defenders, and journalists, highlighting a pattern of state complicity and structural impunity.69 JS3 and JS1 recommended conducting independent, effective and impartial investigations into attacks against human rights defenders; adopting measures to prevent and bring an end to their criminalization; 70 refraining from using surveillance technologies against them; and establishing a protection mechanism that incorporates an intersectional gender perspective.71 Amnesty International regretted the lack of progress made towards adopting the bill to protect journalists and human rights defenders, despite the commitments made,72 and recommended that it be adopted.73
30. JS5 affirmed that the government supported one recommendation on freedom of peaceful assembly but had not implemented it.74 JS1 noted that during peaceful "Gen Z" demonstrations in September 2025 authorities used open-source intelligence systems and cyber-patrol tools to monitor participants without judicial authorisation, and demonstrations were violently suppressed.75 JS5 expressed concern that Law No. 1.066/1997 (March�dromo Law) proscribed time and place restrictions on demonstrations and the obligation to notify the police, granting authorities excessive discretion to restrict them.76 JS5 recommended repealing or amending Law No. 1.066/97, eliminating arbitrary restrictions; dropping charges against peaceful protesters; ensuring judicial recourse and effective remedy; ensuring protest observers monitor police conduct without fear; and updating existing human rights training for police and security forces according to the UN Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms.77
31. JS12 reported that women accounted for only 23.2% of members of Congress and recommended the adoption of the bill on democratic parity, in accordance with the Constitution.78
Right to privacy
32. Tecnolog�a, Educaci�n, Desarrollo, Investigaci�n y Comunicaci�n (TEDIC) referred to the lack of transparency of surveillance policies and practices, and that Paraguay had obtained tools to conduct surveillance without an appropriate legal framework. 79 The regulation of drones remained fragmented and weak.80 JS1 expressed concern at the lack of independent oversight mechanisms in the acquisition and use of mass surveillance technologies, raising serious privacy-related concerns.81
33. TEDIC recommended adopting an adequate regulatory framework in line with international principles and standards to guarantee the transparency and accountability in the acquisition of surveillance technology and regulate the use of surveillance technology by the State or other state authorised actors. This framework should protect people against potential abusers, by ensuring any surveillance measures respect the principles of necessity and proportionality; by guaranteeing independent judicial authorisation, appropriate reporting procedures and meaningful information regarding the scope and extent of the use of private surveillance technology; and by establishing independent oversight bodies to audit, investigate and prosecute abuse in the use of surveillance technologies.82
Prohibition of all forms of slavery, including trafficking in persons
34. European Centre for Law and Justice (ECLJ) reported that, according to the 2023 Global Slavery Index, an estimated 46,000 people lived in conditions of modern slavery in Paraguay, exploited for labor and sexual services83 via false promises.84 Joint Submission 11 (JS11) stated that Paraguay was among the countries with the highest number of victims of trafficking in persons, with alarming numbers of disappeared children and adolescents and a lack of systematic records, protocols and rapid response mechanisms.85 ECLJ stated that,

GE.26-02004

5

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/3
although between 2019 and 2023 authorities had opened cases, the number of human trafficking cases that opened every year had decreased since 2019 86 due to corruption, impunity, lack of resources and inadequate victim support.87 Two communications noted that trafficking in persons and sexual and economic exploitation mainly affected women, girls, boys and adolescents belonging to vulnerable groups.88
35. Several submissions recommended that Paraguay weed out corruption, provide resources, open shelters, and offer help to victims,89 as well as strengthen inter-institutional coordination, comprehensive protection, training, and prevention measures.90
Right to work and to just and favourable conditions of work
36. Joint Submission 9 (JS9) reported that various forms of abuse and exploitation, including violence and sexual harassment, had been directed at Indigenous domestic workers by their employers,91 and recommended that labour inspections and reporting mechanisms be strengthened.92
Right to an adequate standard of living
37. According to JS3, Paraguay was marked by a high concentration of land ownership, low levels of public investment in the rural sector and the increasing criminalization of campesino activism. Campesinos had limited access to land, despite the regulations in force. A national commission for exploring mechanisms for recovering public agricultural land illegally awarded during the 1954-1989 dictatorship has not been established. JS3 recommended establishing mechanisms for recovering public land to ensure the right to adequate food for the rural population; implementing policies for land redistribution; ensuring the participation of campesinos in decisions relating to agricultural policy; and promoting food sovereignty.93
Right to health
38. JS3 emphasized that free public healthcare was not guaranteed and that public spending was insufficient to increase access to, and the quality of, services.94 JS11 regretted the low level of funding allocated to mental health.95 JS9 stated that Indigenous women and girls faced additional barriers to healthcare.96
39. Joint Submission 13 (JS13) referred to the criminalization of abortion in Paraguay, which is authorized only when a woman's life or health is at risk and is not governed by a clear protocol.97 In 2024, the Ministry of Health registered 4,691 abortions and, as of June 2025, 19 women had died. Under current legislation, women were forced to seek clandestine abortions. 98 Two communications recommended guaranteeing the right to terminate a pregnancy when the person's life and mental or physical health are at risk; decriminalizing abortion, at least in cases of rape or abuse;99 adopting a law on sexual and reproductive health that guarantees universal access to safe abortion;100 and offering humane, non-stigmatizing and confidential services.101
40. Center for Family and Human Rights (C-Fam) recommended to ensure adequate and affordable maternal health care, investing in infrastructure and ensuring pregnant women in remote areas have access to adequate antenatal care.102
41. JS13 noted that no significant progress had been made towards preventing early pregnancies and protecting the sexual and reproductive rights of women and girls.103 In 2024, the Ministry of Health recorded 350 births to girls aged between 10 and 14 years who were not given the option of terminating the pregnancy, 104 putting their lives, life plans and physical and mental health at risk.105 JS6 stated that the lack of comprehensive sexuality education undermined efforts to prevent sexual violence and forced pregnancy.106 JS2 noted that access to sexual and reproductive health services was limited and responses to sexual violence were ineffective.107 JS13 recommended budgeting for the National Sexual and Reproductive Health Plan 2024-2030 and the National Comprehensive Adolescent Health Plan;108 adopting measures to prevent sexual abuse, such as implementing comprehensive sexuality education109 and a comprehensive national plan for preventing and responding to sexual violence;110 ensuring the provision of comprehensive support with measures to prevent

6

GE.26-02004

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/3

revictimization; 111 establishing a single registry of cases of sexual violence; 112 and strengthening the training of judges and justice officials.113
Right to education
42. JS2 noted that school attendance rates had improved but dropout rates remained high among rural and low-income students as a result of poverty, the lack of infrastructure, poor quality education, violence and lack of vocational guidance.114 It also noted that there was a marked disparity between State and private schools.115 Two communications referred to the persistent educational gap and structural restrictions affecting access to education for Indigenous Peoples,116 disproportionately affecting Indigenous girls.117
43. JS2 considered that the implementation of the National Plan for Human Rights Education had been partial and uneven. Despite the legislative developments made, significant gaps remained that would require urgent measures to be taken in relation to infrastructure, teacher training, inclusive policies and educational reform.118 It recommended increasing investment in infrastructure and educational resources in rural areas and Indigenous communities in order to ensure appropriate conditions for access and retention, with a focus on inclusive and bilingual secondary and technical education; and implementing programmes to reduce school dropout rates and discrimination.119 Joint Submission 10 (JS10) mentioned the low quality of early childhood education.120
Development, the environment, and business and human rights
44. JS3 stated that Paraguay had taken insufficient action to tackle the challenges of climate change, particularly with regard to halting deforestation caused by the expansion of monoculture farming and the use of forest fires to expand agricultural land. JS3 recommended institutionally strengthening the agencies responsible for preventing deforestation and expanding their coverage to the entire territory.121
2. Rights of specific persons or groups
Women
45. According to Amnesty International, 78.5% of women experienced gender-based violence and, in 2024, an average of 103 people per day submitted reports of domestic violence.122 Despite the commitments made by Paraguay,123 legislative initiatives such as a bill to ban gender mainstreaming and another to eliminate the Ministry for Women involved a serious risk of regression.124 A number of communications recommended including in the national budget the resources necessary to implement Act No. 5777 on Comprehensive Protection for Women against All Forms of Violence;125 strengthening the fourth National Equality Plan;126 and strengthening the independence of the Ministry for Women127 and comprehensive care services for victims, particularly victims of sexual violence.128
46. A number of communications referred to cases of femicide,129 with the majority of victims being murdered by their current or former partners. 130 JS2 questioned the effectiveness of early warning systems.131 Two communications recommended including resources for the implementation of Act No. 6806132 and adopting a national protocol for the prevention of femicide to ensure swift inter-agency responses.133
47. Madres Aut�nomas Paraguay (Madresaut�nomaspy) stated that vicarious violence was a form of gender-based violence that involved sons and daughters being weaponized in order to cause pain to their mothers.134 It pointed out that, according to the Public Prosecution Service, there were 4,251 cases involving failure to comply with legal maintenance obligations in 2025, which constituted economic and institutional violence135 in a context of impunity, with a conviction rate of only 1%.136 Madresaut�nomaspy recommended that vicarious violence be recognized and that the misuse of the child court system be halted.137
48. JS4 highlighted violence against women in digital spaces. 138 Act No. 5777/16 recognized cyberviolence. 139 However, according to JS1, this legislation was limited in scope, leaving other forms of technology-facilitated gender-based harassment and abuse uncovered and creating legal and protection gaps. 140 A number of communications recommended developing regulatory frameworks on cybersecurity; recognizing online

GE.26-02004

7

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/3
gender-based violence as a violation of human rights; amending article 6 of Act No. 5777/16 to include the various forms of online violence against women;141 preventing misuse of the Act to unjustifiably restrict journalistic work;142 and training justice officials to respond appropriately to digital violence.143
49. Unidas en la Esperanza explained that stigma and discrimination against sex workers facilitated violations of rights,144 including violations that harmed their physical integrity145 and resulted in arbitrary detention146 and the denial of access to justice.147 Unidas en la Esperanza recommended training law enforcement agents and justice officials and treating violence against women sex workers as gender-based violence.148
Children
50. JS2 expressed concern about discrimination, structural exclusion and the unequal progress made in improving the health situation of various groups of children, particularly in Indigenous and rural communities, where access to education, healthcare, drinking water and legal documentation is limited.149
51. JS11 noted that unpaid domestic child labour (criadazgo), which involved placing poor children and adolescents in other people's homes on the promise that they will receive food, housing and education, continued to be practised. 150 According to JS9, criadazgo particularly affected Indigenous girls, who performed domestic work without compensation and were exposed to abuse, receiving insufficient support and care from the State.151 JS6 argued that this practice exposed children and adolescents to multiple violations, exploitation, and sexual violence152 and that no policies have been adopted to tackle it.153 It also pointed out that the National Congress had rejected a bill aimed at protecting children against criadazgo on the grounds that it was part of Paraguayan culture. 154 A number of communications recommended prohibiting criadazgo in law, ensuring school retention and adopting a national strategy based on a preventive, comprehensive and systemic approach.155
52. JS11 expressed concern about the persistence of child unions and marriages, including those endorsed by the State, given that the law continued to allow marriage from the age of 16 years with the authorization of a court.156 JS9 highlighted the vulnerability of Indigenous adolescents to early marriage and pregnancy.157 JS12 recommended eliminating exceptions to the minimum age for marriage.158
Persons with disabilities
53. JS2 drew attention to the fact that Indigenous children and children with disabilities faced significant barriers and discrimination in gaining access to education and greater obstacles to remaining in the education system. 159 JS2 recommended strengthening the implementation of inclusive public policies and awareness-raising campaigns, ensuring equitable access. 160 JS12 recommended adopting legislation against all forms of discrimination, including on grounds of disability.161
54. JS12 referred to the clear difference between men with disabilities in employment and women with disabilities. It recommended implementing measures to reduce the wage and employment gap for women with disabilities and to promote their full inclusion in public and private employment.162
Indigenous Peoples
55. JS9 reported that Paraguay had made no progress in implementing the recommendations on Indigenous Peoples emanating from the third cycle. It expressed concern about poverty resulting from land dispossession and the requirement to have an identity card to gain access to social programmes intended to reduce poverty.163 It also referred to the precarious nature of Indigenous housing, which is subject to significant gaps in access to electricity, drinking water and sanitation services.164
56. Amnesty International reported that the National Plan for Indigenous Peoples 2020-2030 lacked adequate funding and that the National Institute of Indigenous Affairs165 had been weakened. According to JS9, the Indigenous Peoples had reported that there was a lack of political will and limited State financial capacity for the effective implementation of

8

GE.26-02004

Notes

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/3
the Plan. 166 Two communications recommended strengthening the Plan with sufficient funding167 and enhancing the operational and legal capacity of the National Institute of Indigenous Affairs.168
57. JS3 reported that little progress had been made towards the restitution of Indigenous territories.169 JS9 mentioned conceptual limitations in land restitution policies, under which areas of land were conceived as physical spaces rather than as territories essential for the exercise of self-determination by the Indigenous Peoples. 170 Two communications denounced the legal uncertainty faced by Indigenous communities in respect of their territories, the lack of land titles, the slow and fragmented administrative procedures, forced evictions, the lack of comprehensive public policies on access to drinking water, health and education in Indigenous territories171 and encroachments on these territories.172
58. Joint Submission 8 (JS8) stated that the protocol on consultation and free, prior and informed consent had structural shortcomings that hindered its effective implementation: the protocol lacked binding legal mechanisms or sanctions for non-compliance and failed to ensure substantive participation by Indigenous Peoples based on their own timelines, languages and organizational structures.173 JS9 expressed concern about projects carried out without free, prior and informed consent, causing the destruction of ecosystems, displacement and the fragmentation of the social fabric.174 JS8 recommended ensuring that consent procedures were binding and in compliance with the right of Indigenous Peoples to self-determination. 175 JS3 recommended strengthening land restitution mechanisms, guaranteeing Indigenous participation in the formulation of public policy and ensuring equitable access to essential resources in their territory.176
59. JS8 reported that sacred sites had been violated.177
60. JS9 expressed concern about the selective and unequal implementation of the ZavalaRiera Act, which increased penalties for encroaching on private property, affecting poor and rural communities and Indigenous Peoples. It recommended amending the Zavala-Riera Act and the national unified registry to prevent them from being used in a discriminatory manner and from having a regressive impact.178
Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex persons
61. REPAR+ stressed that the situation of the LGBTQ+ population in Paraguay remained marked by the absence of legislation, by institutional and social discrimination, and the rise of hate speech.179 Ultra-conservative political and religious sectors targeted the LGBTQ+ community as a threat to the family and national values resulting in increased violence against them, normalising harassment in public and private life and stigmatisation.180 REPAR+ stated that the lack of legal recognition of civil unions between same sex couples generated inability to access certain rights and benefits as well as indirect discrimination in housing policies.181
62. REPAR+ noted the absence of an administrative procedure for the legal recognition of self-perceived gender and the change of name under civil legislation being obstructed when requested by a trans person.182 It recommended to establish an agile, accessible and free administrative procedure for that purpose.183

9	National report submitted pursuant to Human Rights Council resolutions 5/1 and 16/21*
10	Paraguay
11	
12	* The present document is being issued without formal editing. GE.26-02845 (E) 110326 110326
13	
14	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/1
15	Introduction
16	1. The Republic of Paraguay presents its national report on the implementation of the recommendations received in 2021 during the third cycle of the universal periodic review. On that occasion, Paraguay accepted 202 of the 210 recommendations received.
17	2. This report brings together information on the efforts made, measures taken, progress and achievements realised, and pending challenges and obstacles, based on information provided by representatives of around 66 State agencies and entities of the three branches of government (executive, legislative and judicial) and the autonomous government bodies that make up the network of focal points operating under the Recommendations Monitoring System (SIMORE Plus), the national mechanism for implementation, reporting and follow-up, coordinated by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Justice.
18	3. For ease of reference, a list of initialisms, acronyms and abbreviations is included in Annex I.
19	Follow-up to recommendations
20	Ratification of international instruments1
21	4. Paraguay has ratified most of the universal human rights instruments, demonstrating an ongoing willingness to cooperate with international mechanisms.
22	5. In this regard, it considers that the potential ratification of new instruments should result from an internal process of analysis involving the various stakeholders and relevant sectors. This approach enriches discussions of social, political and economic factors and ensures that any parliamentary decision is made on the basis of an objective assessment and is in line with national capacities, needs and priorities. Therefore, the question of whether to incorporate new international commitments into domestic law is determined by the sovereign decisions that each State adopts in accordance with its situation and possibilities, and is subject to the conclusions that arise from the aforementioned internal deliberation process.
23	6. In this connection, Paraguay ratified the Convention against Discrimination in Education in 2025. In December 2025, it approved accession to the Inter-American Convention on Protecting the Human Rights of Older Persons.
24	7. With regard to the Inter-American Convention against Racism, Racial Discrimination and Related Forms of Intolerance, Paraguay notes that it is a State Party to the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination and considers that the obligations and guarantees provided for in this treaty already encompass the rights established in the inter-American instrument.
25	8. It also points out that it has assumed a solid framework of international commitments relating to economic, social and cultural rights, particularly through the American Convention on Human Rights and the mechanisms of the inter-American system. In this regard, the possible ratification of the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights continues to be the subject of internal analysis, taking into account the need to avoid overlap and ensure adequate coordination between the universal and regional systems.

In addition, it implemented a preferential interest rate of financing of 0% for women and 4% for men for the purchase of plots of land, along with a protocol for preventing and responding to property-related violence. These measures led to an increase in women's participation: from 35% to 46% in respect of land allocation; from 34% to 48% in respect of land titling; and from 54% to 58% in access to rural housing.
205	108. The Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock promotes the equitable participation of women in agricultural development, guaranteeing their access to land, credit, training and technical assistance. In 2024, women accounted for 53% of registered producers and 45% of recipients of technical assistance.
206	109. Vocational training activities have been carried out, with a significant level of participation by women, including rural and Indigenous women, contributing to capacity-building and integration into the labour market in traditional and non-traditional sectors. Between 2018 and 2023, 54,196 women were trained, including 497 Indigenous women.
207	
208	12
209	
210	GE.26-02845
211	
212	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/1
213	110. For the first time since 2024, the Centre for Military Instruction and the Training of Reserve Officers opened enrolment to women, enabling more than 1,000 women to be trained. A total of 62% of participants in the call for applications in 2026 are women.
214	111. Procedures for reporting, preventing and investigating sexual harassment in the workplace have been established, including the mandatory establishment of internal protocols in private companies, with more than 1,000 internal regulations having been approved. State institutions have specific protocols for addressing, preventing and dealing with cases of workplace violence.
215	112. Mention should be made of the "Women Leaders" mentoring programme run by the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Finance, the purpose of which is to strengthen women's leadership in the civil service.
216	113. The State has stepped up its efforts to prevent and combat violence against women and girls by taking measures under Act No. 5777/2016 on the Comprehensive Protection of Women from All Forms of Violence, supplemented by Act No. 7239/2024, declaring a social emergency in respect of violence against women, children and adolescents and strengthening strategies for promoting change in the sociocultural patterns of conduct that perpetuate inequality between men and women.
217	114. In 2024, Paraguay launched a comprehensive strategy for family protection, the purpose of which is to prevent domestic violence and reduce the rate of femicide.
218	115. The Inter-institutional Working Group for the Prevention of Violence against Women, which is made up of public institutions and civil society organizations, has the primary function of advising the lead agency and recommending appropriate strategies and measures to tackle violence. In 2024, six departmental committees and four district committees were established to tackle violence against women, strengthening local coordination.
219	116. In 2023, the Protocol for Inter-Agency Action on Femicide and High-Risk Violence was updated. In addition, high-impact national campaigns, such as "Zero Violence", "Emergency!", "Stop Femicide!", "Let's Tell It Like It Is", "Dating without Violence", "Let's Talk in Time" and "Face Mask 37", were promoted to raise awareness, promote early prevention and transform sociocultural patterns of conduct.
220	117. In addition, courses are being implemented to strengthen detection, response and referral capacities. In that connection, the Ministry of Women coordinates training and technical activities at the Tape Jojar� Higher Technical Institute for Training in Gender Equality. Under Act No. 7239/2024, the Ministry of Women and the National Civil Service Institute have promoted the implementation of mandatory training courses on equal rights, non-discrimination and violence against women and children for civil servants of all ranks throughout the country. At the time of writing, there are 65,193 certified officials.
221	118. Attention should also be drawn to the initiative "Opening Paths: Towards a Response to Violence against Indigenous Women", the purpose of which is to organize training courses and train trainers to strengthen the response to cases of violence against Indigenous women.
222	119. In 2025, a protocol on the intercultural perspective in addressing and dealing with cases of violence against Indigenous women was developed along with a training manual for public officials on responding to violence against Indigenous women.
223	120. The Public Prosecution Service has 11 units that specialize in combating domestic violence and are authorized to respond to cases of gender-based violence in the capital and the departments of Alto Paran� and Guair�. In the rest of the country, ordinary crime units are in operation. These units also conduct their investigations on the basis of institutional instruments such as the Protocol for the Criminal Investigation of Femicide, which adopts the Latin American Model Protocol for the Investigation of Gender-related Killings of Women.
224	121. The Public Defence Service strengthens access to justice by employing public defenders who specialize in cases of physical, psychological and domestic violence, offences against dignity, and femicide. A protocol on specialized responses, which includes amendments relating to the rights of Indigenous women, has been approved and updated.
225	
226	GE.26-02845
227	
228	13
229	
230	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/1
231	122. Access to justice is promoted under the National Courthouse Programme, which provides guidance, referrals and services at the community level, and through the provision of training for officials involved in the care and investigation pathway.
232	123. Paraguay has consolidated a comprehensive model for the support and protection of women in situations of violence. At the local level, progress is being made in establishing and consolidating regional centres and shelters. Mention should also be made of the presentation and progressive implementation of the coordinated model for the protection and comprehensive care of women at the local level, which is designed to ensure swift, effective and specialized responses to restore rights and provide comprehensive reparation. Currently, the first model in Alto Paran� is at an advanced stage of implementation.
233	124. The Women's Support Service provides comprehensive assistance, delivering more than 25,500 comprehensive services in 2025. The capacities of the Service have been strengthened two-fold through the recruitment of new professionals.
234	125. The toll-free "SOS Mujer" hotline (137) has nationwide coverage and operates around the clock. The hotline received more than 4,000 calls reporting violence in 2025 and provided more than 10,500 services. A customer service channel on WhatsApp was launched in 2026.
235	126. The Women's City Centre operates as a comprehensive centre with five modules (registration and initial care; the prevention of violence and responses to it; economic empowerment; comprehensive health; and early childhood). This model is expanded through the "Mobile Women's City" programme, which brings services to rural areas with the support of the Office of the First Lady: 74 districts were visited and almost 20,000 women and their families were reached. The inclusive nature of the campaign was ensured by the National Secretariat for the Human Rights of Persons with Disabilities, which supported workshops by providing more than 8,747 services.
236	127. The National Plan for the Prevention of Gender-based Violence and Care for Victims within the National Health System 2020-2025 sets out priorities and measures for responding to domestic violence, sexual violence and other forms of violence against women, children and adolescents, including trafficking in persons, forced labour and child labour. In addition, a handbook on comprehensive care for victims of domestic, sexual or gender-based violence sets out technical guidelines and protocols for comprehensive care.
237	128. Attention should be drawn to the launch of a monitoring system that uses electronic devices in the form of electronic ankle bracelets. This tool is made available by court order for prosecuted or convicted persons with the aim of reducing domestic violence and femicide and helping to reduce prison overcrowding. The State has invested approximately $3 million in contracting the service. The Ministry of the Interior has approved a manual on police conduct and coordination for a comprehensive response to domestic violence that sets out specific provisions for responding to cases involving women and girls from Indigenous communities.
238	129. In order to strengthen information and data systems, the Ministry of Women, in coordination with the Ministry of Information and Communications Technology, has developed a computer system for reporting violence against women. The system, which is currently being implemented, will enable inter-agency coordination, real-time monitoring of cases and a more timely response within the State protection system, contributing to the traceability of actions and preventing revictimization.
239	130. The National Institute of Statistics, in conjunction with other State agencies and entities, is working on standardizing records, constructing disaggregated indicators and designing a national system of statistics on gender-based violence that incorporates data from surveys and administrative records. In this connection, attention should be drawn to the Gender Atlas, which is a tool for highlighting gender gaps and guiding the formulation of evidence-based public policies.
240	131. In 2025, the Ministry of Women organized a workshop on gender statistics that focused on the collection, analysis and presentation of sex-disaggregated data, the development of indicators, and the strategic use of information for inclusive public policies.
241	
242	14
243	
244	GE.26-02845
245	
246	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/1
247	132. The strengthening of the statistical system is complemented by relevant sector-based progress. The Public Defence Service has implemented a system for managing indicators relating to access to justice that makes it possible to systematically collect data on gender-based violence from all public defender's offices throughout the country. Since 2022, within the framework of the Inter-institutional Working Group for the Prevention of Violence against Women, an inter-agency process has been conducted to develop indicators and methodological guidelines on femicide, attempted femicide, domestic violence and family violence. Plans are in place to expand the process to include trafficking in persons and the sexual abuse of children and adolescents. The Public Prosecution Service has implemented an integrated electronic case management system. Through its Observatory, it publishes regular disaggregated reports on femicide, child sexual abuse, and domestic violence that inform more effective public policies.
248	133. The Ministry of Women has a Gender Observatory that highlights the structural inequalities affecting women in various areas of social, economic and political life. In 2025, it launched the first national competition for scientific articles with a gender focus as a mechanism to promote critical thinking, innovation in equality policies and inclusive development. Lastly, mention should be made of the launch in 2025 of the updated Gender Observatory of the Judiciary and the judiciary's first excellence award for the incorporation of the right to equality and non-discrimination in judicial decisions.
249	134. The budgetary resources allocated to guarantee women's rights have been progressively strengthened. In this connection, the Ministry of Women was allocated a budget of 24,124,867,588 guaranies (G)16 in 2024 and G 25,213,520,78517 in the general national budget for 2025 in order to strengthen its operational capacity. Subsequently, an additional increase of G 1.5 billion was added, which made it possible to adjust and strengthen the initial allocation, consolidating the sustainability of prevention, care and protection services for women.18
250	135. The Ministry of Economic Affairs and Finance has developed a methodological guide for measuring investment in gender that provides guidance on gender-sensitive budgeting in public programmes. In 2024, it issued an evaluation report on the impact of public spending on gender gaps.
251	Rights of children and adolescents19
252	136. The State implements comprehensive policies for protecting children and adolescents, preventing all forms of violence and strengthening the family environment. The "Seeds of the Future" programme is a priority initiative that seeks to guarantee rights from conception, with a historic level of investment until 2028. Under the programme, 100 comprehensive early childhood care centres have been constructed in 17 departments, 1,900 professionals have been hired and baby libraries have been incorporated, promoting timely stimulation, respectful child-rearing and the strengthening of families.
253	137. The purpose of the Comprehensive Care Programme for Child and Adolescent Victims is to prevent sexual abuse and provide comprehensive and specialized care to victims by coordinating actions with the protection system. It offers psychological, medical, legal and social assistance, as well as family support and digital follow-up of cases. Since its launch, it has provided support to 1,036 girls and adolescents, including Indigenous girls.
254	138. The #TodosSomosResponsables (We Are All Responsible) campaign is being implemented on an ongoing basis, promoting the prevention and reporting of violence against children and adolescents and disseminating a guide to the prevention of child sexual abuse to 3.5 million people.
255	139. An inter-institutional road map for a comprehensive response to the sexual abuse of children and adolescents has been distributed to more than 200,000 professionals and leaders in the prevention of sexual abuse. Between 2023 and 2025, 21,062 children and adolescents participated in prevention workshops that focused on self-protection, reporting channels and support networks. This initiative forms part of the mandatory course content established under Act No. 7239/24.
256	
257	GE.26-02845
258	
259	15
260	
261	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/1
262	140. The National Registry of Sex Offenders against Children contains permanent records of persons who have been handed final convictions for sexual offences against children.
263	141. The Abrazo Programme is the main public policy for the social protection of children and adolescents at risk or in dangerous child labour situations. It is implemented in 56 districts with 74 care centres, covering 5,500 families and 14,000 children and adolescents, providing them with social support, financial assistance and guaranteed access to rights. Support is provided for Indigenous children and adolescents under the Comprehensive Programme for Indigenous Children and Adolescents. In that connection, work is carried out directly in the field to strengthen protective environments through protection centres in the communities of Punta Por�, J. Manuel Frutos, Tarumandymi and Guavirami. In 2025, support was provided to 11,647 children and adolescents.
264	142. The State set up an inter-agency technical committee to draft a bill aimed at eradicating unpaid domestic child labour (criadazgo) on the basis of the National Strategy for the Prevention and Eradication of Child Labour. Although the bill presented in 2024 was not passed, the National Commission for the Eradication of Child Labour, together with the Ministry for Children and Adolescents and the Ministry of Labour, Employment and Social Security, plans to resume the legislative process in order to define this practice as an offence and establish criminal penalties. The implementation of the Adolescent Labour Register has strengthened the oversight and monitoring of protected adolescent labour.
265	143. A proposal for regulatory reform to eliminate exceptions to the minimum age for marriage and impose a total ban on marriage between adolescents is currently under consideration.
266	144. With regard to the right to identity, the Directorate General of the Civil Registry implements a single register of persons that allows for the online registration of births and facilitates registration through offices established within hospitals. Such offices currently operate in 21 locations across the country and will soon be installed in comprehensive early childhood care centres.
267	145. The National Programme for Alternative Care and Adoption ("Guardian Families") is a flagship public policy implemented to guarantee the fundamental right of children and adolescents to live in a family. The Programme is operationalized through the allocation of resources and the implementation of Act No. 6486/20, leading to the decentralization of technical teams, greater training for foster and adoptive families and the protection of 900 children and adolescents.
268	Indigenous Peoples20
269	146. The National Plan for Indigenous Peoples 2020-2030 is in force. A cross-cutting theme of the Plan is the implementation of a process of consultation and free, prior and informed consent with Indigenous Peoples in respect of all decision-making. Between 2022 and 2025, 637 consultation processes were carried out.
270	147. In addition, Act No. 7008/22 was adopted, establishing the National Commission for the Strengthening, Promotion and Appreciation of Indigenous Languages in Paraguay.
271	148. In 2024, a specific inter-agency cooperation agreement between the High Court of Electoral Justice and the National Institute of Indigenous Affairs was renewed with the primary objective of promoting, disseminating, registering, re-registering and updating the data in the registry in order to guarantee the effective exercise of the civil and political rights of Indigenous communities. Since 2023, a specific box for identifying members of Indigenous communities has been included in the relevant registration form. Between 2021 and 2024, fieldwork, including documentation campaigns and civic and electoral capacity-building, was carried out in different departments in the country. New polling stations were set up in Indigenous territories.
272	
273	16
274	
275	GE.26-02845
276	
277	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/1
278	149. The National Institute of Indigenous Affairs strengthened its institutional capacity by establishing the Directorate of Territorial Management, which is a specialist body responsible for securing land rights. Between 2020 and 2025, the State acquired 3,115 ha for Indigenous communities.
279	150. The Ministry of Urban Planning, Housing and the Human Environment implemented programmes aimed at Indigenous communities, resulting in the construction of 15,323 homes for these communities between 2021 and 2025. At the end of this period, 1,533 homes were under construction and work on 198 homes was about to begin.
280	151. The Ministry of Labour, Employment and Social Security implements training programmes for the Indigenous population, including projects run in partnership with civil society organizations. Between 2021 and 2023, 856 Indigenous people received certificates. Of those people, 497 were women and 359 were men.
281	152. The National Council for Indigenous Peoples' Health, the National Directorate for Indigenous Peoples' Health and the secretariats established in several departmental governments guarantee access to health services for Indigenous peoples and the recognition, respect and strengthening of their own healthcare systems. The teams attached to the family health units make ongoing efforts to bring public health services closer to the communities located furthest from health facilities.
282	153. The Public Defence Service has a team of experts in Indigenous culture who assist both Indigenous Peoples in court proceedings and justice officials by providing advice at different stages of criminal proceedings involving Indigenous Peoples.
283	154. The Supreme Court promotes regular training for justice officials on the protocol for intercultural justice in order to mainstream Indigenous law and the human rights perspective in the adjudication of cases. The second edition of the protocol, released in 2022, was translated into Guaran�.
284	155. The State has made progress in complying with judgments handed down by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights.
285	156. The Yakye Axa community has been definitively settled on the 11,312 ha restored to it. The access road has been completed, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights deemed the work to be finished in 2025. The community was also given a rainwater catchment system, as well as improved access to water from cisterns and full electrification. A total of 50 new homes were delivered in 2025.
286	157. The Sawhoyamaxa community now occupies the 14,404 ha expropriated in its favour. In 2024, internal roads were rehabilitated and a connecting branch road was opened. The community also has wells with a storage capacity of 100,000 litres, a regular supply of water and four schools that benefit from the "Zero Hunger" programme. Furthermore, 200 homes have been built and the electricity grid is being expanded.
287	158. The X�kmok K�sek community lives on 7,701 ha and has two access roads. The National Institute of Indigenous Affairs requested the expropriation of an additional 2,999 ha for the community. A total of 13 wells, a reservoir with a mill, a newly completed family health unit, and 80 homes were installed. In addition, the electrical grid was expanded, and additional improvements are planned in order to stabilize the service.
288	People of African descent21
289	159. In 2022, Act No. 6940 was enacted, establishing mechanisms and procedures to prevent and punish acts of racism and discrimination against people of African descent. The Act also provides for the development of a national plan and the establishment of a national registry of people of African descent, among other measures.
290	160. In this connection, the National Council of People of African Descent was established to act as an advisory body and to promote the implementation of the Act, with the participation of several State agencies and entities and three representatives of organizations of people of African descent in the country. The national plan is currently being developed.
291	
292	GE.26-02845
293	
294	17
295	
296	A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/1
297	
298	Persons with disabilities22
299	161. The National Action Plan for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 2015-2030 is currently being implemented. Furthermore, the National Commission on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities was strengthened. The Commission is a joint body in which the State and civil society organizations evaluate public policies on a quarterly basis. Ten thematic technical committees operate to ensure that public policies are in compliance with international human rights standards and meet the real needs of persons with disabilities.
300	162. Regional offices have been opened and strengthened to bring rehabilitation services, assistive devices and disability certification services closer to the interior of the country, reducing access gaps resulting from geographical factors. Furthermore, the establishment of disability secretariats in municipal and departmental government offices has been promoted.
301	163. In 2023, the Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare approved technical guidelines on the appropriate and respectful treatment of persons with disabilities by health workers, which were developed through a participatory process. The Ministry also has a guide to sexual and reproductive healthcare for adolescents with disabilities.
302	164. Specific protocols have been developed to ensure access to justice for persons with psychosocial disabilities and care for persons with disabilities who are deprived of their liberty.
303	165. Disability is mainstreamed in the national risk management policy in accordance with article 11 of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Georeferenced records have been established to identify persons with disabilities in flood-prone areas, ensuring that evacuation plans are accessible and prioritizing the bodily integrity and autonomy of persons with disabilities.
304	166. The disability certification process has been modernized, migrating to a digital system that makes it easier to obtain the relevant document, which is essential for gaining access to all social programmes.
305	167. Laws have been adopted on exemption from customs duties and VAT on the importation of vehicles and adaptation mechanisms; exemption from charges for the renewal of identity cards and police records; the amendment of the Electoral Code to guarantee the exercise of the right to vote for persons with disabilities; the use of canes for persons who are blind, blind-deaf or visually impaired; the establishment of inclusive and accessible tourism; and the guarantee of the full exercise of legal rights for persons with disabilities.
306	168. The First Atlas on Disability, which incorporates information from six public institutions to highlight gaps in health, education, employment and access to services, has been developed. Plans are in place to move towards a second stage that will focus on harmonizing administrative records and ensuring the quality and sustainability of statistical information.
307	
308	Notes
309	
310	Challenges
311	169. Paraguay reaffirms that it remains committed to making its best efforts to follow up on and give effect to all the recommendations, thereby confirming the importance it attaches to the international human rights protection system and, in particular, its open and transparent collaboration with the universal periodic review.

United Nations
General Assembly

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/1
Distr.: General 2 March 2026 English Original: Spanish

Human Rights Council
Working Group on the Universal Periodic Review Fifty-second session Geneva, 4-15 May 2026
National report submitted pursuant to Human Rights Council resolutions 5/1 and 16/21*
Paraguay

* The present document is being issued without formal editing. GE.26-02845 (E) 110326 110326

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/1
Introduction
1. The Republic of Paraguay presents its national report on the implementation of the recommendations received in 2021 during the third cycle of the universal periodic review. On that occasion, Paraguay accepted 202 of the 210 recommendations received.
2. This report brings together information on the efforts made, measures taken, progress and achievements realised, and pending challenges and obstacles, based on information provided by representatives of around 66 State agencies and entities of the three branches of government (executive, legislative and judicial) and the autonomous government bodies that make up the network of focal points operating under the Recommendations Monitoring System (SIMORE Plus), the national mechanism for implementation, reporting and follow-up, coordinated by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Justice.
3. For ease of reference, a list of initialisms, acronyms and abbreviations is included in Annex I.
Follow-up to recommendations
Ratification of international instruments1
4. Paraguay has ratified most of the universal human rights instruments, demonstrating an ongoing willingness to cooperate with international mechanisms.
5. In this regard, it considers that the potential ratification of new instruments should result from an internal process of analysis involving the various stakeholders and relevant sectors. This approach enriches discussions of social, political and economic factors and ensures that any parliamentary decision is made on the basis of an objective assessment and is in line with national capacities, needs and priorities. Therefore, the question of whether to incorporate new international commitments into domestic law is determined by the sovereign decisions that each State adopts in accordance with its situation and possibilities, and is subject to the conclusions that arise from the aforementioned internal deliberation process.
6. In this connection, Paraguay ratified the Convention against Discrimination in Education in 2025. In December 2025, it approved accession to the Inter-American Convention on Protecting the Human Rights of Older Persons.
7. With regard to the Inter-American Convention against Racism, Racial Discrimination and Related Forms of Intolerance, Paraguay notes that it is a State Party to the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination and considers that the obligations and guarantees provided for in this treaty already encompass the rights established in the inter-American instrument.
8. It also points out that it has assumed a solid framework of international commitments relating to economic, social and cultural rights, particularly through the American Convention on Human Rights and the mechanisms of the inter-American system. In this regard, the possible ratification of the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights continues to be the subject of internal analysis, taking into account the need to avoid overlap and ensure adequate coordination between the universal and regional systems.
National Human Rights Plan2
9. The State's Human Rights Network, which is coordinated by the Ministry of Justice, implements the National Human Rights Plan. Within this framework, the fourth Action Plan of the Human Rights Network (2024-2028) was approved in 2024 with the strategic aim of promoting inter-agency and intersectoral coordination to implement the National Human Rights Plan, strengthening mechanisms for defending, protecting and promoting human rights by coordinating the policies, plans and programmes of the State agencies and entities that make up the Network.

2

GE.26-02845

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/1
Cooperation with international human rights mechanisms3
10. With regard to the open and standing invitation to the special procedures, as a result of effective inter-agency coordination, official visits were received in 2022 from the Special Rapporteur on the implications for human rights of the environmentally sound management and disposal of hazardous substances and wastes and the Special Rapporteur on minority issues.
11. Paraguay is up to date with its reporting obligations to the treaty bodies, having submitted reports to the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women, the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination, the Committee against Torture, the Committee on the Rights of the Child, the Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, the Committee on Enforced Disappearances, the Committee on Migrant Workers (follow-up report) and the midterm report on the implementation of the recommendations arising from the universal periodic review. The country also actively participated in the constructive dialogues relating to its second periodic report for the Committee on Migrant Workers; its combined second and third periodic reports for the Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities; and its combined fourth to sixth periodic reports for the Committee on the Rights of the Child.
12. In addition, the national report and questionnaire on the implementation of the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action and the second voluntary national report on the implementation of the Montevideo Consensus on Population and Development were submitted.
13. Paraguay successfully completed its second term as a member of the Human Rights Council (2022-2024), consolidating its presence, visibility and international standing. During this period, it held the regional vice-presidency, led thematic initiatives and co-sponsored side events, including activities related to strengthening national mechanisms responsible for implementation, monitoring and reporting.
14. The participation of the President of Paraguay in the high-level segment of the fifty-fifth session of the Human Rights Council constituted the first address made by a President of Paraguay before this body, reaffirming the Government's political commitment at the highest level.
15. Paraguay has used inter-agency coordination mechanisms to respond regularly and in a coordinated manner to questionnaires sent by special procedures, thereby strengthening constructive dialogue and ongoing cooperation with these mandates.
16. The 180th session of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights was successfully organized in Asunci�n. The session coincided with the twentieth anniversary of the first session of the Court to be held away from its headquarters in Costa Rica, which also took place in Paraguay, in 2005, reinforcing the country's pioneering role in the decentralization of the Court's sessions and the promotion of human rights in the region.
Office of the Ombudsman4
17. The Office of the Ombudsman was re-accredited with category A status by the Subcommittee on Accreditation of the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions. 18. Between 2021 and 2024, the monetary poverty rate in Paraguay fell from approximately 26% to 20% of the population, reaching one of the lowest levels ever recorded. The extreme poverty rate also fell to around 4% and the multidimensional poverty rate was reduced to around 15.6%.
19. The Cabinet Council on Social Affairs within the Office of the President is implementing the social protection system to promote social inclusion and cohesion, with a special focus on Indigenous Peoples, children aged 4 years or under, women, persons with disabilities and persons living in poverty, guaranteeing access to fundamental rights such as education, health and employment. This comprehensive public policy is structured across the life course of beneficiaries and focuses on three fundamental pillars: social integration; integration into the labour market and productive activities; and social welfare.
20. The National Development Plan 2050 is the State's guiding instrument for long-term planning. Its purpose is to align public policies, investment and State actions with a vision of sustainable, inclusive and people-centred development, ensuring the continuity of State policies.

22. The "Zero Hunger in Schools" programme is a school meals strategy whose purpose is to ensure that lunches are provided to all students in the education system. Since its launch, the Government has invested more than $350 million, achieving 100% coverage nationwide and feeding more than 1,050,000 children and adolescents every day. This programme has created formal employment opportunities for 17,231 people, 94% of whom are women.
23. The Tekopor� Programme, which is aimed at households living in poverty and extreme poverty, prioritizes groups in vulnerable situations and combines cash transfers with social and family support and shared responsibilities in the areas of health and education, contributing to the reduction of extreme poverty and the prevention of its intergenerational transmission. 24. Other programmes that have been implemented: (1) the Tekoha Programme, the purpose of which is to guarantee access to land ownership for vulnerable families living in poverty by legalizing and organizing the occupation of areas in and on the periphery of cities (6,826 sales contracts between 2021 and 2025); (2) the Tenonder� Programme, the purpose of which is to promote the socioeconomic inclusion of families living in poverty and in vulnerable situations who are beneficiaries of the Tekopor� Programme by building their capacities and increasing their productive and financial assets for starting or strengthening businesses (42,269 beneficiaries in the period 2021-2025).
