122. Access to justice is promoted under the National Courthouse Programme, which provides guidance, referrals and services at the community level, and through the provision of training for officials involved in the care and investigation pathway.
123. Paraguay has consolidated a comprehensive model for the support and protection of women in situations of violence. At the local level, progress is being made in establishing and consolidating regional centres and shelters. Mention should also be made of the presentation and progressive implementation of the coordinated model for the protection and comprehensive care of women at the local level, which is designed to ensure swift, effective and specialized responses to restore rights and provide comprehensive reparation. Currently, the first model in Alto Paran� is at an advanced stage of implementation.
124. The Women's Support Service provides comprehensive assistance, delivering more than 25,500 comprehensive services in 2025. The capacities of the Service have been strengthened two-fold through the recruitment of new professionals.
125. The toll-free "SOS Mujer" hotline (137) has nationwide coverage and operates around the clock. The hotline received more than 4,000 calls reporting violence in 2025 and provided more than 10,500 services. A customer service channel on WhatsApp was launched in 2026.
126. The Women's City Centre operates as a comprehensive centre with five modules (registration and initial care; the prevention of violence and responses to it; economic empowerment; comprehensive health; and early childhood). This model is expanded through the "Mobile Women's City" programme, which brings services to rural areas with the support of the Office of the First Lady: 74 districts were visited and almost 20,000 women and their families were reached. The inclusive nature of the campaign was ensured by the National Secretariat for the Human Rights of Persons with Disabilities, which supported workshops by providing more than 8,747 services.
127. The National Plan for the Prevention of Gender-based Violence and Care for Victims within the National Health System 2020-2025 sets out priorities and measures for responding to domestic violence, sexual violence and other forms of violence against women, children and adolescents, including trafficking in persons, forced labour and child labour. In addition, a handbook on comprehensive care for victims of domestic, sexual or gender-based violence sets out technical guidelines and protocols for comprehensive care.
128. Attention should be drawn to the launch of a monitoring system that uses electronic devices in the form of electronic ankle bracelets. This tool is made available by court order for prosecuted or convicted persons with the aim of reducing domestic violence and femicide and helping to reduce prison overcrowding. The State has invested approximately $3 million in contracting the service. The Ministry of the Interior has approved a manual on police conduct and coordination for a comprehensive response to domestic violence that sets out specific provisions for responding to cases involving women and girls from Indigenous communities.
129. In order to strengthen information and data systems, the Ministry of Women, in coordination with the Ministry of Information and Communications Technology, has developed a computer system for reporting violence against women. The system, which is currently being implemented, will enable inter-agency coordination, real-time monitoring of cases and a more timely response within the State protection system, contributing to the traceability of actions and preventing revictimization.
130. The National Institute of Statistics, in conjunction with other State agencies and entities, is working on standardizing records, constructing disaggregated indicators and designing a national system of statistics on gender-based violence that incorporates data from surveys and administrative records. In this connection, attention should be drawn to the Gender Atlas, which is a tool for highlighting gender gaps and guiding the formulation of evidence-based public policies.
131. In 2025, the Ministry of Women organized a workshop on gender statistics that focused on the collection, analysis and presentation of sex-disaggregated data, the development of indicators, and the strategic use of information for inclusive public policies.

14

GE.26-02845

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/1
132. The strengthening of the statistical system is complemented by relevant sector-based progress. The Public Defence Service has implemented a system for managing indicators relating to access to justice that makes it possible to systematically collect data on gender-based violence from all public defender's offices throughout the country. Since 2022, within the framework of the Inter-institutional Working Group for the Prevention of Violence against Women, an inter-agency process has been conducted to develop indicators and methodological guidelines on femicide, attempted femicide, domestic violence and family violence. Plans are in place to expand the process to include trafficking in persons and the sexual abuse of children and adolescents. The Public Prosecution Service has implemented an integrated electronic case management system. Through its Observatory, it publishes regular disaggregated reports on femicide, child sexual abuse, and domestic violence that inform more effective public policies.
133. The Ministry of Women has a Gender Observatory that highlights the structural inequalities affecting women in various areas of social, economic and political life. In 2025, it launched the first national competition for scientific articles with a gender focus as a mechanism to promote critical thinking, innovation in equality policies and inclusive development. Lastly, mention should be made of the launch in 2025 of the updated Gender Observatory of the Judiciary and the judiciary's first excellence award for the incorporation of the right to equality and non-discrimination in judicial decisions.
134. The budgetary resources allocated to guarantee women's rights have been progressively strengthened. In this connection, the Ministry of Women was allocated a budget of 24,124,867,588 guaranies (G)16 in 2024 and G 25,213,520,78517 in the general national budget for 2025 in order to strengthen its operational capacity. Subsequently, an additional increase of G 1.5 billion was added, which made it possible to adjust and strengthen the initial allocation, consolidating the sustainability of prevention, care and protection services for women.18
135. The Ministry of Economic Affairs and Finance has developed a methodological guide for measuring investment in gender that provides guidance on gender-sensitive budgeting in public programmes. In 2024, it issued an evaluation report on the impact of public spending on gender gaps.
Rights of children and adolescents19
136. The State implements comprehensive policies for protecting children and adolescents, preventing all forms of violence and strengthening the family environment. The "Seeds of the Future" programme is a priority initiative that seeks to guarantee rights from conception, with a historic level of investment until 2028. Under the programme, 100 comprehensive early childhood care centres have been constructed in 17 departments, 1,900 professionals have been hired and baby libraries have been incorporated, promoting timely stimulation, respectful child-rearing and the strengthening of families.
137. The purpose of the Comprehensive Care Programme for Child and Adolescent Victims is to prevent sexual abuse and provide comprehensive and specialized care to victims by coordinating actions with the protection system. It offers psychological, medical, legal and social assistance, as well as family support and digital follow-up of cases. Since its launch, it has provided support to 1,036 girls and adolescents, including Indigenous girls.
138. The #TodosSomosResponsables (We Are All Responsible) campaign is being implemented on an ongoing basis, promoting the prevention and reporting of violence against children and adolescents and disseminating a guide to the prevention of child sexual abuse to 3.5 million people.
139. An inter-institutional road map for a comprehensive response to the sexual abuse of children and adolescents has been distributed to more than 200,000 professionals and leaders in the prevention of sexual abuse. Between 2023 and 2025, 21,062 children and adolescents participated in prevention workshops that focused on self-protection, reporting channels and support networks. This initiative forms part of the mandatory course content established under Act No. 7239/24.

GE.26-02845

15

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/1
140. The National Registry of Sex Offenders against Children contains permanent records of persons who have been handed final convictions for sexual offences against children.
141. The Abrazo Programme is the main public policy for the social protection of children and adolescents at risk or in dangerous child labour situations. It is implemented in 56 districts with 74 care centres, covering 5,500 families and 14,000 children and adolescents, providing them with social support, financial assistance and guaranteed access to rights. Support is provided for Indigenous children and adolescents under the Comprehensive Programme for Indigenous Children and Adolescents. In that connection, work is carried out directly in the field to strengthen protective environments through protection centres in the communities of Punta Por�, J. Manuel Frutos, Tarumandymi and Guavirami. In 2025, support was provided to 11,647 children and adolescents.
142. The State set up an inter-agency technical committee to draft a bill aimed at eradicating unpaid domestic child labour (criadazgo) on the basis of the National Strategy for the Prevention and Eradication of Child Labour. Although the bill presented in 2024 was not passed, the National Commission for the Eradication of Child Labour, together with the Ministry for Children and Adolescents and the Ministry of Labour, Employment and Social Security, plans to resume the legislative process in order to define this practice as an offence and establish criminal penalties. The implementation of the Adolescent Labour Register has strengthened the oversight and monitoring of protected adolescent labour.
143. A proposal for regulatory reform to eliminate exceptions to the minimum age for marriage and impose a total ban on marriage between adolescents is currently under consideration.
144. With regard to the right to identity, the Directorate General of the Civil Registry implements a single register of persons that allows for the online registration of births and facilitates registration through offices established within hospitals. Such offices currently operate in 21 locations across the country and will soon be installed in comprehensive early childhood care centres.
145. The National Programme for Alternative Care and Adoption ("Guardian Families") is a flagship public policy implemented to guarantee the fundamental right of children and adolescents to live in a family. The Programme is operationalized through the allocation of resources and the implementation of Act No. 6486/20, leading to the decentralization of technical teams, greater training for foster and adoptive families and the protection of 900 children and adolescents.
Indigenous Peoples20
146. The National Plan for Indigenous Peoples 2020-2030 is in force. A cross-cutting theme of the Plan is the implementation of a process of consultation and free, prior and informed consent with Indigenous Peoples in respect of all decision-making. Between 2022 and 2025, 637 consultation processes were carried out.
147. In addition, Act No. 7008/22 was adopted, establishing the National Commission for the Strengthening, Promotion and Appreciation of Indigenous Languages in Paraguay.
148. In 2024, a specific inter-agency cooperation agreement between the High Court of Electoral Justice and the National Institute of Indigenous Affairs was renewed with the primary objective of promoting, disseminating, registering, re-registering and updating the data in the registry in order to guarantee the effective exercise of the civil and political rights of Indigenous communities. Since 2023, a specific box for identifying members of Indigenous communities has been included in the relevant registration form. Between 2021 and 2024, fieldwork, including documentation campaigns and civic and electoral capacity-building, was carried out in different departments in the country. New polling stations were set up in Indigenous territories.

16

GE.26-02845

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/1
149. The National Institute of Indigenous Affairs strengthened its institutional capacity by establishing the Directorate of Territorial Management, which is a specialist body responsible for securing land rights. Between 2020 and 2025, the State acquired 3,115 ha for Indigenous communities.
150. The Ministry of Urban Planning, Housing and the Human Environment implemented programmes aimed at Indigenous communities, resulting in the construction of 15,323 homes for these communities between 2021 and 2025. At the end of this period, 1,533 homes were under construction and work on 198 homes was about to begin.
151. The Ministry of Labour, Employment and Social Security implements training programmes for the Indigenous population, including projects run in partnership with civil society organizations. Between 2021 and 2023, 856 Indigenous people received certificates. Of those people, 497 were women and 359 were men.
152. The National Council for Indigenous Peoples' Health, the National Directorate for Indigenous Peoples' Health and the secretariats established in several departmental governments guarantee access to health services for Indigenous peoples and the recognition, respect and strengthening of their own healthcare systems. The teams attached to the family health units make ongoing efforts to bring public health services closer to the communities located furthest from health facilities.
153. The Public Defence Service has a team of experts in Indigenous culture who assist both Indigenous Peoples in court proceedings and justice officials by providing advice at different stages of criminal proceedings involving Indigenous Peoples.
154. The Supreme Court promotes regular training for justice officials on the protocol for intercultural justice in order to mainstream Indigenous law and the human rights perspective in the adjudication of cases. The second edition of the protocol, released in 2022, was translated into Guaran�.
155. The State has made progress in complying with judgments handed down by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights.
156. The Yakye Axa community has been definitively settled on the 11,312 ha restored to it. The access road has been completed, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights deemed the work to be finished in 2025. The community was also given a rainwater catchment system, as well as improved access to water from cisterns and full electrification. A total of 50 new homes were delivered in 2025.
157. The Sawhoyamaxa community now occupies the 14,404 ha expropriated in its favour. In 2024, internal roads were rehabilitated and a connecting branch road was opened. The community also has wells with a storage capacity of 100,000 litres, a regular supply of water and four schools that benefit from the "Zero Hunger" programme. Furthermore, 200 homes have been built and the electricity grid is being expanded.
158. The X�kmok K�sek community lives on 7,701 ha and has two access roads. The National Institute of Indigenous Affairs requested the expropriation of an additional 2,999 ha for the community. A total of 13 wells, a reservoir with a mill, a newly completed family health unit, and 80 homes were installed. In addition, the electrical grid was expanded, and additional improvements are planned in order to stabilize the service.
People of African descent21
159. In 2022, Act No. 6940 was enacted, establishing mechanisms and procedures to prevent and punish acts of racism and discrimination against people of African descent. The Act also provides for the development of a national plan and the establishment of a national registry of people of African descent, among other measures.
160. In this connection, the National Council of People of African Descent was established to act as an advisory body and to promote the implementation of the Act, with the participation of several State agencies and entities and three representatives of organizations of people of African descent in the country. The national plan is currently being developed.

GE.26-02845

17

A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/1

Persons with disabilities22
161. The National Action Plan for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 2015-2030 is currently being implemented. Furthermore, the National Commission on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities was strengthened. The Commission is a joint body in which the State and civil society organizations evaluate public policies on a quarterly basis. Ten thematic technical committees operate to ensure that public policies are in compliance with international human rights standards and meet the real needs of persons with disabilities.
162. Regional offices have been opened and strengthened to bring rehabilitation services, assistive devices and disability certification services closer to the interior of the country, reducing access gaps resulting from geographical factors. Furthermore, the establishment of disability secretariats in municipal and departmental government offices has been promoted.
163. In 2023, the Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare approved technical guidelines on the appropriate and respectful treatment of persons with disabilities by health workers, which were developed through a participatory process. The Ministry also has a guide to sexual and reproductive healthcare for adolescents with disabilities.
164. Specific protocols have been developed to ensure access to justice for persons with psychosocial disabilities and care for persons with disabilities who are deprived of their liberty.
165. Disability is mainstreamed in the national risk management policy in accordance with article 11 of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Georeferenced records have been established to identify persons with disabilities in flood-prone areas, ensuring that evacuation plans are accessible and prioritizing the bodily integrity and autonomy of persons with disabilities.
166. The disability certification process has been modernized, migrating to a digital system that makes it easier to obtain the relevant document, which is essential for gaining access to all social programmes.
167. Laws have been adopted on exemption from customs duties and VAT on the importation of vehicles and adaptation mechanisms; exemption from charges for the renewal of identity cards and police records; the amendment of the Electoral Code to guarantee the exercise of the right to vote for persons with disabilities; the use of canes for persons who are blind, blind-deaf or visually impaired; the establishment of inclusive and accessible tourism; and the guarantee of the full exercise of legal rights for persons with disabilities.
168. The First Atlas on Disability, which incorporates information from six public institutions to highlight gaps in health, education, employment and access to services, has been developed. Plans are in place to move towards a second stage that will focus on harmonizing administrative records and ensuring the quality and sustainability of statistical information.

Notes

Challenges
169. Paraguay reaffirms that it remains committed to making its best efforts to follow up on and give effect to all the recommendations, thereby confirming the importance it attaches to the international human rights protection system and, in particular, its open and transparent collaboration with the universal periodic review.

content.thinking:
Now I have all three Paraguay documents in view. Paraguay's official picture shows a State reporting substantial activity: the SIMORE Plus follow-up system, poverty reduction from 26% to 20% between 2021-2024, a universal old-age pension law from 2024, full coverage under Zero Hunger in Schools, a 2022 mental health act, and a National Plan for Indigenous Peoples with hundreds of consultation processes and land restitution to several Indigenous communities.

But I'm also weighing serious gaps and regressions: the absence of a comprehensive anti-discrimination law, the 2024 "Garrote Act" restricting NGO freedom of association, resolutions banning gender/CSE topics in schools, criminalized abortion with dozens of deaths since 2025, a rejected bill on criadazgo (child servitude), and child marriage still legally permitted from age 16 with court authorization.

Beyond that, I'm noting the Escazú Agreement and OP-ICESCR remain unratified, alongside a severe prison crisis with extreme overcrowding, accountability findings against Paraguay for killings of two girls by the Joint Task Force, stalled protection legislation for human rights defenders and journalists despite ongoing attacks, and significant VAW response measures like Act 5777 and Act 7239/2024. I'm also weighing mixed compliance on indigenous land restitution and the Ombudsman's regained A-status despite concerns about a non-merit-based selection process, before turning to Paraguay's key thematic priorities: equality and non-discrimination, violence against women, and other emerging issues.

Now I'm starting to build out `countries/paraguay/assess.py`, planning around 26 thematic clusters and about 10 keywords, drawing from the National Report, UN Compilation, and Stakeholder summary documents. For the first cluster on equality and non-discrimination, I'm drafting a C-grade assessment recommending Paraguay adopt a comprehensive anti-discrimination law, given persistent gaps flagged across review cycles and by the Special Rapporteur.

Meanwhile Paraguay's own reply cites the Constitution's equality clause as sufficient even without implementing legislation. For violence against women, I'm noting Paraguay's protective laws, emergency declarations, and support services like the SOS Mujer hotline, while also flagging that the UN country team and Amnesty International report femicide rates and prevalence remain very high.

Now I'm looking at the third recommendation, on strengthening the Ombudsman's Office as the national human rights institution—noting it regained GANHRI category A status in 2025 with an increased budget, but the UN country team flags it still has one of the lowest budgets among agencies, while civil society points to an unregulated, non-transparent selection process leaving it open to political capture.

Then I move to the fourth issue, freedom of association, recommending repeal of Act No. 7363/2024 (the so-called "Ley Garrote"), which imposes oversight restrictions on NGOs.

Additional quotes confirm Act No. 7363's abusive restrictions on freedom of association and the recommendation to repeal it, along with its 2025 implementing decree.

Now I'm moving to the administration of justice category, noting Paraguay's digitalization efforts and judicial-ethics training, but weighing this against the Special Rapporteur's finding that the judicial system remains slow with most human-rights complaints left uninvestigated, and civil society's concerns about judicial independence.

Then I'm shifting to the right to education category, focused on quality, inclusive and non-discriminatory education.

Paraguay expanded its Zero Hunger in Schools meals program to full national coverage and set up inclusion support centres, but disability rights bodies flag under-investment in inclusive education, persistent segregated special education, high dropout rates among rural, low-income and Indigenous students, and a concerning ministry restriction on gender and sexuality education.

Now I'm noting that on ratification of international instruments, Paraguay ratified the Convention against Discrimination in Education in 2025 and approved accession to the Inter-American Convention on Older Persons in December 2025, though it still hasn't ratified certain outstanding optional protocols.

Adding another quote citing the failure to ratify the Escazú Agreement, then moving to the right to health category, where I'm noting Paraguay's decentralized health teams, mammography expansion, mental-health legislation, and maternal mortality reduction plan, weighed against persistent quality gaps flagged for rural and Indigenous areas.

1,200-place women's prison in Emboscada and adopted a 2024 protocol on pre-trial detention alternatives, but the UN country team and National Mechanism for the Prevention of Torture describe a structural crisis: 70% of prisoners held pre-trial, 435% overcrowding nationwide (over 1,100% in some units), and maximum-security conditions amounting to torture.

For trafficking, Paraguay ran its National Plan to Combat Trafficking 2020-2024, extended to 2025-2026, with the Ministry of the Interior now leading a dedicated fund, plus the new Ñasaindy Protection Centre and a specialized prosecution unit—though the Committee on Migrant Workers still finds standards unsatisfactory, case numbers have declined since 2019, and CRC wants a national strategy addressing criadazgo.

Moving to sexual and reproductive health rights, Paraguay adopted a National Sexual and Reproductive Health Plan 2024-2030 and a maternal mortality reduction plan, but abortion remains criminalized.

The CRC quote calls for repealing Resolution 933/2023 and decriminalizing abortion entirely, ensuring safe and quality abortion and post-abortion care.

Turning to abortion-related statistics, I note that in 2024 the Ministry of Health registered 4,691 abortions, and by June 2025 nineteen women had died due to clandestine procedures forced by current legislation. Paraguay's National Sexual and Reproductive Health Plan 2024-2030 aims to promote more equitable and inclusive access to care.

Now looking at women's political participation, I'm categorizing this under partial recommendations since Paraguay has training academies and an observatory for political participation, though women hold only about 23% of positions.

For that same theme, I'm noting the specific figures: women accounted for 23.2% of Congress members according to one submission, with a call for adopting the democratic parity bill, while state data shows women averaging 22.6% of the legislature in 2023 with acknowledged ongoing challenges.

Moving to indigenous peoples' issues, I'm assessing this as a partial recommendation too, since Paraguay has a National Plan for Indigenous Peoples 2020-2030 and conducted 637 consultation processes between 2022 and 2025.

Now I'm moving to human rights defenders: a bill to protect journalists and defenders, required by an Inter-American Court ruling, has stalled in Congress since 2021, while the UN country team and civil society report continued attacks, reprisals, and criminalization of defenders.

Then poverty: monetary poverty dropped from about 26% to 20% between 2021 and 2024 as Paraguay implements the Ñaime Porã program.

Poverty Reduction Plan, Tekoporã cash transfers reaching 573,478 people, and a universal old-age pension under Act No. 7322/2024 covering 340,203 beneficiaries; the CRC and other stakeholders still flag large numbers of children in poverty, sharp rural-urban and Indigenous disparities, and high land concentration.

Now I'm moving to the persons-with-disabilities theme, which aligns with SDG cluster C. Paraguay has implemented a National Action Plan for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 2015-2030, modernized disability certification, and strengthened its National Commission, though the CRPD notes limited implementation of the accessibility law, involuntary psychiatric treatment, a persisting medical model under Act No. 7018/2022, and under-resourced institutions.

Next I'm looking at children's themes—definition, juvenile justice, family environment—which map to cluster B, covering child protection, violence against children, and criadazgo. Paraguay operates programs like "Seeds of the Future," the Abrazo child-labour initiative, a National Registry of Sex Offenders, and a Guardian system.

For right to life and use of force, I'm noting how the Committee on the Rights of the Child held Paraguay accountable for grave violations in the 2020 killings of two 11-year-old girls during a Joint Task Force operation against the Paraguayan People's Army, calling for truth-finding and stronger law-enforcement accountability, while the National Report only mentions complaint procedures without legal reform.

Moving to torture and ill-treatment, I categorize this as C: while Paraguay approved 2023-2024 protocols for monitoring prisons and recording torture allegations, the National Mechanism for the Prevention of Torture documents maximum-security regimes amounting to torture, prolonged inhumane detention, and torture cases without charges, alongside CRC findings of torture and ill-treatment of children in police stations.

Next I look at migrants and refugees, also C: a migration bill has languished for over five years, with the Committee on Migrant Workers pressing for its adoption aligned with the ICRMW, along with regular regularization mechanisms, alternatives to administrative detention, and repeal of emergency measures.

Then I move to cultural rights and bilingualism, category C: Paraguay's Act No. 7008/22 established a Commission for Indigenous Languages, but the Special Rapporteur on minority issues notes six of the 19 Indigenous languages remain endangered and calls for stronger legislative protection.

Paraguay enacted Act No. 6940 (2022) to prevent and punish racism against people of African descent, but the UN country team notes implementation still pending, leaving the Afro-descendant minority largely invisible in official data.

Next, I'm looking at environment and hazardous substances issues -- Paraguay reports progress on hazardous-waste management and a 2022 Climate Adaptation Plan, but the Special Rapporteur on hazardous substances describes alarming pesticide exposure among rural and Indigenous communities, widespread non-compliance with environmental laws, and Paraguay's failure to implement Human Rights Committee Views in the Campo Agua'ẽ and Colonia Yerutí cases.

Moving to national human rights action plans, I'm noting Paraguay approved its fourth Human Rights Network Action Plan for 2024-2028, coordinating implementation efforts.

I'm noting Paraguay's cooperation with UN mechanisms—hosting Special Rapporteur visits in 2022, maintaining an open invitation, staying current on treaty reporting, and serving on the Human Rights Council, though civil society flags unpaid reparations ordered by the Human Rights Committee. Moving next to the right to work.

For labour rights, I'm capturing Paraguay's National Employment Plan 2022-2026, its formalisation strategy, and upcoming forced labour and child labour strategies, while noting the UN's recommendation to ratify ILO Convention 190 and reports of abuse against Indigenous domestic workers.

Now I'm setting up keyword overrides, starting with one that flags references to Act No. 7363, NGO oversight, or freedom of association as evidence for repealing the 2024 NGO oversight law, then moving into another override pattern related to gender theory and comprehensive sexuality education.

For the second override, I'm noting that Resolution No. 933/2023 and decision No. 29.664 from the Ministry of Education restricted teaching on gender and reproductive health in schools, and pending legislation to ban gender mainstreaming and eliminate the Ministry for Women represents a regression against prior recommendations. I'm gathering the relevant quotes from the Committee on the Rights of the Child and the UN country team documenting these restrictions.

Now I'm mapping abortion decriminalization to category C, since abortion remains criminalized except when life or health is at risk with no clear protocol -- the CRC recommends full decriminalization, and stakeholders report 19 maternal deaths by June 2025 tied to clandestine abortions.

Next I'm categorizing criadazgo (child domestic servitude) also under C, noting a 2024 bill to criminalize it was rejected by Congress and no protective policies exist yet, though the government intends to revive the legislative effort.

Then I'm flagging the minimum marriage age issue under C too — the law still permits marriage at 16 with court approval, while CRC and UNESCO push for a strict age-18 threshold, and reform remains only "under consideration."

Next, I'm marking the recommendation to ratify OP-ICESCR under C, noting the Special Rapporteur, UN country team, and UNESCO all called on Paraguay to do so.

I'm continuing with pattern 7, matching Escazú Agreement ratification calls to category C, citing Amnesty International's joint submission on the failure to ratify the regional environmental access agreement. Then I'm starting pattern 8, catching references to comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation.

I'm noting that Amnesty International and REPAR+ point to impunity for hate speech and rising discrimination against LGBTIQ+ people due to absent legislation. Next I'm mapping the journalist and human rights defender protection mechanism category, noting a pending bill remains unpassed.

Also mapping the Ombudsman/NHRI pattern to the "Strengthen the Ombudsman" cluster, and noting Paraguay's compliance with Inter-American Court judgments on Yakye Axa, Sawhoyamaxa, and Xákmok Kásek land restitution, even as broader Indigenous land regularisation remains stalled amid rising forced evictions.

For Paraguay, I'm seeing a high D count of 32, with several themes falling through the cracks — children's protection against exploitation, right to participate in public affairs and vote, discrimination against women, identity and nationality rights, land and property rights, governance and corruption, and marriage and family rights.

# Denmark — Implementation of 2021 (3rd cycle) UPR Recommendations

Assessment of Denmark's implementation of the 288 recommendations received in the 3rd UPR cycle (A/HRC/48/10, 38th session, 2021-05-06), using the Human Rights Committee A–E grading system (CCPR/C/108/2). Evidence is the 4th-cycle pre-sessional documentation (7 May 2026 (session 52) review).

**Sources**

- **National Report** — A/HRC/WG.6/52/DNK/1, 20 February 2026
- **UN Compilation** — A/HRC/WG.6/52/DNK/2, OHCHR, 6 February 2026 (UN treaty bodies, UNHCR, UNESCO)
- **Stakeholders' Summary** — A/HRC/WG.6/52/DNK/3, OHCHR, 28 January 2026 (16 submissions + the Danish Institute for Human Rights)

Grades: **A** largely satisfactory · **B** partially satisfactory · **C** not satisfactory / no relevant action · **D** no information · **E** measures contrary to, or rejection of, the recommendation.

This is a **first-pass assessment for expert review**. Recommendations are grouped by their OHCHR theme; within a theme, near-identical asks share a grade, with separate blocks where the substance (and grade) differ. Each block notes the position Denmark took at the review (supported / noted / supported-noted); a *noted* recommendation was not accepted.

## Summary

| Grade | Count | Share |
|---|---:|---:|
| **A** — Largely implemented / action largely satisfactory | 10 | 3% |
| **B** — Partially implemented / steps taken, further action needed | 177 | 61% |
| **C** — Not implemented / no relevant action taken | 78 | 27% |
| **D** — No information available on implementation | 8 | 3% |
| **E** — Contrary measures taken, or recommendation rejected | 15 | 5% |
| **Total** | 288 | 100% |

Denmark reports concrete follow-up on many recommendations, so **partial implementation (B)** is the dominant outcome (ratification of the Enforced Disappearance Convention, a consent-based rape law, action plans on racism, trafficking and intimate-partner violence). Persistent gaps remain (no stand-alone torture offence, the retained "Parallel Society" laws) and asylum externalisation is a clear regression (**E**).

---
name: project-us-upr-cycle3-assessment
description: Python + SQLite tool assessing implementation of UPR recommendations (US + Denmark, Namibia, Paraguay)
metadata:
  type: project
---

**Location:** `C:\Users\rolan\OneDrive - Centre for Civil and Political Rights\Claude\Assessment of recommendations`

**Goal:** grade the level of implementation of each recommendation a country
received in one UPR cycle, using the *next* cycle's pre-sessional documentation
as evidence. Grade scale = adapted Human Rights Committee A–E (CCPR/C/108/2):
A largely implemented, B partial, C no action, D no information, E contrary/rejected.

**Countries done (all cycle 3 → cycle 4):**
- **United States** — 347 recs (A/HRC/46/15). Evidence: A/HRC/WG.6/50/USA/2 + /3 (no national report). Result 0A/7B/219C/0D/121E.
- **Denmark** — 288 recs (A/HRC/48/10). Evidence: A/HRC/WG.6/52/DNK/1,2,3. Result 10A/177B/78C/8D/15E.
- **Namibia** — 283 recs (A/HRC/48/4). Evidence: A/HRC/WG.6/52/NAM/1,2,3. Result 4A/88B/180C/11D/0E.
- **Paraguay** — 210 recs (A/HRC/48/9). Evidence: A/HRC/WG.6/52/PRY/1,2,3. Result 1A/77B/123C/5D/4E.

Tanzania/Suriname/Thailand were requested but their cycle-4 pre-sessionals do
not exist yet (reviewed Nov 2021, cycle 4 ≈ 2027).

**Structure:**
- `recommendations/` package (stdlib only): db, models (Grade/Position), repository,
  `thematic_list.py` (OHCHR "Thematic List of Recommendations" .docx parser),
  `uhri.py` (UHRI .xlsx parser), cli.
- `scripts/`: `countries.py` (registry), `build_country.py` (import),
  `assess.py` (generic `run()` — grades by thematic cluster + keyword overrides,
  each rule carries verbatim quotes from doc 1/2/3), `make_report.py`,
  `fill_thematic_list.py`. All take a country slug arg.
- `countries/<slug>/`: `assess.py` (the per-country CLUSTERS + KEYWORDS analytical
  content — the real work), `<slug>.db`, `evidence/` (PDFs + .txt), `output/`
  (report .md, assessment .csv, thematic list .docx with column 4 filled).
- US files sit in the repo root (`recommendations.db`, `output/`, `apply_assessment.py`).

**Run a country:** `python -m countries.<slug>.assess && python -m scripts.make_report <slug> && python -m scripts.fill_thematic_list <slug>`

content.text:
Done — all three countries assessed with the same method as the US.

## What was done

For each country: pulled the **cycle‑3 recommendations** (OHCHR "UPR38 Thematic List", May 2021) and the **cycle‑4 evidence** (session 52, review May 2026) — the **National Report**, **UN Compilation** and **Stakeholders' Summary**. Read all nine evidence documents, built a per‑country thematic assessment, and generated three deliverables per country: a narrative report grouped by theme, a per‑recommendation CSV, and the thematic list with column 4 filled in.

## Results (adapted HR Committee A–E)

| Country | Recs | A | B | C | D | E | Picture |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| **Denmark** | 288 | 10 | 177 | 78 | 8 | 15 | Mostly **partial (B)** — a cooperative State with real follow‑up (Enforced Disappearance Convention ratified, consent‑based rape law, action plans); gaps on torture criminalisation and the "Parallel Society" laws; asylum externalisation is a regression (E) |
| **Namibia** | 283 | 4 | 88 | 180 | 11 | 0 | Mostly **no action (C)** — some concrete steps (ILO C190, free tertiary education 2026, majority‑female Cabinet, GBV law reform), but the Torture Bill, anti‑discrimination law, OP‑CAT and Indigenous recognition all still pending |
| **Paraguay** | 210 | 1 | 77 | 123 | 5 | 4 | Mostly **no action (C)** — lots of activity (SIMORE Plus, poverty 26→20%, universal old‑age pension, IACtHR land compliance), but long‑standing asks unmet (anti‑discrimination law, migration law, abortion, criadazgo); regressions (E): the 2024 NGO "Garrote" law and school gender/sexuality‑education bans |

Every grade carries a reasoned assessment and verbatim quotes from the National Report / Compilation / Stakeholders' Summary, with the body or organisation named.

## Caveats

- Same as before: **first‑pass, cluster‑based, for expert review**. The `D` grades (8/11/5) are 1‑2‑recommendation themes with no specific evidence.
- **Tanzania, Suriname, Thailand** could not be done — their cycle‑4 pre‑sessionals don't exist yet (reviewed Nov 2021; cycle 4 ≈ 2027).

content.text:
Yes. In brief:

**The procedure (CCPR/C/108/2, refined in later notes up to CCPR/C/161).**

1. **Selection.** When the Human Rights Committee adopts Concluding Observations on a State party's periodic report, it picks a small number — normally **3** (occasionally 4) — of recommendations for follow-up. Criteria: implementable within ~2 years, and serious or urgent.
2. **State reply.** The State party must submit written information on those recommendations within **two years** (earlier cycles used one year). Remaining CO recommendations are picked up at the next periodic review.
3. **Special Rapporteur for follow-up on concluding observations** — a Committee member who runs the process, issues reminders, and can request a meeting with the Permanent Mission if the State does not reply.
4. **Other stakeholders.** NHRIs and NGOs submit their own concise follow-up reports (the "alternative" follow-up information), which the Committee weighs alongside the State reply.
5. **Grading.** The Committee (via the Special Rapporteur, adopted in plenary) assigns each recommendation — often each sub-part — a grade:
   - **A** information/action largely satisfactory
   - **B** partially satisfactory — more information or action needed
   - **C** not satisfactory — reply received but not relevant / doesn't implement
   - **D** no cooperation (no reply, even after reminder)
   - **E** measures taken are contrary to, or reflect rejection of, the recommendation
6. **Follow-up progress reports.** Each session the Committee publishes a report listing, per State, the recommendation, the information received, its assessment, the grade and the next step (renew request / new deadline / defer to next review). A "D" is flagged in the next dialogue and next COs.
7. It is separate from the **Views (individual communications) follow-up** procedure, which grades *remedies* on its own scale.

This is the scale our project borrows. One difference worth keeping in mind: the Committee grades the **State's reply** on its **3 selected** recommendations, whereas we've been grading **implementation on the ground** across **all** the country's UPR recommendations.

content.text:
Understood, and noted — thanks for the corrections:

- **3 years** after the dialogue, not 2 — the State submits its follow-up report on the 3 priority recommendations, then NGOs (and the NHRI) submit their own assessment.
- The Special Rapporteur's grade is a **desk assessment** — purely on the documents received, no mission, no independent fact‑finding.
- So the grade tracks **the information on the file**, not necessarily the situation on the ground. If civil society files nothing, the Rapporteur is left with the State's own account, and the grade tends to come out **more favourable** (more A/B, fewer C). The reverse when NGOs document gaps in detail.

That's a useful frame for what we've been doing. Our UPR exercise is also a desk assessment on the A–E scale, with the same dependency on what's in the sources — the difference being that for cycle‑4 we have the OHCHR **Stakeholders' Summary**, which already consolidates civil‑society input, so the "no NGO information" failure mode is less of a risk (though a thin summary still pulls grades up).

If this is heading toward a task — e.g. contributing an NGO follow‑up assessment for a specific country's CCPR concluding observations, or benchmarking our UPR grades against the Committee's official follow‑up grades — tell me the country and I'll set it up.

content.text:
Exactly — and that's the important part. The five one‑line definitions in CCPR/C/108/2 are just the skeleton. Fifteen-plus years of follow‑up progress reports are effectively a casebook of how Committee members actually apply them, and some fairly settled conventions have emerged:

- **The grade attaches to the specific ask, not the theme.** "Adopt law X" is graded on whether law X was adopted — not on whether the underlying situation improved.
- **Sub‑grading is normal.** One recommendation routinely comes back as, say, "16(a): B; 16(b): C". The Committee is comfortable with a split.
- **A is genuinely rare** — reserved for a completed measure *plus* some evidence of effect. The Committee often still asks for confirmation in the next report but closes the follow‑up point.
- **B is the workhorse**: bill adopted but not in force; policy adopted but unfunded / no indicators; institution created but under‑resourced; data collection started but incomplete; substantial information provided but specifics still needed.
- **C** covers two distinct situations: (i) a reply that restates the pre‑CO legal framework or is otherwise not responsive, and (ii) only intentions — "under consideration", a bill stalled in parliament for years, general statements. A "draft bill pending since 2019" reliably gets **C**, not B.
- **D** is literally no reply after the reminder — rare for engaged States.
- **E** is used sparingly, for a measure going the other way or an express rejection.
- **Reiteration is a tell**: if the next Concluding Observations repeat a recommendation, the follow‑up grade was almost always C or D.

This bears directly on our four assessments. Where we can sharpen them against Committee practice:

1. Grade each **distinct sub‑ask** rather than a whole thematic cluster uniformly.
2. Be **stricter on A** — several of our A's (e.g. Denmark's ILO/ICPPED ratifications) would likely survive, but "free tertiary education from 2026" for Namibia is a *future* measure and the Committee would more probably call that B.
3. We're already close on the C conventions (Namibia Torture Bill, Paraguay migration law → C).

If useful, I can pull a representative sample of the actual CCPR follow‑up progress reports from that page — including any that exist for the US, Denmark, Namibia, Paraguay — and distil the working grading conventions into a short calibration reference, then re‑check our four assessments against it.

29	Paragraph 16: Violence against women
30	The State Party should redouble its efforts to prevent and combat all forms of violence against women effectively, including domestic and sexual violence, in particular by:
31	(a) Revising the law on domestic violence to ensure a victim-centred approach that guarantees access to immediate means of redress and protection;
32	(b) Establishing an effective mechanism to encourage the reporting of cases of violence against women and by intensifying efforts to address the social stigmatization of victims;
33	(c) Ensuring that all cases of violence against women are promptly and thoroughly investigated, that perpetrators are prosecuted and, if convicted, are punished with appropriate sanctions and that victims have access to effective remedies and means of protection, including sufficient, safe and adequately funded shelters and suitable medical, psychosocial, legal and rehabilitative support services throughout the country, during the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic and beyond;

41	Summary of the information received from the State Party
42	(a) On 1 July 2024, amendments to the 2017 Law on the Prevention of Domestic Violence, the Protection of Victims of Domestic Violence and the Restoration of Peace in the Family entered into force, including amendment of the title to "Law on the Prevention of Family and Domestic Violence and the Protection of Persons Subjected to Family and Domestic Violence" and changes to 11 of the 23 articles. The amendments are aimed at increasing the effectiveness of the fight against domestic violence, raising public awareness and improving social and psychological support services provided to victims of violence.
43	The existing definitions and main concepts in the Law were clarified and brought into line with the definitions in the Criminal Code. For example, the definition of domestic violence was changed to include violence regardless of the circumstances of cohabitation and that committed between partners, former partners or former family members, and a child who witnessed the violence or suffered the negative consequences thereof is now considered a victim of violence. The definition of the conciliation procedure has been repealed, and the Law establishes free and preferential medical care and services for persons subjected to domestic violence. The deadlines for the implementation of urgent intervention and protection-oriented decisions have been revised.
44	Furthermore, a centralized data-collection system was launched to register cases of domestic violence, in order to streamline activities to protect persons subjected to domestic violence. The data collected will serve as a basis for developing further strategic plans and activities.
45	(b) Work is under way to launch a mobile application, entitled "SAFE YOU", which will allow victims of violence to promptly call the police and receive support.
46	To raise public awareness of domestic violence, information corners have been set up in police units, providing literature on domestic violence, including information leaflets and "SAFE YOU" application posters, and information on support centres, hotlines and organizations providing services to victims of domestic violence.
47	(c) The Investigative Committee produces semi-annual and annual reports on cases of domestic violence.
48	In 2023, 1,848 criminal proceedings related to domestic violence were investigated by the Investigative Committee, compared to 730 in 2020, 556 in 2021 and 960 in 2022. Of the 1,848 criminal proceedings investigated in 2023: 338 were completed with indictments (compared to 144 in 2020, 129 in 2021 and 122 in 2022); 8 proceedings were completed with final acts (proceedings of medical coercion) and sent to court; 557 proceedings were terminated (compared to 358 in 2020, 252 in 2021 and 301 in 2022), of which 463 were terminated on rehabilitative grounds, 90 on non-rehabilitative grounds and 4 on other grounds; 144 are in a passive stage; 14 were forwarded to the appropriate jurisdiction; 179 were combined; and 608 proceedings were passed to the following year.
49	Of the 349 defendants involved in the 338 criminal proceedings completed with indictments, 259 were victims' spouses. A total of 359 individuals were recognized as victims. For 152 individuals, criminal prosecution was not initiated or was terminated on non-rehabilitative grounds.
50	(d) A strategic plan for the implementation of gender policy in Armenia for the period 2024-2028 is currently being developed. The current document sets out six priorities: overcoming gender discrimination in all areas of management and at the decision-making level; encouraging gender-sensitive approaches in work activities and reducing the gender gap in the workforce; overcoming gender discrimination in the field of education and science; ensuring equal opportunities for women and men in the health sector; ensuring prevention of and protection from gender-based violence and discrimination; and developing gendersensitive and gender-responsive approaches to climate change.
51	Under the fifth priority of the strategic plan, action is envisaged to ratify the Council of Europe Convention on Preventing and Combating Violence against Women and Domestic Violence.

59	The Office of the Human Rights Defender notes that, despite legislative progress, gaps remain in the prevention and elimination of domestic violence, particularly concerning the legal provisions and their implementation. Article 12 (1) of the 2017 Law prohibits the application of emergency intervention or protection orders against minors or incapacitated persons, which is problematic as regards the application of protection measures for victims. Misconceptions and stereotypes regarding women and domestic violence persist and are rooted throughout society, including discriminatory approaches among law enforcement and judicial authorities, which have led to cases of professional misconduct. The Human Rights Defender has recommended the provision of mandatory and ongoing training for relevant professionals on domestic and international standards.
60	Support services for victims, such as shelters and psychological and economic assistance, remain insufficient and unevenly distributed throughout the country. There are gaps in interdepartmental coordination in law enforcement, and legislative mechanisms for protecting child victims are incomplete. Furthermore, Armenia lacks a comprehensive national strategy and action plan for preventing domestic and family violence; a draft strategy for 2024-2028 has been developed but not yet adopted.
61	Committee's evaluation
62	[B]
63	While welcoming the amendments to the law that is now entitled the "Law on the Prevention of Family and Domestic Violence and the Protection of Persons Subjected to Family and Domestic Violence", including the provisions establishing free and preferential medical care and services for persons subjected to domestic violence, the Committee is concerned about the reports of the discriminatory application of protection orders. It further regrets the lack of concrete information, including statistical data, on the means of redress provided to victims. It reiterates its recommendation in this regard, and requests further information on the new amendments to the legislative framework, their practical application and their impact on ensuring adequate enforcement and monitoring of protection orders.
64	The Committee welcomes the work carried out to launch the "SAFE YOU" mobile application to facilitate immediate support to victims, and the provision of information in police stations to increase public awareness of domestic violence. It regrets, however, the reports indicating that misconceptions and stereotypes regarding women and domestic violence persist, leading to cases of professional misconduct for discriminatory approaches, including among law enforcement authorities. It reiterates its recommendation in this regard, and requests further information on efforts made to increase awareness among the general public of gender stereotypes and domestic violence, tackling also the root causes and negative effects of domestic violence, and to address the social stigmatization of victims. It further requests information on the progress of development of the mobile application and its expected launch date, and information as to whether mechanisms will be put in place to evaluate the impact of the mobile application on the reporting of cases of violence against women.
65	The Committee notes the data provided on relevant criminal proceedings, and requests additional information on the number of eventual convictions and the sanctions imposed, and on the medical, psychosocial, legal and rehabilitative support services received by victims. It regrets the reports indicating that support services for victims remain insufficient, and reiterates its recommendation in this regard. The Committee requests additional information on the steps taken to increase the number of shelters in the State Party and to ensure their adequate funding.

74	Paragraph 40: Right of peaceful assembly and excessive use of force
75	In line with the Committee's general comment No. 37 (2020), the State Party should:
76	(a) Strengthen its efforts to ensure that all law enforcement officers found responsible for excessive use of force during the March 2008, June 2015, July 2016 and April 2018 events, including those with command responsibility, are held accountable and appropriately sanctioned, and that all the victims of those acts receive adequate compensation and rehabilitation;
77	(b) Review the amendments to the law on freedom of assemblies to bring it into conformity with article 21 of the Covenant;
78	(c) Refrain from undue interference with assembly participants and reduce police presence at peaceful demonstrations;
79	(d) Ensure that impartial and thorough investigations are undertaken without delay by the public prosecutor's office into all allegations of the excessive use of force and arbitrary arrest and detention by State agents at protests, and ensure that the perpetrators are prosecuted and, if found guilty, that they are punished, and that the victims have access to adequate remedies;
80	(e) Ensure that domestic laws and regulations on the use of force are in full conformity with the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials and the United Nations Human Rights Guidance on Less-Lethal Weapons in Law Enforcement, that all law enforcement officers systematically receive training on the use of force, especially in the context of demonstrations, and the employment of non-violent means and crowd control, and that the principles of necessity and proportionality are strictly adhered to in practice during the policing of demonstrations.
81	Summary of the information received from the State Party
82	(a) Following the fatal injury of a police officer during the riots in Yerevan 1 March 2008, the case was referred for pretrial investigation in accordance with article 225 (3) of the Criminal Code (2003). Report on follow-up to the concluding observations of the Human Rights Committee*
Addendum

Evaluation of the information on follow-up to the concluding observations on Armenia

Concluding observations (133rd session): CCPR/C/ARM/CO/3, 3 November 2021

Follow-up paragraphs:

16, 40 and 42

Information received from State Party: CCPR/C/ARM/FCO/3, 21 January 2025

16 [B], 40 [C] [B] and 42 [B]

Paragraph 16: Violence against women
The State Party should redouble its efforts to prevent and combat all forms of violence against women effectively, including domestic and sexual violence, in particular by:
(a) Revising the law on domestic violence to ensure a victim-centred approach that guarantees access to immediate means of redress and protection;
(b) Establishing an effective mechanism to encourage the reporting of cases of violence against women and by intensifying efforts to address the social stigmatization of victims;
(c) Ensuring that all cases of violence against women are promptly and thoroughly investigated, that perpetrators are prosecuted and, if convicted, are punished with appropriate sanctions and that victims have access to effective remedies and means of protection, including sufficient, safe and adequately funded shelters and suitable medical, psychosocial, legal and rehabilitative support services throughout the country, during the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic and beyond;
(d) Considering ratifying the Council of Europe Convention on Preventing and Combating Violence against Women and Domestic Violence.

* Adopted by the Committee at its 144th session (23 June-17 July 2025). 1 Submission available at
https://tbinternet.ohchr.org/_layouts/15/TreatyBodyExternal/FollowUp.aspx?Treaty=CCPR&Lang=e n.
GE.25-11922 (E) 240725 240725

CCPR/C/144/2/Add.1
Summary of the information received from the State Party
(a) On 1 July 2024, amendments to the 2017 Law on the Prevention of Domestic Violence, the Protection of Victims of Domestic Violence and the Restoration of Peace in the Family entered into force, including amendment of the title to "Law on the Prevention of Family and Domestic Violence and the Protection of Persons Subjected to Family and Domestic Violence" and changes to 11 of the 23 articles. The amendments are aimed at increasing the effectiveness of the fight against domestic violence, raising public awareness and improving social and psychological support services provided to victims of violence.
The existing definitions and main concepts in the Law were clarified and brought into line with the definitions in the Criminal Code. For example, the definition of domestic violence was changed to include violence regardless of the circumstances of cohabitation and that committed between partners, former partners or former family members, and a child who witnessed the violence or suffered the negative consequences thereof is now considered a victim of violence. The definition of the conciliation procedure has been repealed, and the Law establishes free and preferential medical care and services for persons subjected to domestic violence. The deadlines for the implementation of urgent intervention and protection-oriented decisions have been revised.
Furthermore, a centralized data-collection system was launched to register cases of domestic violence, in order to streamline activities to protect persons subjected to domestic violence. The data collected will serve as a basis for developing further strategic plans and activities.
(b) Work is under way to launch a mobile application, entitled "SAFE YOU", which will allow victims of violence to promptly call the police and receive support.
To raise public awareness of domestic violence, information corners have been set up in police units, providing literature on domestic violence, including information leaflets and "SAFE YOU" application posters, and information on support centres, hotlines and organizations providing services to victims of domestic violence.
(c) The Investigative Committee produces semi-annual and annual reports on cases of domestic violence.
In 2023, 1,848 criminal proceedings related to domestic violence were investigated by the Investigative Committee, compared to 730 in 2020, 556 in 2021 and 960 in 2022. Of the 1,848 criminal proceedings investigated in 2023: 338 were completed with indictments (compared to 144 in 2020, 129 in 2021 and 122 in 2022); 8 proceedings were completed with final acts (proceedings of medical coercion) and sent to court; 557 proceedings were terminated (compared to 358 in 2020, 252 in 2021 and 301 in 2022), of which 463 were terminated on rehabilitative grounds, 90 on non-rehabilitative grounds and 4 on other grounds; 144 are in a passive stage; 14 were forwarded to the appropriate jurisdiction; 179 were combined; and 608 proceedings were passed to the following year.
Of the 349 defendants involved in the 338 criminal proceedings completed with indictments, 259 were victims' spouses. A total of 359 individuals were recognized as victims. For 152 individuals, criminal prosecution was not initiated or was terminated on non-rehabilitative grounds.
(d) A strategic plan for the implementation of gender policy in Armenia for the period 2024-2028 is currently being developed. The current document sets out six priorities: overcoming gender discrimination in all areas of management and at the decision-making level; encouraging gender-sensitive approaches in work activities and reducing the gender gap in the workforce; overcoming gender discrimination in the field of education and science; ensuring equal opportunities for women and men in the health sector; ensuring prevention of and protection from gender-based violence and discrimination; and developing gendersensitive and gender-responsive approaches to climate change.
Under the fifth priority of the strategic plan, action is envisaged to ratify the Council of Europe Convention on Preventing and Combating Violence against Women and Domestic Violence.

2

GE.25-11922

CCPR/C/144/2/Add.1
Summary of the information received from the national human rights institution
The Office of the Human Rights Defender notes that, despite legislative progress, gaps remain in the prevention and elimination of domestic violence, particularly concerning the legal provisions and their implementation. Article 12 (1) of the 2017 Law prohibits the application of emergency intervention or protection orders against minors or incapacitated persons, which is problematic as regards the application of protection measures for victims. Misconceptions and stereotypes regarding women and domestic violence persist and are rooted throughout society, including discriminatory approaches among law enforcement and judicial authorities, which have led to cases of professional misconduct. The Human Rights Defender has recommended the provision of mandatory and ongoing training for relevant professionals on domestic and international standards.
Support services for victims, such as shelters and psychological and economic assistance, remain insufficient and unevenly distributed throughout the country. There are gaps in interdepartmental coordination in law enforcement, and legislative mechanisms for protecting child victims are incomplete. Furthermore, Armenia lacks a comprehensive national strategy and action plan for preventing domestic and family violence; a draft strategy for 2024-2028 has been developed but not yet adopted.
Committee's evaluation
[B]
While welcoming the amendments to the law that is now entitled the "Law on the Prevention of Family and Domestic Violence and the Protection of Persons Subjected to Family and Domestic Violence", including the provisions establishing free and preferential medical care and services for persons subjected to domestic violence, the Committee is concerned about the reports of the discriminatory application of protection orders. It further regrets the lack of concrete information, including statistical data, on the means of redress provided to victims. It reiterates its recommendation in this regard, and requests further information on the new amendments to the legislative framework, their practical application and their impact on ensuring adequate enforcement and monitoring of protection orders.
The Committee welcomes the work carried out to launch the "SAFE YOU" mobile application to facilitate immediate support to victims, and the provision of information in police stations to increase public awareness of domestic violence. It regrets, however, the reports indicating that misconceptions and stereotypes regarding women and domestic violence persist, leading to cases of professional misconduct for discriminatory approaches, including among law enforcement authorities. It reiterates its recommendation in this regard, and requests further information on efforts made to increase awareness among the general public of gender stereotypes and domestic violence, tackling also the root causes and negative effects of domestic violence, and to address the social stigmatization of victims. It further requests information on the progress of development of the mobile application and its expected launch date, and information as to whether mechanisms will be put in place to evaluate the impact of the mobile application on the reporting of cases of violence against women.
The Committee notes the data provided on relevant criminal proceedings, and requests additional information on the number of eventual convictions and the sanctions imposed, and on the medical, psychosocial, legal and rehabilitative support services received by victims. It regrets the reports indicating that support services for victims remain insufficient, and reiterates its recommendation in this regard. The Committee requests additional information on the steps taken to increase the number of shelters in the State Party and to ensure their adequate funding.
While noting with satisfaction the information that a strategic plan for the implementation of gender policy in Armenia for the period 2024-2028 is being developed, and that action is envisaged under one of the plan's priorities to ratify the Council of Europe Convention on Preventing and Combating Violence against Women and Domestic Violence, the Committee regrets the reports indicating that the plan has yet to be adopted. It requests further information on the progress of the adoption and implementation of the plan and on the

(b) The Constitution and the Electoral Code define the mechanisms and procedures for the implementation of the right to elect and to be elected, including mechanisms of restriction and general criteria. The right to be elected may be restricted on two grounds: (a) persons lacking active legal capacity as declared by a civil judgment of a court having entered into force; and (b) persons sentenced by a criminal judgment having entered into force and serving a punishment.
The limitation of a person's legal capacity inevitably leads to a possible restriction of the rights and freedoms of this person in certain legal relations. For this reason, the approach enshrined in the Constitution and Electoral Code is justified and legitimate.
Not all persons with intellectual and/or psychosocial disabilities are recognized as "incapacitated"; therefore, legislatively and in practice, persons with disabilities (including intellectual and/or psychosocial disabilities) have the right to vote and exercise that right.
Another reason for the deprivation of the right to be elected is the conviction and serving of a punishment under a sentence that has entered into force for any crimes.
The non-nomination of persons as candidates at the time of imprisonment is not a deprivation of the electoral right, but a temporary suspension. When the sentence is complete and the individual is released, the individual will enjoy the right to be elected. As such, the constitutionally fixed restrictions on the right to be elected are justified, meeting the interests of society and complying with the principle of proportionality of fundamental rights and freedoms.
(c) Under article 17 of the Electoral Code, local authorities must ensure that polling stations are accessible to voters with limited mobility or visual impairments. The Central Electoral Commission may set additional accessibility standards, as outlined in its decision No. 17-N of 24 March 2022.
In September 2024, a revised legislative package was submitted to the National Assembly, proposing reforms to enhance electoral transparency, fairness and efficiency. Some of the key reforms include the following:
� Stronger financial oversight of political parties, with distinct mechanisms for election and non-election periods.
� Improved voting access for individuals with mobility impairments, including the option to vote at a more accessible polling station. The application for inclusion in the voter list of an accessible polling station may be submitted electronically.
� Stricter standards for the selection of polling stations, ensuring ease of entry and mobility for persons with disabilities. Certain measures are also planned to facilitate the exercise of voting rights for individuals with visual impairments, ensuring they can fully participate in the electoral process.
Taking into account the rapid development of technologies, the Central Electoral Commission is considering the most up-to-date and effective solutions for voters with visual impairments.

GE.25-11922

7

CCPR/C/144/2/Add.1
Summary of the information received from the national human rights institution
The Office of the Human Rights Defender notes that there are several systemic barriers to the political and public participation of persons with disabilities in Armenia. These barriers primarily concern: (a) inaccessible election precincts and environmental obstacles, such as lack of ramps and absence of nearby transport and proper road crossings, which hinder independent access to polling stations; (b) inaccessible digital platforms, such as e-draft.am, the website used for public consultations on draft legislation; (c) legal restrictions under article 48 (4) of the Constitution, which deny voting rights to individuals declared by a court to be "incapacitated"; and (d) limited accommodation for persons with mobility impairments during elections.
Comprehensive reforms are required to ensure accessibility in electoral processes, public consultations and infrastructure, including legal amendments, improved monitoring, inclusive construction standards and expanded training and education programmes.
Committee's evaluation
[B]
The Committee welcomes the reforms included in the legislative package submitted to the National Assembly in September 2024 proposing amendments and supplements to the Electoral Code, in particular regarding the implementation of new tools for financial oversight and the measures established to increase the accessibility of polling stations to persons with disabilities. It is, however, concerned about the information indicating that institutional barriers to the political participation of persons with disabilities remain. It regrets that legal restrictions under article 48 (4) of the Constitution remain, denying persons recognized by a court as "incapacitated" the right to elect and to be elected and the right to participate in referendums. The Committee reiterates its recommendations in this regard and requests further information: (a) on whether any administrative proceedings were initiated by the Central Electoral Commission during the reporting period and, if so, whether any violations were found to be substantiated; (b) on any further steps taken to revise eligibility requirements to ensure there are no undue limitations on the right to stand for presidential and legislative elections; and (c) on the progress of the adoption of the legislative package and on the new tools to be implemented.
Recommended action: A letter should be sent informing the State Party of the discontinuation of the follow-up procedure. The information requested should be included in the State Party's next periodic report.
Next periodic report due: 2028 (country review in 2029, in accordance with the predictable review cycle).

Looking at this Armenia example, I can already see clear grading patterns emerging: a B grade tends to correspond to concrete legislative action taken but with gaps in implementation or evidence, while a C grade reflects described investigations or proceedings that remain pending, unresolved, or lack follow-through like compensation.

For para 42, I notice something interesting — even a legislative package merely *submitted* to parliament (not yet adopted) earned a B because it had substantive reform content and was paired with other partial measures, contrasting with cases where a "bill stalled for years" only earns a C. This suggests the grading weighs concreteness and momentum of reform, not just formal completion, and the recommended action here was discontinuation of the follow-up procedure, folding the remainder into the next periodic review.

The core distinction I'm seeing between B and C grades is whether the State took concrete steps toward the specific recommendation — amending a law, adopting a system, submitting a substantive bill — versus simply describing the existing framework or reporting activity without demonstrating the actual outcome asked for. With 13 addenda downloaded covering roughly 250-350 graded sub-items, I have enough material for a solid analysis.

Both are good and they're complementary — the first is "study the casebook", the second is "sit the exam". I'd do them in that order.

I've started. From that page I've pulled the Committee's own **follow‑up assessment reports** (the `CCPR/C/<session>/2/Add.*` addenda) for its **138th, 141st, 144th and 145th sessions** (2023–2025) — ~40 country evaluations, each with 3 follow‑up paragraphs, State reply, NGO/NHRI input, the Committee's reasoning, and the grade (often sub‑graded, e.g. "40 [C][B]").

Already, from one entry (Armenia, 144th session), the conventions are visible:
- **B** — law amended *and in force*, data system launched, but statistics/implementation evidence missing → partial.
- **B** — a substantive reform **bill submitted** to parliament with real content, plus partial administrative measures → still B (contrast with a bill merely "pending for years", which is C).
- **C** — investigations and activity *described*, but the recommended outcome (accountability, compensation) not shown → "information provided but does not implement".

**Plan**

1. **Now** — I read all the addenda I've pulled and produce a calibration guide: operational criteria per grade, the decision rules at each boundary (A/B, B/C, C/E), and real worked examples. Saved into the project as a reference the grading scripts can be checked against.
2. **Then** — the blind test. You give me the State follow‑up report + the NGO/NHRI submissions for cases **outside** sessions 138/141/144/145 (so it's genuinely blind), I grade each paragraph, and we compare to the Rapporteur's final grades.

28	The State Party should take all steps necessary to ensure that all acts relating to the assignment of a sex to intersex children performed without their free and informed consent are specifically prohibited, except in cases where such interventions are absolutely necessary for medical reasons and the best interests of the child have been duly taken into account. The State Party should also ensure that all victims have access to remedies, including through a revision of the application of statutes of limitation for violations in childhood, taking steps to ensure that all victims have access to their health records and considering the establishment of a dedicated compensation fund.
29	Summary of the information received from the State Party
30	Under the Act on the Protection of Children with Variations in Sexual Development, effective from 22 May 2021, a new section 1631e was inserted in the Civil Code. According to section 1631e, it is prohibited to align children diagnosed with sexual development variants to an assigned sex if they are unable to consent. Parents or court-appointed curators may not consent on behalf of the child. Under section 1631e (2) and (3), surgical intervention on a child's internal or external genitalia is permitted with parental consent only if the procedure cannot wait until the child is able to consent, and only following ratification by the family court.
