content.thinking:
I have complete records now for Denmark, Namibia, and Paraguay, so I'll commit blind grades for these three before handling the US separately, starting with Denmark's follow-up paragraphs on domestic violence, solitary confinement, and migrant/asylum rights.

For domestic violence, the state's follow-up describes ex officio prosecution with binding DPP guidelines on interrelational violent crimes, mandatory training and risk-assessment tools for investigators, the 2014-2017 national action plan, and a new government-funded national unit against family violence launching October 2017 with a hotline and legal counselling, plus separate mention of Greenland's strategy.

Now I'm noting Greenland and Faroe's new protective legislation from 2017, including marriage rape provisions, alongside the DIHR's concern that psychological violence still lacks its own criminal offence and isn't consistently applied by courts or covered in DPP guidelines despite links to intimate-partner homicides. Overall Denmark's response shows a well-developed framework with concrete recent steps, though the psychological violence gap remains unresolved.

Moving to para 24 on solitary confinement, I'm laying out its three parts—abolishing it for minors, reducing permissible duration for remand detainees, and requiring regular evaluation to develop alternatives—then checking Denmark's response on the minors provision.

Denmark reports it's largely prohibited but permitted up to 4 weeks (longer for serious crimes, beyond 6 months only for the most serious), with very few actual cases: 1 minor 2009-2015, 2 in 2016, plus 13 minors in disciplinary solitary that year. A January 2017 working group recommended capping disciplinary solitary for minors at 3 days (7 in exceptional cases) with daily association time, and the Ministry of Justice says it's now considering amending the law accordingly. On the remand limb, I'm noting the statutory caps by offence severity and the 2016 figures on solitary confinement usage.

DIGNITY's counter-narrative is that no real reform has happened -- solitary of minors is still legally allowed up to 4 weeks, court-ordered isolation of remand minors persists, and the January 2017 recommendations remain unenacted. Most strikingly, they report disciplinary solitary confinement actually increased from 2,579 cases in 2015 to roughly 2,995 in 2016, following an August 2016 amendment that tripled the length of disciplinary sanctions.

Now assessing item (a) on minors: given no legislative change, only a "being considered" working group recommendation, and Denmark explicitly defending its right to keep remand minors in solitary, this looks like a C-level response at best -- the State reiterated its existing framework without real implementing action, possibly even trending toward E given the concerning rise in numbers.

For (b), remand solitary confinement length: the statutory caps remain unaltered, and though Denmark supplied usage data (37 cases, none exceeding 8 weeks), the actual recommendation was to shorten the permissible length itself, not merely report on how it's used -- so this also lands as C, a reply received but the specific ask unaddressed.

For (c), evaluating effects of disciplinary solitary: Denmark points to its existing reporting and monitoring structure (quarterly/annual reports, monthly checks on minors), which reads as ongoing review rather than the deeper regular evaluation the recommendation called for.

I'm also noting the reporting chain tracks numbers, not effects, and there's no evidence of alternatives being developed -- combined with NGO reports that disciplinary use actually increased, this looks like another C. The DIGNITY submission adds that disciplinary solitary confinement rose while sanction lengths tripled in August 2016, a retrogression signal, though it sits on the disciplinary/Sentence Enforcement Act track rather than the remand/minors focus of the original recommendation -- still relevant since para 24(c) explicitly calls for continued reduction.

Weighing each sub-point: no legislative abolition step (just "considering") points to C; no actual reduction in use points to C; and monitoring without evaluation of effects or alternatives, against an adverse trend, points to C again. The one complication is a January 2017 working-group report with concrete recommendations under MoJ review, which is more substantial than a mere "considering" and could arguably nudge the first sub-point toward B -- though per the calibration standard, anything short of enacted change still defaults to C, so I'm leaning C there while flagging the working-group process as a possible mitigating factor the Committee might credit differently.

I'm also checking whether the rise in adult disciplinary solitary confinement and tripled sanctions falls under any of the paragraph's limbs -- it doesn't, since that paragraph specifically concerns minors, remand length, and evaluation, not adult disciplinary practice, so I won't grade it there but will note it as a flag. My working grade is 24 [C][C][C], with the first limb as the closest candidate for B given the concreteness of the working group's recommendations -- limiting minors' disciplinary confinement to three days and enabling association, which would move it out of solitary confinement under the Mandela Rules definition -- and the MoJ's active consideration of amending the law, which is a step beyond a bare intention.

Still, since nothing has been formally adopted and the working group doesn't touch remand-related solitary confinement of minors (the more serious court-imposed case), while Denmark's response reads as defending the status quo, I'll settle on C for that limb while flagging B as plausible.

Now I'm moving to paragraph 32 on the rights of migrants and asylum seekers, which has five limbs: ensuring non-refoulement guarantees in return and expulsion; making sure migrant/asylum detention is reasonable, necessary, and proportionate with real alternatives in practice; reducing detention length for those awaiting deportation and improving conditions, particularly at Vridsløselille; repealing the November 2015 Aliens Act amendment so detained migrants get full access to legal safeguards including judicial review; and repealing a related amendment I'm still identifying.

Looking at Denmark's response to each: on non-refoulement, it cites the RAB's automatic appeal process, free legal counsel, individualized assessments, and the 2017 suspension of Dublin transfers to Hungary, concluding the recommendation is already fully implemented. On detention proportionality, it points to a preference for less restrictive measures and automatic court review within three days. On conditions, it notes a six-month cap (eighteen in exceptional cases), detention as a last resort, and significant improvements at Vridsløselille since autumn 2016 — reduced lock-up time, more employment and social activities, and at least an hour of outdoor access daily, with the Parliamentary Ombudsman who'd previously criticized conditions now acknowledging the changes in December 2016.

Now I'm looking at Denmark's stance on the remaining recommendations: the government defends keeping the §37k suspension rule since it hasn't yet needed activation and detained migrants can still request judicial review, and it flatly states there are no plans to repeal the asset-seizure rules, despite having confiscated roughly DKK 174,000 across seven cases (with sentimental items like wedding rings exempted). I'm also noting DIGNITY's counterpoint about the broader pattern of restriction — dozens of new limits on asylum seekers, and the February 2017 tightening of the "tolerated stay" regime, where the Minister reportedly said conditions should be made "as unbearable as possible."

I'm now turning to the Danish Helsinki Committee's critique in Annex B: they dispute that Denmark has fully implemented non-refoulement obligations, pointing to UN treaty bodies still finding violations in deportation cases involving Iraq and Egypt, gaps in identifying torture survivors among asylum seekers, and concerns over reliance on diplomatic assurances. They also flag that accompanied children aren't interviewed individually, so risks like FGM or persecution based on sexuality go unassessed, and raise the issue of Somali residence permits being revoked. On detention, they note the latest Aliens Act amendments were explicitly meant to expand its use, and they're pushing Denmark to reconsider — while also questioning how much real scrutiny judges apply in practice.

Denmark simply asserts the framework is "already fully implemented" without taking any new measures, while NGO reports and treaty-body findings point to ongoing violations, gaps in identifying torture victims, and unassessed risks to children. This points toward a C grade: a reply was received restating the existing framework and claiming compliance, but with no concrete steps taken and credible reports contradicting that claim.

For detention, Denmark again just restates the necessity/proportionality framework while NGOs note recent amendments actually increased detention rather than expanding alternatives "in practice" — another C.

For conditions at Vridsløselille, though, Denmark points to a genuine, evidenced improvement in autumn 2016, confirmed independently when the previously critical Parliamentary Ombudsman withdrew its concerns in December 2016. That's a real step forward on the conditions limb, even though detention length wasn't reduced — so this sub-issue merits a B rather than a C.

For §37k specifically, Denmark explicitly refuses to repeal the November 2015 amendment despite the recommendation to do so, defending it on the basis that review "upon request" remains available. That's a clear E — the State openly rejects the recommendation and maintains the very provision it was told to repeal, though the fact it's never been activated is a mitigating factor worth noting, and I could see an argument for C if the Committee weighs "retained access upon request plus never activated" as partial compliance.

Similarly for (e), Denmark explicitly states it has no plans to repeal the asset confiscation rules, defending them on principle. So I'm leaning toward para 32 grading as C/C/B/E/E — mixed, with (c) getting B for genuine improvement, (a)/(b) at C for restating existing framework without new measures, and (d)/(e) at E for outright refusal to repeal. Though I'm second-guessing whether the Committee would be more lenient on (d)/(e), treating limited access or exemptions as mitigating factors worth a C instead.

Locking in my Denmark grades: para 20 as B, para 24 as C/C/C (with (a) possibly closer to B), and para 32 as C/C/B/E/E (with (d)/(e) possibly softer at C). Moving on now to Namibia's follow-up report, which covers non-discrimination in paragraph 10 and prohibition of torture in paragraph 22.

For Namibia's state response — there's no NGO or NHRI submission to cross-reference, and the state's own follow-up is quite thin at just three pages. On 10(a), the state points to bills on marriage and intestate succession that were drafted and submitted to the Minister of Justice after years of research, but these haven't even reached Parliament yet, let alone been enacted. On 10(b), regarding anti-discrimination and hate crime legislation, the state's response reiterates its existing position that Namibian law doesn't discriminate.

The state cites the Constitution and existing acts, essentially arguing that LGBT people aren't discriminated against, which sidesteps the actual recommendation rather than addressing sexual-orientation-specific protections or hate crime legislation directly. Recommendation 10(c), about decriminalizing sodomy and extending domestic violence protections to same-sex relationships, isn't addressed at all. Moving to 10(d) on disability and HIV-positive persons, the state points to the National Human Rights Action Plan's objectives in this area.

Turning to recommendation 22 on torture prevention, I see a bill to criminalize torture is said to be forthcoming in parliament, defined consistently with the Convention Against Torture. The Namibian Police have created an Internal Investigation Directorate to probe torture and ill-treatment claims, with the Ombudsman providing additional oversight, though I need to check what's said about protecting sex workers from prosecution when reporting crimes.

Moving to recommendation 24 on violence against women, I'm reviewing what's reported on awareness campaigns involving traditional leaders, investigations into "passion killings," barriers to prosecuting domestic violence, shelter operations, victim protection from stigmatization, and training for police and judicial officials.

Namibian Police also established a GBV Unit with specially trained officers leading sexual/domestic violence investigations, with some sent for training in Botswana and Hungary. But now assessing without NGO input, I have to weigh the State's account carefully—it's thin and largely restates the framework or describes activity predating the Concluding Observations, with several law reform bills only drafted and submitted to the Minister rather than enacted by Parliament.

For sub-paragraph (a), the marriage/succession reform bills remain at a future-tense drafting stage, not even before Parliament after a decade, so I'm grading this **C**. For (b), the State offers no new legislation and simply denies discrimination occurs without engaging the sexual-orientation-specific ask, so that's also **C** as non-responsive rather than a full refusal. For (c), it isn't addressed at all, which per calibration also merits **C**. I'm now looking at whether (d) is addressed with anything more substantive or if it's similarly generic.

Moving to paragraph 22 on torture: the Bill is only "soon to be tabled," not yet before Parliament, so that legislative ask is **C**. Sub-limb (a) on prosecution and compensation has no concrete information provided. Sub-limb (b) on independent investigation shows an IID established within the Police plus an Ombudsman role — but since the IID sits inside the Police Force itself, it's questionable whether it truly counts as independent, even though the Ombudsman is; there's a partial measure here but no data on actual investigations or outcomes. Sub-limb (c) on sex workers isn't addressed. I'm now checking what's said about training measures.

Given Namibia's repeated pattern of promising this torture bill across multiple reporting cycles without delivery, I'll classify this as C.

For para 24, the (a) awareness campaigns cited are pre-CO or expired frameworks like the 2012-2016 GBV plan, so no new measure exists in the current period — that's a C. The (b) "passion killings" investigation isn't addressed at all, another C, and (c) on magistrate numbers for protection orders shows flat or slightly declining figures with only a proposed structural increase from the Commission.

I'm noting the DV Act training for social workers as some activity, but since it doesn't meet the specific 24-hour protection order requirement, that stays C with maybe a B nod for the training piece. Shelters (d) aren't addressed at all — another C. But (e), on witness protection legislation, gets a clear B since the Witness Protection Act No. 11 of 2017 was actually enacted, alongside the Whistleblower Protection Act.

For (f), police/prosecutor/judge training happened (GBV Unit, officers trained abroad in 2015) but the specific ask about pending legislation on prosecuting sexual violence when a victim withdraws wasn't addressed, so I'm landing on C overall for that limb since the core legislative element is missing. That puts recommendation 24 at [C][C][C][C][B][C].

Turning to Namibia: recommendation 10 comes out C across all limbs since drafts only went to the Minister, the framework was just restated or denied, and other parts weren't addressed or were generic. Recommendation 22 also lands at C given the torture Bill wasn't tabled, the IID isn't independent, and two limbs weren't addressed. For recommendation 24, most limbs are C but (e) stands out as B since Namibia actually enacted the Witness Protection Act No. 11 of 2017. Without an NGO submission to cross-check against, my grades might skew a bit higher than they should — but the State's own report here is genuinely thin, full of bills still pending and frameworks merely restated rather than concrete implementation.

Now moving on to Paraguay's follow-up paragraphs, which cover dictatorship-era violations, pretrial detention safeguards, and judicial independence.

With no NGO submission but a fairly detailed state report, I'm looking at para 13's response documenting the Special Human Rights Unit's progress, including convictions in the Almada-Pérez case and case 53/2017, plus several pending cases against former officials — real concrete progress worth noting.

For reparations under Act 838/96, I'm seeing a mixed picture: compensation processing continued with 17,000 cases handled between 2019-2023, but many claims were refused for not meeting the law's rigid legal criteria, and there's now a pending bill trying to address these gaps.

For the missing persons search, I'm noting concrete but limited progress — the Genetic Databank contacted over 200 families in Paraguay and around 100 in Argentina, collected samples tied to 158 missing persons cases, identified 4 individuals by name, and recovered 37 sets of skeletal remains.

Cooperation with the Argentine Forensic Anthropology Team and exploratory work in Caaguazú show real activity, but budget shortfalls are still stalling excavations at roughly a dozen identified sites, so I'm landing on B — real steps and results, but resources remain insufficient.

Moving to paragraph 29 on pretrial detention, I'm looking at whether Paraguay reduced its use and expanded non-custodial alternatives like bail and electronic monitoring, and whether detention stayed exceptional and brief, including for adolescents — starting with the passage of Act 6350/19, which repealed prior provisions.

There's also a pending bill on lifting pretrial detention once constitutional time-limits expire, a December 2021 cooperation agreement establishing a Committee on Alternative Measures to Deprivation of Liberty across the Supreme Court, Prosecution, and Public Defence, Supreme Court Resolution 1511 setting guidelines to limit pretrial detention and trigger ex officio reviews, and updates to electronic monitoring legislation with ministry-driven regulation and inter-institutional coordination meetings through 2023.

B**, given the concrete legislative and policy steps plus juvenile justice results, though electronic monitoring remains undelivered and there's no data on overall detention reduction. For safeguard (b) — informing detainees of reasons/rights and access to lawyer/family from the outset — the response just restates constitutional articles 12/16/17 and describes existing Public Defence Service and training programs, without offering a concrete new measure ensuring these protections from the very beginning of detention. That's a **C**: generic framework restatement without addressing the specific "from the outset" requirement.

Moving to para 35 on judicial independence, I'm looking at part (a) on combating judicial corruption — measures include the National Anti-Corruption Secretariat, an anti-corruption portal and transparency platform, the 2021-2025 Integrity Plan (Decree 4458/20), prosecution training programs, the Supreme Court's 2020 anti-corruption campaign, the Judicial Ethics Office, and specialized economic crimes courts under Act 6379/19.

This includes Act 6430/19 on transnational bribery and the Special Unit for Economic Crimes with 14 prosecutors handling notable convictions up to 15 years. Given the substantial institutional framework and some concrete results, though the focus is mostly on general corruption and training rather than judicial interference specifically, this warrants a **B** rating.

For part (b) on eradicating interference by other branches and prosecuting related allegations, I'm not finding concrete measures addressing interference specifically — the response focuses on corruption prosecution and ethics offices rather than institutional interference itself.

For part (c) on reviewing laws governing judicial institutions, judge/prosecutor appointments, and prosecutorial independence, I see the constitutional nomination process through the Council of the Judiciary, plus **Act 6814/21**, which established procedures for prosecuting and removing judges, prosecutors, and public defenders, replacing the previous enjuiciamiento law — a meaningful legislative reform touching judicial independence.

I'm also noting **Act 6721/21**, which created a national commission tasked with reviewing administration-of-justice legislation, though it has four years to report so nothing concrete yet, and **Supreme Court Decision 1309/20**, which standardized entrance-exam and promotion criteria for the judiciary. These are real legislative steps addressing the specific ask, but with outcomes still pending given the commission's timeline and no proof yet that independence has improved in practice — so I'm landing on **B** for this item, giving **35 [B][C][B]** overall.

Compiling my blind grades across the Paraguay recommendations: 13 comes out **[B][B][B]**, 29 as **[B][C]**, and 35 as **[B][C][

B]**. Without NGO input to calibrate against, these might run a bit generous, but Paraguay's follow-up report genuinely documents concrete legislative and institutional measures with some tangible results, justifying B for most limbs — the C grades reflect places where the state either just restated the existing framework or sidestepped the specific ask.

With Denmark, Namibia, and Paraguay's blind grades locked in, I'm turning to the US now, which is a heavier lift — the April 2015 State follow-up report won't text-extract, though I do have the October 2015 supplementary reply and the 2017 addendum, plus around fifteen NGO submissions to work through across the US's multiple assessment rounds.

I think the honest path is to post the three completed countries now and take on the US separately rather than rush it.

For Denmark, I want to reconsider the §32(d)/(e) grading — I lean toward E given their explicit refusal to repeal, but I should flag that C is a plausible alternative reading before finalizing.

I'll commit to (d) C for the mitigated response, (e) E for the flat refusal defended on principle. Final Denmark 32: [C][C][B][C][E].

Moving to Denmark 24(a), the working group's concrete recommendations plus MoJ's active consideration of amendment represents more than mere intention but less than a bill submitted to parliament—I'll go with C while noting B remains plausible.

Denmark 24 overall settles as [C][C][C]. Time to write this up.

I have complete, clean records for **Denmark, Namibia and Paraguay** (Concluding Observations + State follow‑up report; for Denmark also the DIHR/NHRI and DIGNITY‑coalition submissions; Namibia and Paraguay had **no** civil‑society submission). I have **not** opened `CCPR/C/125/2/Add.4`, `CCPR/C/126/2/Add.4` or `CCPR/C/140/2/Add.2`.

Here are my committed blind grades for these three. The US is document‑heavy and had multiple assessment rounds — I'll post it in the next message.

---

## DENMARK — CCPR/C/DNK/CO/6 (117th session); follow‑up ¶¶ 20, 24, 32

**¶20 Domestic violence — [B]**
Denmark took concrete measures in the reporting period: a new government‑funded national unit against family/intimate‑partner violence (operational 1 Oct 2017), rollout of evidence‑based risk‑assessment tools (116 investigators certified since 2015), and new legislation in Greenland (April 2017) and the Faroe Islands (March 2017, incl. marital rape and stalking). But no outcome data (reporting/prosecution/sanction figures, uniform district enforcement) and the DIHR documents a real gap — psychological violence still not effectively criminalised or prosecuted. Concrete steps, more needed → **B**.

**¶24 Solitary confinement — [C] [C] [C]**
- (a) *abolish for minors*: not done. Remand solitary confinement of under‑18s remains lawful (up to 4 weeks); the State restates the framework. A January 2017 working group recommended a 3‑day disciplinary‑cell cap and association, and the MoJ "is currently considering" amending the law — process only, nothing enacted → **C** *(could be B if the Committee credits the working‑group process)*.
- (b) *reduce permissible length for remand detainees*: statutory caps unchanged; the State reports usage figures instead of reducing the limits → **C**.
- (c) *regularly evaluate the effects*: a quarterly/annual reporting chain on numbers exists, but no evaluation of *effects* and no development of alternatives; DIGNITY documents that disciplinary solitary confinement actually **increased** (2,579→~2,995 from 2015 to 2016) after sanctions were tripled → **C**.

**¶32 Rights of migrants/asylum seekers — [C] [C] [B] [C] [E]**
- (a) *non‑refoulement guarantees*: the State restates its framework and asserts it has "already… fully implement[ed]" the recommendation; no new measure, and NGO/treaty‑body decisions show continuing violations and unidentified torture victims → **C**.
- (b) *detention reasonable/necessary/proportionate; alternatives in practice*: framework restated; DIGNITY notes the latest Aliens Act amendments were intended to *increase* detention → **C**.
- (c) *reduce length / improve conditions at Vridsløselille*: conditions at Vridsløselille were "significantly improved" in autumn 2016 and the Parliamentary Ombudsman (a former critic) withdrew his concerns in December 2016 — a genuine, independently confirmed step; length not reduced → **B**.
- (d) *repeal the Nov 2015 §37k judicial‑review suspension amendment*: not repealed; the State defends it (review "upon request" retained; never activated) → **C** *(borderline E)*.
- (e) *repeal the asset‑confiscation amendment*: the State expressly states it "does not have any plans on repealing the rules" and defends them on principle → **E** (reflects rejection of the recommendation).

---

## NAMIBIA — CCPR/C/NAM/CO/2 (116th session); follow‑up ¶¶ 10, 22, 24 — *no civil‑society submission; 3‑page State report*

**¶10 Non‑discrimination — [C]**
- (a) marriage/succession bills "drafted and submitted to the Minister of Justice", "will repeal" apartheid‑era laws — drafting stage only → **C**.
- (b) no new legislation; the State asserts "Namibian law does not discriminate" and "LGBT people are not discriminated" — restates the framework, doesn't engage the sexual‑orientation‑specific ask → **C**.
- (c) abolition of the sodomy offence / same‑sex protection under the DV Act — not addressed → **C**.
- (d) disability/HIV discrimination — only a generic reference to NHRAP 2015‑2019 objectives → **C**.

**¶22 Prohibition of torture — [C]**
Anti‑torture Bill "will soon be tabled in parliament" (not tabled/enacted, and long promised); an Internal Investigation Directorate was set up *within the Police Force* (not an independent mechanism as recommended) plus the Ombudsman; sub‑limbs (a) prosecution/compensation and (c) sex workers not addressed. → **C** *(the IID + Ombudsman element is the closest to B)*.

**¶24 Violence against women — [C] [C] [C] [C] [B] [C]**
- (a) awareness with traditional leaders: campaigns cited are 2008–2010 (pre‑CO); National Plan of Action on GBV 2012–2016 expired → **C**.
- (b) investigate "passion killings": not addressed → **C**.
- (c) barriers to prosecuting DV / 24‑hour protection orders / more magistrates: magistrate numbers roughly flat (84/98/92), some training on the DV Act; nothing on 24‑hour availability → **C**.
- (d) operationalise/expand shelters: not addressed → **C**.
- (e) protect victims from stigmatisation/reprisals; **adopt witness‑protection legislation**: the **Witness Protection Act No. 11 of 2017** (and Whistleblower Protection Act No. 10 of 2017) were enacted — a concrete legislative step on the witness‑protection element → **B**.
- (f) train police/prosecutors/judges; adopt pending legislation to continue sexual‑violence prosecutions after a withdrawn complaint: training described; the pending‑legislation element not addressed → **C**.

---

## PARAGUAY — CCPR/C/PRY/CO/4 (126th session); follow‑up ¶¶ 13, 29, 35 — *no civil‑society submission*

**¶13 Dictatorship‑era violations — [B] [B] [B]**
- (a) investigate/prosecute/punish: convictions obtained in the period (case 3154/89, three convicted Dec 2019; case 53/2017, 7 years) plus several active indictments/appeals listed — concrete progress, most cases still pending → **B**.
- (b) prompt/full reparation "irrespective of when the claim was filed": the compensation programme is operating with statistics and a partly‑restored budget (cut in 2021, back to ~2019 level by 2023), but many claims are refused for not meeting Act 838/96 criteria and the fix for older claims is only a pending bill → **B** *(borderline C)*.
- (c) accelerate the search for the missing / identify remains / resource it: Genetic Databank created, families of 158 missing persons sampled, four individuals identified, exhumations and cooperation with the Argentine Forensic Anthropology Team — evidenced progress, but "budgetary challenges" still hinder excavations at ~12 sites → **B**.

**¶29 Pre‑trial detention & safeguards — [B] [C]**
- (a) reduce pre‑trial detention; non‑custodial alternatives incl. for adolescents: Act 6350/19 repealed the restrictive Act 4431/11; Supreme Court Resolution 1511 (2021) on exceptional use and ex‑officio review; an inter‑institutional committee on alternatives; a restorative juvenile‑justice programme with a measurable fall in detained adolescents. Electronic‑monitoring (Act 5863/17 as amended) still not regulated/operational; no overall pre‑trial‑detention figures. Concrete legislative + policy steps, incomplete → **B**.
- (b) inform detainees of reasons/rights, lawyer and family contact from the outset: the State restates constitutional guarantees and existing Public Defence services and training — no concrete new measure on the "from the very beginning of detention" ask → **C**.

**¶35 Independence of the judiciary — [B] [C] [B]**
- (a) combat corruption in the judiciary / awareness among judges, prosecutors, police: extensive institutional build‑out — Anti‑Corruption Secretariat and portal, National Integrity/Transparency/Anti‑Corruption Plan 2021‑2025, specialised economic‑crime/anti‑corruption courts (Act 6379/19), a 14‑prosecutor special unit with sentences up to 15 years → **B**.
- (b) eradicate inter‑branch interference; investigate/prosecute interference: the specific ask (interference by other branches) is not addressed; the corruption measures don't reach it → **C**.
- (c) review the laws/institutions on appointing and disciplining judges and prosecutors to guarantee independence: concrete legislative steps — Act 6814/21 (new discipline/removal procedure), Act 6721/21 (justice‑reform review commission, 4‑year deadline), Supreme Court Decision 1309/20 (merit‑based entry/promotion); outcomes pending → **B**.

---

Summary of my committed calls:

| | Denmark | Namibia | Paraguay |
|---|---|---|---|
| ¶ / grade | 20 **B** · 24 **C/C/C** · 32 **C/C/B/C/E** | 10 **C** · 22 **C** · 24 **C** (24(e) **B**) | 13 **B/B/B** · 29 **B/C** · 35 **B/C/B** |

US next.

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   - **Original**: Set up a basic Python project with a database to store a human rights recommendation, its source, and an implementation status.
   - **Evolved into**: A tool to assess implementation of UN Universal Periodic Review (UPR) recommendations, grading each on the Human Rights Committee's **A–E scale** (CCPR/C/108/2, per ccprcentre.org/follow-up-and-assessment): A = largely implemented/satisfactory, B = partially/steps taken, C = not implemented/no relevant action, D = no information, E = contrary measures/rejection.
   - **US analysis (done)**: Assess implementation of the **347 cycle-3 (2020, A/HRC/46/15) UPR recommendations to the United States** against the cycle-4 pre-sessional documents A/HRC/WG.6/50/USA/2 (OHCHR Compilation) and /3 (Stakeholders' Summary). Output: narrative report grouped by theme + per-recommendation CSV + the OHCHR thematic list `.docx` with column 4 filled. Format must follow a "Malawi example" the user pasted: grouped recommendations (collapsed number ranges), short action phrase in parentheses after the numbers, an **Evidence:** list quoting sources verbatim with the body/organisation named, a reasoned **Assessment:** line.
   - **Denmark/Namibia/Paraguay analysis (done)**: Same method for cycle-3 (2021, UPR38) recommendations graded against cycle-4 (session 52, May 2026) documents — National Report (/1), Compilation (/2), Stakeholders' Summary (/3). User explicitly: "Make sure you get the rights recommendations - not from the last cycle (4th) from the 3rd (2021)." Tanzania/Suriname/Thailand were requested but impossible (no cycle-4 pre-sessionals published yet).
   - **Grading calibration training (done)**: "I want you to train on how to grade for you to know when to give a A, or a B, or a C, or a E." — study the ~15 years of Committee follow-up practice ("jurisprudence") from its own follow-up progress reports and distil the working conventions.
   - **Blind grading test (IN PROGRESS)**: For Denmark (CCPR/C/DNK/CO/6, 117th session), Namibia (CCPR/C/NAM/CO/2, 116th), Paraguay (CCPR/C/PRY/CO/4, 126th), US (CCPR/C/USA/CO/4, 110th): grade the follow-up paragraphs blind from the same documents the Special Rapporteur had (Concluding Observations + State follow-up report + NGO/NHRI follow-up submissions), commit grades in writing, then compare to the Rapporteur's actual grades. **CHEATING PROHIBITION (verbatim commitment)**: do NOT open the Committee's follow-up assessment addendum (`CCPR/C/<session>/2/Add.N` and `INT/CCPR/FUL/...` / `INT/CCPR/FUD/...` letters) for any test country until after posting grades; only read CO + State FCO + NGO/NHRI submissions; only sessions outside 138/141/144/145; post grades before comparing with no post-hoc revision; flag and switch if I already recall a grade.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - UN Universal Periodic Review (UPR) cycles 3 (2017–2022) and 4 (2022–2027); session 36 (US cycle 3), session 38 (DNK/NAM/PRY cycle 3), session 50 (US cycle 4), session 52 (DNK/NAM/PRY cycle 4, May 2026).
   - Human Rights Committee (ICCPR treaty body) follow-up to Concluding Observations: ~3 selected "priority" recommendations, State follow-up report ~3 years after review, NGO/NHRI submissions, Special Rapporteur desk assessment with A–E grades (often sub-graded per lettered limb), follow-up progress reports `CCPR/C/<session>/2` + addenda.
   - Document sourcing: OHCHR cloudfront pattern `https://d2oervbip9wfy4.cloudfront.net/en/<A/HRC/...symbol>` (returns PDF directly); OHCHR treaty body DownloadDraft mechanism (Telerik RadGrid on FollowUp.aspx, 3-level expand; NGO symbols `INT/CCPR/NGS/<CC>/<num>`; fetch `Download.aspx?symbolno=...` page → regex `DownloadDraft.aspx\?key=([^"'&]+)` → curl/urllib with URL-encoded self-authenticating key).
   - Text extraction: `pdftotext -nopgbrk` (Git for Windows); docx via `C:\Users\rolan\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\docx_dump.py` (stdlib zipfile + xml.etree) or `python-docx`.
   - Python stack: stdlib-only `recommendations/` package; helper `scripts/` use `python-docx`. Cluster-based grading (theme → default grade + summary + rationale + verbatim quotes) with regex KEYWORD overrides (last match wins).
   - SQLite schema with `UNIQUE(document_symbol, paragraph)`, `Grade`/`Position` enums, migration via `PRAGMA table_info` + `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN`.

3. Files and Code Sections:
   - `recommendations/db.py` — SQLite connection + `SCHEMA` (recommendations table) + `init_db` with `_migrate()` adding `assessment_evidence` and `action_summary` columns. `DEFAULT_DB_PATH`.
   - `recommendations/models.py` — `Grade(str,Enum)` {NOT_ASSESSED,A,B,C,D,E} with `.label`, `.committee_meaning`; `_GRADE_LABELS`, `_COMMITTEE_MEANINGS`; `Position(str,Enum)` {supported,noted,supported_noted,unknown} with `.parse()`; `Recommendation` dataclass (fields incl. text, country, mechanism, cycle, session, document_symbol, paragraph, recommending_state, position, themes, affected_persons, sdgs, date_issued, annotation_id, source_url, grade, action_summary, assessment_rationale, assessment_sources, assessment_evidence, assessed_at) with `.citation`, `.from_row()`.
   - `recommendations/repository.py` — `RecommendationRepository`: `add`, `add_many` (INSERT OR IGNORE), `get`, `list(grade,position,theme,paragraph)`, `count_by_grade`, `set_grade(rec_id, grade, rationale, sources, evidence, action)`, `delete`, context manager.

The Human Rights Committee (CCPR) ccpr@ohchr.org

SUBMISSION OF FOLLOW-UP DOCUMENT TO THE UNITED NATIONS HUMAN RIGHTS COMMITTEE IN RELATION TO THE CONCLUDING OBSERVATIONS ON THE SIXTH PERIODIC REPORT OF DENMARK (CCPR/C/DNK/CO/6)

21 AUGUST 2017

On 15 August 2017, the UN Human Rights Committee requested Denmark in its concluding observations to provide the Committee within one year with follow-up information in response to the Committee's recommendations relating to paragraphs 20 (domestic violence), 24 (solitary confinement) and 32 (rights of aliens, including migrants, refugees and asylum seekers).
Denmark provided the Committee with a report containing follow-up information on the above-mentioned recommendations on 19 July 2017.
On this background, the Danish Institute for Human Rights - Denmark�s National Human Rights Institution (DIHR) hereby submits the following comments on the follow-up information provided by Denmark on 19 July 2017.
Please be advised, that the following comments should be read in conjunction with the follow-up report submitted by Denmark.
COMMENTS REGARDING RECOMMENDATION 20:
Psychological violence Regarding Denmark's efforts to effectively combat domestic violence, DIHR would like to emphasise that the UN CEDAW Committee in its concluding observations on Denmark's eight periodic report (2015)i repeated its concern that Denmark has no explicit provisions to ensure the protection of women from psychological violence. On this basis, the Committee recommended that Denmark should adopt a legislative framework that explicitly provides for the protection of women from

psychological violence, in line with article 33 of the Istanbul Conventionii. However, the Danish Ministry of Justice states in a state report to the Group of Experts on Action against Violence against Women and Domestic Violence (2017)iii that article 33 of the Istanbul Convention on psychological violence does not require change of legislation as it is already criminalized in sections 245(2)iv, 260v and 266vi of the Danish Criminal Codevii. Thus, the exercise of psychological violence is still not recognised as a separate criminal offense in the Danish Criminal Code and no concrete definitions of psychological violence have been developed.
DIHR would like to accentuate that the present state of play concerning Danish case law shows that psychological violence despite the legal possibility to apply the above sections is not recognized as a crime by the judiciaries. Studies of case law (2012-2013)viii on sections 245(2) and 260 of the Danish Criminal Code shows that neither sections have been applied in judgements to state psychological violence against a current partner. Nor have the scant judgements passed on section 266 of the Danish Criminal Code against a former partner referred to the offense as psychological violence. Further, DIHR would like to draw the Committee's attention to a recent Danish study (2016)ix that indicates a specific link between psychological violence and killings of women by their intimate partners in Denmark.
In relation to para. 3 in Denmark's follow-up report, it follows that the Director of Public Prosecution has issued binding guidelines for the police and the prosecutors on handling of criminal cases, including cases on domestic violence (guidelines on Interrelational Violent Crimes updated on 1 July 2016x). In that connection, DIHR would like to note that these guidelines do not entail information or relevant case law regarding threats and other forms of psychological violence.
Further, it follows from para. 6 in Denmark's follow-up report that the Director of Public Prosecution has developed binding guidelines on how the police and prosecution service must handle cases concerning restraining orders, exclusion- and expulsion orders.xi DIHR, however, notes that these guidelines do not refer to psychological violence.
COMMENTS REGARDING RECOMMENDATION 24:
Children placed in isolation In relation to the numbers concerning children placed in isolation, DIHR would like to draw the Committee's attention to the fact that recent figures by the Danish Director of Public Prosecution shows, that children suspected of criminal activities in 15 cases was placed into isolation during the year 2016.
2/4

Further, the numbers show that one out of the 15 cases was conducted with no legal basis in the Danish Administration of Justice Act. Additionally, nine of the 15 cases was inconsistent with the Danish Administration of Justice Act.xii
The Danish Director of Public Prosecution stated in April 2017 that he found the use of isolation in the cases unfortunate, and requested the local police in question to follow up on the cases. Furthermore, he stated that he intended to closely monitor the area during 2017.
COMMENTS REGARDING RECOMMENDATION 32:
Non-refoulement in cases concerning children In relation to Denmark's assessment of non-refoulement in cases concerning children DIHR would like to inform the Committee of the following practice that has come to the attention of DIHR:
According to information received by DIHR accompanied children is generally not heard individually in the asylum procedure (exceptions might occur on a very limited basis), but parents are instead asked about their child's potential conflicts if returned.
The result of this procedure is that if the child has experienced a conflict relevant for the asylum case, but unknown to the parent (e.g. if the child is homosexual and has not informed his/her parents) or the child risks inhumane treatment etc. from the parents or with the parents' consent (e.g. if the parents plan to allow their girl-child be circumcised), a sufficiently thorough assessment of the child's risk of refoulement is not properly ensured.
Immature unaccompanied minors It follows from para. 45 in Denmark's follow-up report, that all unaccompanied minors, who are assessed to be mature enough for the asylum proceedings, have access to an individual asylum procedure.
In this connection DIHR would like to emphasise that in accordance with Danish Aliens Act (section 9 c (3)(1)), children who are deemed immature to undergo an asylum procedure will not have their asylum claim processed until a later stage where they are deemed sufficiently mature. They can be granted a residence permit as an unaccompanied child, if they will be in an emergency situation upon return to their country of origin. But if they e.g. have contact to family relations at their country of origin, they cannot be granted this residence permit. They can however also not be returned, as their asylum claim has not yet been processed.
3/4

NGO's have reported to DIHR that they have become aware of examples of children in the asylum process, who are not granted a temporary residence permit under the special regulation for unaccompanied children, e.g. because they have family in the country of origin. They therefore remain in the asylum centres until they are sufficiently mature to undergo an asylum process. The NGO's report that this is an amendment in practice, as the children previously were allowed to live with relatives or be part of normal society, whereas the authorities state that no amendment has taken place. Regardless, the consequence is that the children will remain as unaccompanied in the asylum facilities for children, awaiting being mature enough to have their case handled by authorities. The group reportedly concerns some 26 children as young as 9/10 years old. Yours sincerely, Christoffer Badse Department Director, Monitoring

import sys, urllib.request, urllib.parse, ssl, json, os
ctx = ssl.create_default_context(); ctx.check_hostname = False; ctx.verify_mode = ssl.CERT_NONE

# argv: outdir  jsonspec
# jsonspec = {"prefix": {"id": "key", ...}, ...}
outdir = sys.argv[1]
spec = json.loads(sys.argv[2])
os.makedirs(outdir, exist_ok=True)
for prefix, d in spec.items():
    for k, key in d.items():
        u = "https://tbinternet.ohchr.org/_layouts/15/TreatyBodyExternal/DownloadDraft.aspx?key=" + urllib.parse.quote(key, safe="")
        req = urllib.request.Request(u, headers={"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0"})
        try:
            b = urllib.request.urlopen(req, context=ctx, timeout=90).read()
        except Exception as e:
            print(prefix, k, "ERR", e); continue
        ext = "pdf" if b[:4] == b"%PDF" else ("docx" if b[:2] == b"PK" else "bin")
        p = os.path.join(outdir, f"{prefix}_{k}.{ext}")
        open(p, "wb").write(b)
        print(prefix, k, len(b), ext)

    i=x.lower().find('follow-up',i+1)
    if i>60000: break
"

21	Paragraph 20: Domestic violence
22	The State party should continue its efforts to combat domestic violence effectively, in particular violence against women, by ensuring effective reporting on acts of domestic violence, investigations, prosecutions and sanctions of perpetrators. The State party should ensure that guidelines on the application of its legislation are enforced by all police districts in a uniform manner. It should continue to provide training to all professionals involved in preventing and combating domestic violence.

25	The police initiates investigations upon receiving a complaint or ex officio when there is a reasonable presumption that an offence has been committed. The Prosecution Service initiates criminal proceedings ex officio when evidence of a crime is found. A new

The Director also developed guidelines on restraining, exclusion and expulsion orders.
37	Under the national action plan against violence in intimate relations (2014-2017), a number of projects were implemented to educate professionals. Basic training in the handling of criminal cases, including domestic violence, is mandatory for all new legal staff in the Prosecution Service. Students at the Police Academy are trained in the prevention and detection of violence. The national centre for crime prevention, established in 2012, offers a two-day training course on the evidence-based risk assessment tools (116 investigators and caseworkers have obtained certification since 2015).
38	The State party reiterates information contained in its sixth periodic report (CCPR/C/DNK/6, para. 110) on the strategy and action plan against violence (2014-2017) in place in Greenland. The Danish act on restraining, exclusion and expulsion orders entered into force for Greenland (with adjusted conditions) on 1 April 2017. It enables the Chief Police Constable in Greenland to, inter alia, issue restraining orders.
39	Various measures have also been taken by the government in the Faroe Islands, including information pamphlets on avenues for protection and counselling; new legislation in force since March 2017 containing provisions protecting persons from violence, assault, harassment and stalking, authorizing the temporary expulsion of abusive persons from the home and providing for clear rules regarding restraining orders; and Criminal Code amendments in force since March 2017 that, inter alia, extend the statute of limitations for certain sexual offences, expand the definition of rape to include coercion and abuse of a person in a helpless state/situation, and add offences committed within marriage.
40	Information from the national human rights institution
41	There is no concrete definition or criminalization of psychological violence as a separate crime. The Ministry of Justice considers psychological violence to be criminalized under sections 245 (2), 260 and 266 of the Criminal Code on offences generally relating to bodily harm and coercion by violence or threats. Despite these provisions, case law shows that psychological violence is not recognized as a crime by the judiciary. A Danish study (2016) found a specific link between psychological violence and killings of women by their intimate partners.
42	There is no reference to psychological violence in the guidelines issued by the Director of Public Prosecutions referred to by the State party.
43	Committee's evaluation
44	[A]: The Committee welcomes the various legislative and policy measures taken to prevent and combat domestic violence in Denmark, Greenland and the Faroe Islands, including the update to the guidelines on interrelational violent crimes (1 July 2016), the operationalization of the national unit to combat violence in family and intimate relations (1 October 2017), the extension of the Danish Act on Restraining, Exclusion and Expulsion Orders to Greenland (1 April 2017), and the new legislation and Criminal Code amendments passed in the Faroe Islands (March 2017) that, inter alia, provide for clear rules regarding restraining orders, extend the statute of limitations for certain sexual offences and expand the definition of rape. The Committee requires further information on: (a) the practical impact of these measures, including of the national action plan (2014-2017) and the strategy and action plan against violence (2014-2017) of Greenland, on preventing domestic violence and facilitating the reporting of domestic violence, and on ensuring investigations, prosecutions and the sanctioning of perpetrators in Denmark, Greenland and the Faroe Islands (please provide relevant statistics since 2016); (b) the content of the latest

50	Paragraph 24: Solitary confinement
51	The State party should bring its legislation and practice on solitary confinement into line with international standards as reflected in the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (the Nelson Mandela Rules), by abolishing solitary confinement of minors and reducing the total length of permissible solitary confinement for remand detainees even if it is used as a measure of last resort. The State party should regularly evaluate the effects of solitary confinement in order to continue to reduce it and to develop alternative measures where necessary.
52	Summary of State party's reply
53	The Administration of Justice Act sets out strict limits for the use of solitary confinement and requires compliance with the principles of necessity and proportionality. Solitary confinement of persons under 18 for up to four weeks is possible in exceptional circumstances when the nature of the crime and risk of tampering with the investigation warrants it, and extension is possible beyond six months for persons suspected of the most serious crimes. Two minors were held in solitary confinement during pretrial detention in 2016 (charged with terrorism and severe violations of weapons legislation). Pretrial detention, including solitary confinement, is ordered by district courts and can be appealed to the High Court and to the Supreme Court under certain conditions.
54	Solitary confinement can also be ordered by administrative decision for either punitive (disciplinary cell) or preventive reasons (exclusion from association). It concerns only a limited number of minors (13 in 2016), given that most minors get suspended sentences/community service or may serve their sentence outside the prison system. Time in solitary confinement is generally served in normal cells, with access to books, television and occupational activities. The Ministry of Justice was considering amendments to the law following the recommendations made by a working group under the Danish Prison and Probation Service in January 2017 that placement in a disciplinary cell should not exceed three days (seven days in exceptional circumstances) and should be implemented in ways that permit association with others for a few hours during work or study (this would not constitute solitary confinement as defined by the Nelson Mandela Rules).
55	Under the Administration of Justice Act, solitary confinement during pretrial detention cannot exceed two weeks when charges can lead to imprisonment of up to four years; four weeks where the maximum sentence faced would be six years; and eight weeks where the maximum sentence faced would be more than six years. It may be extended beyond eight weeks (up to six months) if crucial consideration regarding the investigation so requires and if the offence is expected to lead to imprisonment of at least two years; and beyond six months in cases involving the most serious forms of crime.
56	The use of solitary confinement is kept under close review, with reporting obligations for police districts (quarterly), State prosecutors (annually) and the Director of Public Prosecutions (annually). The department of prisons and probation conducts monthly monitoring of the use of disciplinary cells in relation to minors to clarify whether such use has been absolutely necessary.

58	
59	CCPR/C/125/2/Add.4
60	Information from the national human rights institution
61	A total of 15 minors suspected of crimes were placed in solitary confinement in 2016; one such placement lacked any legal basis, and nine others were inconsistent with the Administration of Justice Act.
62	Information from non-governmental organizations
63	Solitary confinement continues to be permitted by law. Despite its limited use for minors (15 cases in 2016) and positive efforts to limit prolonged isolation (beyond 15 days), the relevant legislation is contrary to international standards. Prolonged court-imposed solitary confinement for remand prisoners remains a concern; it exceeded two weeks in nearly 60 per cent of the 37 cases in 2016.
64	The rate of use of solitary confinement as a disciplinary measure remains high, except for children. The number of cases in which it was used increased from 2,579 in 2015 to an estimated 2,995 cases in 2016, with half of the cases involving long-term confinement of 15 or more days. The increase was attributed to the recent strict regulation on unlawful possession (and use) of mobile phones (cited in 219 out of the 222 cases of solitary confinement for 15 days or more in 2016).
65	Non-governmental organizations also report on the deleterious health impact of solitary confinement as documented extensively in health studies (see annex A of the submission of non-governmental organizations).
66	Committee's evaluation
67	[C]: While taking note of the extensive information provided on solitary confinement and efforts to monitor and reduce its use, especially for prolonged periods of time, the Committee regrets that the State party neither abolished solitary confinement for minors nor reduced the total length of permissible solitary confinement for remand detainees even if it is used as a measure of last resort. It requires information on any amendments to the law adopted following the issuance of the recommendations regarding placement in a disciplinary cell made by the working group under the prison and probation service in January 2017. The Committee reiterates its recommendations.
68	Paragraph 32: Rights of aliens, including migrants, refugees and asylum seekers
69	The State party should, while taking measures to control immigration, ensure their full compliance with the rights of migrants, including asylum seekers, as protected under the Covenant. In particular, the State party should:
70	(a) Ensure that its policies and practices related to the return and expulsion of migrants and asylum seekers afford sufficient guarantees of respect for the principle of non-refoulement under the Covenant;
71	(b) Ensure that the detention of migrants and asylum seekers is reasonable, necessary and proportionate in the light of the circumstances, in accordance with the Committee's general comment No. 35 (2014) on liberty and security of person, and that alternatives to detention are found in practice;
72	(c) Consider reducing the length of detention for migrants and asylum seekers who are awaiting deportation and improve the detention conditions of such persons, in particular at the detention facility of Vridsl�selille;
73	(d) Repeal the amendment introduced to the Aliens Act in November 2015 in order to ensure that, in all cases, detained migrants have full access to fundamental legal safeguards, in particular to judicial review of the legality of their detention;
74	(e) Repeal the amendment to the Aliens Act relating to the confiscation of asylum seekers' assets.
75	4
76	
77	CCPR/C/125/2/Add.4
78	Summary of State party's reply
79	Reply relating to paragraph 32 (a)
80	The State party elaborates on the information provided on the asylum procedure under the Aliens Act, including on the automatic appeal against negative asylum decisions that is made to the Refugee Appeals Board. Return decisions are not enforced if an alien in principle has the right to asylum under article 7 of the Aliens Act but is excluded from receiving a residence permit under article 10 of the Aliens Act or article 1 (F) of the Convention relating to the Status of Refugees, and is covered by the principle of nonrefoulement. Such individuals may remain in Denmark on a "tolerated stay" basis until the Refugee Appeals Board decides that there is no longer any danger relating to refoulement. As an example of compliance with the principle of non-refoulement, the Board decided on 3 May 2017 to suspend the transfer of asylum seekers to Hungary under the Dublin Regulation due to systemic deficiencies in the Hungarian asylum system.
81	Reply relating to paragraph 32 (b)
82	Under the Aliens Act, the detention of aliens awaiting deportation is always to be necessary and proportionate. Such cases are subject to individual examination and must be brought before the courts automatically within three days. Financial compensation for unlawful deprivation of liberty can be claimed in court.
83	Reply relating to paragraph 32 (c)
84	Under the provisions of the Aliens Act implementing the European Union return directive (2008/115/EC), the maximum period of detention is 6 months, with extension of up to 18 months possible in exceptional circumstances. Detention is a measure of last resort, applied when aliens do not return voluntarily and less restrictive measures prove insufficient.
85	The living conditions for rejected asylum seekers detained at Vridsl�selille significantly improved in autumn 2016. The Parliamentary Ombudsman (designated as the national preventive mechanism), who had previously criticized the conditions at Vridsl�selille, informed the Ministry of Justice on 19 December 2016 that no further action was required.
86	Reply relating to paragraph 32 (d)
87	A new subparagraph - (k) - introduced into paragraph 37 of the Aliens Act in November 2015, providing for the suspension of the automatic judicial review of detention within three days, was adopted for application in urgent situations entailing a significant increase in the number of asylum seekers and immigrants arriving within a short time. If the suspension provision is activated (no instances as at 14 July 2017), judicial review of detention may be initiated upon the alien's request rather than automatically. Thus, access to such review remains available.
88	Reply relating to paragraph 32 (e)
89	Asylum seekers' assets may be seized to cover the expenses for maintenance during the asylum procedure. Any cash exceeding the value of DKr 10,000 (1,300) will be seized. Assets exceeding the same value, except those having sentimental value, may also be seized. These rules have been applied on seven occasions (the seized amount was approximately DKr 174,000 (23,000)) and are in line with the national fundamental principle that if one can sustain oneself, one must, which is also to apply to asylum seekers. There are no plans to repeal those rules.
90	Information from the national human rights institution
91	Under the Aliens Act, children who are deemed too immature to undergo an asylum procedure will not have their asylum claim processed until they reach sufficient maturity. They can be granted a residence permit as unaccompanied children if certain conditions are
92	5
93	
94	CCPR/C/125/2/Add.4
95	met. There are reported instances of denial of such permits, with children remaining in asylum centres until considered mature enough to go through the asylum procedure.
96	Information from non-governmental organizations
97	Information relating to paragraph 32 (a)
98	The regime of "tolerated stay" has been further tightened by Law No. 189 of 28 February 2017, which, inter alia, imposed a duty of notification for persons in Denmark on a "tolerated stay" basis in cases of inability to comply with their residence obligations, and increased the maximum imprisonment faced for non-compliance to 18 months. A few weeks earlier, on 17 January 2017, the Supreme Court concluded in a specific case that the regime of "tolerated stay" entailed a disproportionate limitation of the person's rights.
99	United Nations treaty bodies continue to issue decisions finding Denmark in violation of the principle of non-refoulement, and the lack of identification and examination of torture victims among asylum seekers possibly leads to such violations. The reconsideration by the Refugee Appeals Board of specific cases following decisions adopted in 2017 by the Human Rights Committee and the Committee against Torture did not reflect their criticism and individuals were still at risk of deportation after the reexamination.
100	Information relating to paragraph 32 (b) and (c)
101	The latest amendments to the Aliens Act were aimed at increasing the use of detention for migrants and asylum seekers. While judicial review of detention of rejected asylum seekers is available, judges uphold such detentions in the majority of cases. Moreover, the decisions by first instance courts are taken without documentation as to whether persons are victims of torture or on their health conditions generally.
102	Information relating to paragraph 32 (d)
103	Paragraph 37 (k) of the Aliens Act should be repealed.
104	Committee's evaluation
105	[B] (a) and (b): The Committee takes note of the information on the asylum procedure and on respect for the principle of non-refoulement. It requires additional information on: (a) any measures taken to strengthen compliance with the principle of non-refoulement in practice, including any legal and procedural standards in place to ensure systematic and effective identification of torture victims among asylum seekers and effective medical forensic evaluation to support their non-refoulement claims; (b) the restrictions on "tolerated stay" introduced by Law No. 189 and any subsequent amendments that may have been adopted that affect the rights of persons under the "tolerated stay" regime, including on their compatibility with the Covenant; and (c) clarification as to whether decisions related to residence obligations for persons under the "tolerated stay" regime are subject to appeal, and whether such obligations might be lifted in individual cases.
106	The Committee welcomes the information that detention of aliens awaiting deportation is always to be necessary and proportionate and taken following an individual examination. It notes, however, the limited information provided on alternatives to detention. It requires additional information on: (a) measures taken to ensure that detention of migrants and asylum seekers is justified in practice as reasonable, necessary and proportionate in the light of the circumstances; and (b) alternatives to detention available in practice, including data on the use of alternatives. The Committee also invites the State party to comment on information that the latest amendments to the Aliens Act are aimed at increasing the use of detention of migrants and asylum seekers, and to provide information on the effect of the amendments.
107	[B] (c): The Committee notes that the maximum period of detention for migrants and asylum seekers awaiting deportation remains unchanged. It requires information on consideration given to reducing the length of such detention.
108	6
109	
110	CCPR/C/125/2/Add.4 The Committee appreciates that the conditions for rejected asylum seekers detained at Vridsl�selille have improved since autumn 2016, and requires an update on this matter in the next periodic report. [C] (d): The Committee takes note of the information provided, but regrets that paragraph 37 (k) of the Aliens Act has not been repealed. It requires clarification on whether this provision has been activated since the adoption of the concluding observations and, if so, on how many aliens, out of the total number of those detained, availed themselves of the right to request judicial review of their detention and on the procedural rights afforded to them, including clarification as to the availability of free legal representation in this process. The Committee reiterates its recommendation. [E] (e): The Committee regrets that the State party did not implement the recommendation to repeal the amendment to the Aliens Act relating to the confiscation of asylum seekers' assets. The Committee reiterates its recommendation. Recommended action: A letter should be sent informing the State party of the discontinuation of the follow-up procedure. The requests for additional information will be included, as appropriate, in the list of issues prior to submission of the seventh periodic report of Denmark. Next periodic report: 15 July 2022.

CCPR/C/125/2/Add.4
Summary of State party's reply
Reply relating to paragraph 32 (a)
The State party elaborates on the information provided on the asylum procedure under the Aliens Act, including on the automatic appeal against negative asylum decisions that is made to the Refugee Appeals Board. Return decisions are not enforced if an alien in principle has the right to asylum under article 7 of the Aliens Act but is excluded from receiving a residence permit under article 10 of the Aliens Act or article 1 (F) of the Convention relating to the Status of Refugees, and is covered by the principle of nonrefoulement. Such individuals may remain in Denmark on a "tolerated stay" basis until the Refugee Appeals Board decides that there is no longer any danger relating to refoulement. As an example of compliance with the principle of non-refoulement, the Board decided on 3 May 2017 to suspend the transfer of asylum seekers to Hungary under the Dublin Regulation due to systemic deficiencies in the Hungarian asylum system.
Reply relating to paragraph 32 (b)
Under the Aliens Act, the detention of aliens awaiting deportation is always to be necessary and proportionate. Such cases are subject to individual examination and must be brought before the courts automatically within three days. Financial compensation for unlawful deprivation of liberty can be claimed in court.
Reply relating to paragraph 32 (c)
Under the provisions of the Aliens Act implementing the European Union return directive (2008/115/EC), the maximum period of detention is 6 months, with extension of up to 18 months possible in exceptional circumstances. Detention is a measure of last resort, applied when aliens do not return voluntarily and less restrictive measures prove insufficient.
The living conditions for rejected asylum seekers detained at Vridsl�selille significantly improved in autumn 2016. The Parliamentary Ombudsman (designated as the national preventive mechanism), who had previously criticized the conditions at Vridsl�selille, informed the Ministry of Justice on 19 December 2016 that no further action was required.
Reply relating to paragraph 32 (d)
A new subparagraph - (k) - introduced into paragraph 37 of the Aliens Act in November 2015, providing for the suspension of the automatic judicial review of detention within three days, was adopted for application in urgent situations entailing a significant increase in the number of asylum seekers and immigrants arriving within a short time. If the suspension provision is activated (no instances as at 14 July 2017), judicial review of detention may be initiated upon the alien's request rather than automatically. Thus, access to such review remains available.
Reply relating to paragraph 32 (e)
Asylum seekers' assets may be seized to cover the expenses for maintenance during the asylum procedure. Any cash exceeding the value of DKr 10,000 (1,300) will be seized. Assets exceeding the same value, except those having sentimental value, may also be seized. These rules have been applied on seven occasions (the seized amount was approximately DKr 174,000 (23,000)) and are in line with the national fundamental principle that if one can sustain oneself, one must, which is also to apply to asylum seekers. There are no plans to repeal those rules.
Information from the national human rights institution
Under the Aliens Act, children who are deemed too immature to undergo an asylum procedure will not have their asylum claim processed until they reach sufficient maturity. They can be granted a residence permit as unaccompanied children if certain conditions are
5

CCPR/C/125/2/Add.4
met. There are reported instances of denial of such permits, with children remaining in asylum centres until considered mature enough to go through the asylum procedure.
Information from non-governmental organizations
Information relating to paragraph 32 (a)
The regime of "tolerated stay" has been further tightened by Law No. 189 of 28 February 2017, which, inter alia, imposed a duty of notification for persons in Denmark on a "tolerated stay" basis in cases of inability to comply with their residence obligations, and increased the maximum imprisonment faced for non-compliance to 18 months. A few weeks earlier, on 17 January 2017, the Supreme Court concluded in a specific case that the regime of "tolerated stay" entailed a disproportionate limitation of the person's rights.
United Nations treaty bodies continue to issue decisions finding Denmark in violation of the principle of non-refoulement, and the lack of identification and examination of torture victims among asylum seekers possibly leads to such violations. The reconsideration by the Refugee Appeals Board of specific cases following decisions adopted in 2017 by the Human Rights Committee and the Committee against Torture did not reflect their criticism and individuals were still at risk of deportation after the reexamination.
Information relating to paragraph 32 (b) and (c)
The latest amendments to the Aliens Act were aimed at increasing the use of detention for migrants and asylum seekers. While judicial review of detention of rejected asylum seekers is available, judges uphold such detentions in the majority of cases. Moreover, the decisions by first instance courts are taken without documentation as to whether persons are victims of torture or on their health conditions generally.
Information relating to paragraph 32 (d)
Paragraph 37 (k) of the Aliens Act should be repealed.
Committee's evaluation
[B] (a) and (b): The Committee takes note of the information on the asylum procedure and on respect for the principle of non-refoulement. It requires additional information on: (a) any measures taken to strengthen compliance with the principle of non-refoulement in practice, including any legal and procedural standards in place to ensure systematic and effective identification of torture victims among asylum seekers and effective medical forensic evaluation to support their non-refoulement claims; (b) the restrictions on "tolerated stay" introduced by Law No. 189 and any subsequent amendments that may have been adopted that affect the rights of persons under the "tolerated stay" regime, including on their compatibility with the Covenant; and (c) clarification as to whether decisions related to residence obligations for persons under the "tolerated stay" regime are subject to appeal, and whether such obligations might be lifted in individual cases.
The Committee welcomes the information that detention of aliens awaiting deportation is always to be necessary and proportionate and taken following an individual examination. It notes, however, the limited information provided on alternatives to detention. It requires additional information on: (a) measures taken to ensure that detention of migrants and asylum seekers is justified in practice as reasonable, necessary and proportionate in the light of the circumstances; and (b) alternatives to detention available in practice, including data on the use of alternatives. The Committee also invites the State party to comment on information that the latest amendments to the Aliens Act are aimed at increasing the use of detention of migrants and asylum seekers, and to provide information on the effect of the amendments.
[B] (c): The Committee notes that the maximum period of detention for migrants and asylum seekers awaiting deportation remains unchanged. It requires information on consideration given to reducing the length of such detention.
6

CCPR/C/125/2/Add.4 The Committee appreciates that the conditions for rejected asylum seekers detained at Vridsl�selille have improved since autumn 2016, and requires an update on this matter in the next periodic report. [C] (d): The Committee takes note of the information provided, but regrets that paragraph 37 (k) of the Aliens Act has not been repealed. It requires clarification on whether this provision has been activated since the adoption of the concluding observations and, if so, on how many aliens, out of the total number of those detained, availed themselves of the right to request judicial review of their detention and on the procedural rights afforded to them, including clarification as to the availability of free legal representation in this process. The Committee reiterates its recommendation. [E] (e): The Committee regrets that the State party did not implement the recommendation to repeal the amendment to the Aliens Act relating to the confiscation of asylum seekers' assets. The Committee reiterates its recommendation. Recommended action: A letter should be sent informing the State party of the discontinuation of the follow-up procedure. The requests for additional information will be included, as appropriate, in the list of issues prior to submission of the seventh periodic report of Denmark. Next periodic report: 15 July 2022.

content.thinking:
I'm noting Denmark's actual Committee grades: paragraph 20 on domestic violence received an A, paragraph 24 on solitary confinement a C, and paragraph 32 shows a mixed set of grades B, B, C, and E across its sub-issues.

Comparing this to my blind predictions, I under-graded paragraph 20 — I gave it a B when the Committee awarded A, apparently treating the breadth of legislative and policy measures as satisfactory even without outcome statistics. This suggests I should recalibrate: for "continue efforts" recommendations, strong continued and new measures across relevant jurisdictions can earn an A even absent hard data, as long as the Committee is only requesting more information.

Continuing through the rest: 24 matched at C, but I was again too harsh on 32(a) and 32(b), where the Committee gave B for detailed engagement plus a concrete example (Hungary Dublin suspension) rather than dismissing it as restated framework. 32(c), 32(d), and 32(e) all matched my predictions exactly.

So Denmark ends at 4/7 exact matches, with all three misses being me grading one notch too strict — treating B-level engagement as C, and A-level comprehensive measures as B. That's a clear systematic bias I need to correct for going forward. Now I'm moving on to review Namibia and Paraguay.

content.thinking:
I'm noting the actual grades for Paraguay's CCPR/C/140/2/Add.2 report: paragraph 13 got a single B grade overall, paragraph 29 received B for both parts (a) and (b), and paragraph 35 was also graded B as a whole, covering both the welcome of anti-corruption measures and concerns about missing information.

Comparing to my blind grading: 13 matches, 29(a) matches, but 29(b) I graded C when the actual was B — the same pattern I saw with Denmark, where the state restating existing frameworks and services still earned a B rather than the C I assigned, showing my one-notch-too-strict bias. Para 35(a) also matched, and I'm now checking how the Committee treated 35(b).

Paraguay ends up 3 correct, 1 wrong, all from the same strictness bias. Now I'm assembling the full scorecard comparing my grades against the Committee's actual sub-grades for Denmark, starting with paragraph 20 where I said B but the actual was A.

Denmark comes out to 4 of 7 exact matches, with all three misses being cases where I graded one notch too strict. Now I'm building the same comparison table for Namibia's sub-graded paragraphs, starting with 10(a) and 10(b) where both match.

Checking Paraguay next: 3/4 exact, one miss too strict on 29(b). Overall tally comes to 18/24 exact matches at the Committee's grading grain.

Every miss so far, all six of them, comes from me grading one notch too strict — never the reverse. The pattern is clear: when a State's reply substantively engages the recommendation, elaborates its legal framework, and reports a bill "will soon be tabled," I marked it C for "not enacted yet," but the Committee consistently marks these B since a substantive on-point reply is "partially satisfactory" rather than "not satisfactory" — C is reserved for replies with no real information.

I'm also noticing A is more reachable than I assumed for "continue efforts" recommendations — Denmark 20 got an A for a broad package of legislative and policy measures even without outcome statistics, with the Committee asking for stats only after granting the A, suggesting my instinct to be stricter on A without outcome data was itself miscalibrated.

I'm correcting another rule: "bill will soon be tabled" reads as B rather than C when the State gives a concrete criminalization commitment (Namibia 22a/b) — C should be reserved for bills pending for years with nothing new. My single E grade (Denmark 32e) held up as correctly rare and precise, and I'm confirming the Committee tends to sub-grade less granularly than I did, collapsing multi-part items into one overall grade.
